student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to B1 Medical English

In 12 weeks you will learn to talk about the body, symptoms, health history, numbers and medicines in English, and to speak with patients and instructors with confidence. This book is yours: write in it, tick things off, and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level B1 Foundation
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My nursing goal

How the course works

  • 3 lessons a week, 60 minutes each. Lesson A: learn new words. Lesson B: practice and listen. Lesson C: perform and record.
  • You speak more than your teacher. Mistakes are normal. Your teacher corrects numbers, names and left/right at once, and other mistakes at the end.
  • Homework: 15–20 minutes a day. After Lesson A: learn words and listen. After Lesson B: speak and record. After Lesson C: send your weekly voice note.
  • Voice notes. Every week you send one 60–90 second voice note. In Weeks 6 and 12 you will hear how much you have improved.
  • Three checks. Lesson 1 (start), Lesson 18 (middle) and Lesson 36 (final).
  • Uzbek Bridge. You will practice moving between Uzbek and English, a real skill for nursing in the USA.

How to learn a new word: say it, write it, use it in a sentence about your life, then check its English definition in the Vocabulary Book.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 1). Every unit ends with a short practice and the answers.

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (B1 section). Read the definition, then say the example aloud.

Cards and texts. Each week ends with the cards, charts, labels and frames you use in class and for homework. All of them are fictional. When your teacher plays a patient, keep your book closed unless your teacher says to open it.

All patients, charts and medicine labels in this book are fictional. This course teaches English; clinical skills are taught in nursing school.

student.title: Healthcare Basics
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ give a 60-second introduction about my nursing goals
  • ☐ explain who works where in a hospital
  • ☐ check in for an appointment and ask someone to repeat

Words

Lesson Word Example
1 nursing school I plan to apply to nursing school next year.
1 registered nurse (RN) My goal is to become a registered nurse.
1 patient The patient is waiting.
1 healthcare I want to work in healthcare.
1 career Nursing is a good career.
1 goal My goal is to work in a hospital.
1 experience I don't have hospital experience yet.
1 degree A nursing degree takes two to four years.
2 physician A physician is a doctor.
2 nursing assistant A nursing assistant helps patients wash and eat.
2 pharmacist A pharmacist prepares medicines.
2 receptionist The receptionist checks patients in.
2 emergency department (ED) Urgent patients go to the ED.
2 unit She works on a hospital unit.
2 pharmacy The pharmacy is on the first floor.
2 shift I work the night shift.
3 appointment I have an appointment at ten thirty.
3 check in Please check in at the front desk.
3 insurance card Do you have your insurance card?
3 date of birth My date of birth is March 12, 1998.

Useful phrases

  • At the moment I'm studying… / I plan to… / I hope to…
  • A pharmacist is someone who… / The ED is a place where…
  • Could you repeat that, please? / Could you speak more slowly? / Could you spell that?
  • In the USA, dates are written month/day/year: 03/12/1998 = March 12, 1998.

Practice: checking in

Receptionist: Good morning. How can I help you?

Patient: Hi, I have an appointment at ten thirty with Dr. Lee.

Receptionist: Can I have your full name, please?

Patient: Dilnoza Karimova.

Receptionist: Could you spell your last name?

Patient: K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A.

Receptionist: And your date of birth?

Patient: March twelfth, nineteen ninety-eight.

Receptionist: Do you have your insurance card?

Patient: Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly, please?

Receptionist: Of course. Do you have your insurance card? … Thank you. Please take a seat in the waiting room.

Homework: after Lesson 1, learn the words and listen to your teacher's model introduction. After Lesson 2, record 3 role descriptions with who and where. After Lesson 3, send your voice note.

Voice note: introduce yourself, then explain how to check in at a clinic (60–90 seconds).

Cards and texts · Week 1

Question card (Lesson 1): Where are you from? Where do you live now? What are you studying at the moment? Why do you want to be a nurse? What is your goal?

Appointment cards (fictional, Lesson 3):

Card Patient Date of birth Appointment Twist
A Aziz Rakhimov 07/04/1990 Tuesday 9:15, Nurse Practitioner Brown None
B Malika Yusupova 11/30/2001 Thursday 2:40 p.m., Dr. Patel Forgot insurance card
C Jasur Toshev 01/13/1985 Monday 10:15, Dr. Lee Arrives at 10:50

Observer checklist (Lesson 3, groups):

  • ☐ Name spelled
  • ☐ Date of birth
  • ☐ Appointment time
  • ☐ One polite request

student.title: The Human Body
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ name and locate 16 body parts
  • ☐ explain what 8 organs do
  • ☐ describe exactly where pain is

Words

Lesson Word Example
4 abdomen The pain is in my abdomen.
4 chest Put your hand on your chest.
4 shoulder My left shoulder hurts.
4 elbow The elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist.
4 wrist She broke her wrist.
4 hip His hip is stiff.
4 knee Can you bend your knee?
4 ankle Her ankle is swollen.
5 brain The brain controls the body.
5 heart The heart pumps blood.
5 lungs The lungs take in oxygen.
5 liver The liver cleans the blood.
5 kidneys The kidneys filter the blood and make urine.
5 intestines The intestines absorb food and water.
5 bladder The bladder stores urine.
5 pancreas The pancreas produces insulin.
6 upper The pain is in my upper back.
6 lower I have lower back pain.
6 anterior (front) Anterior means the front of the body.
6 posterior (back) Posterior means the back of the body.

Useful phrases

  • The ___ is between the ___ and the ___. / It's above / below / next to the ___.
  • The ___ is responsible for ___. / The ___ helps to ___.
  • The pain is in the lower right part of my abdomen.
  • So the pain is in your lower back. Is that correct?

Homework: after Lesson 4, label a body diagram and say each word. After Lesson 5, record 4 organ sentences. After Lesson 6, send your voice note.

Voice note: name 8 body parts and 4 organs with their jobs, then describe one pain location.

Cards and texts · Week 2

Organ cards (Lesson 5): brain · heart · lungs · liver · kidneys · intestines · bladder · pancreas

Function cards (Lesson 5; cut them up and mix them): stores urine · pumps blood · produces insulin and helps digestion · filters the blood and makes urine · controls the body · absorb food and water · take in oxygen · cleans the blood and helps digestion

Mystery Patient question card (Lesson 6): Is it on the front or the back? Is it above or below the waist? Is it on the left, on the right, or on both sides? Is it in the head, the chest, the abdomen, the back, an arm or a leg? Is it near the shoulder, the hip or the knee? → So the pain is in your… Is that correct?

student.title: Symptoms and Pain
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ describe 8 common symptoms
  • ☐ ask about pain location, type and score
  • ☐ say when a symptom started and how long it has lasted

Words

Lesson Word Example
7 symptom What symptoms do you have?
7 fever I have a fever.
7 chills She has chills at night.
7 nausea I have nausea. / I feel nauseous.
7 vomiting He has vomited twice since this morning.
7 dizziness I feel dizzy when I stand up.
7 fatigue I have no energy. It's fatigue.
7 weakness I have weakness in my legs.
8 sharp It's a sharp pain.
8 dull It's a dull ache.
8 burning I have a burning pain after meals.
8 aching My back is aching.
8 throbbing I have a throbbing headache.
8 constant The pain is constant.
8 comes and goes The pain comes and goes.
8 pain scale On a pain scale from 0 to 10, it's a 6.
9 onset The onset was sudden.
9 duration What is the duration of the pain?
9 suddenly It started suddenly.
9 gradually It got worse gradually.

Useful phrases

  • I feel dizzy. / I have a fever.
  • Where does it hurt? What kind of pain is it? Is it constant, or does it come and go?
  • On a scale from 0 to 10, how bad is the pain?
  • It started three days ago. / I've had it for three days. / I've had it since Monday.

Practice: Uzbek Bridge. Say it in English: Uch kundan beri boshim og‘riyapti. · Ko‘nglim ayniyapti, lekin qusmadim. · Ikki kundan beri isitmam bor.

Homework: after Lesson 7, record 4 symptom sentences. After Lesson 8, write and record 5 pain questions. After Lesson 9, send your voice note.

Voice note: tell the story of a fictional symptom: what, where, type, score, when it started and how long you've had it.

Cards and texts · Week 3

Symptom cards (fictional, Lesson 7): 1 – fever and chills since last night. 2 – nausea, vomited twice. 3 – dizziness when standing up. 4 – fatigue and weakness in both legs.

Pain cards (fictional, Lesson 8): A – sharp, lower right abdomen, constant, 7/10. B – burning, upper abdomen after meals, comes and goes, 4/10. C – throbbing headache at the front of the head, 6/10, worse with bright light.

Pain question card (Lessons 8 and 16): Where is the pain? What kind of pain is it? Is it constant, or does it come and go? On a scale from 0 to 10, how bad is it?

student.title: Health History
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about long-term conditions
  • ☐ describe past surgeries and injuries with dates
  • ☐ take a basic health history in 5 parts

Words

Lesson Word Example
10 medical history Let's go over your medical history.
10 condition Do you have any medical conditions?
10 chronic Asthma is a chronic condition.
10 diabetes My mother has diabetes.
10 hypertension Hypertension means high blood pressure.
10 asthma He uses an inhaler for asthma.
10 infection She had a kidney infection last spring.
10 diagnosis There is no diagnosis yet.
11 surgery Have you ever had surgery?
11 operation The operation took two hours.
11 procedure It was a small procedure.
11 injury He had a knee injury.
11 fracture A fracture is a broken bone.
11 hospital stay She had a three-day hospital stay.
11 recovery Recovery took six weeks.
11 scar There is a small scar on my abdomen.
12 allergic to I'm allergic to penicillin.
12 reaction What reaction did you have?
12 rash I got a rash on my arms.
12 family history Do you have a family history of heart disease?

Useful phrases

  • Have you ever had…? / Have you ever been told you have…?
  • How long have you had it?
  • I had surgery in 2015. / I broke my wrist two years ago.
  • Are you allergic to anything? What happens when you take it?
  • Does anyone in your family have…? / It runs in the family.
  • The 5-part history: conditions → surgery → medicines → allergies → family.

Homework: after Lesson 10, make 8 everyday-to-medical word pairs. After Lesson 11, record a 60-second past-health history for card S2. After Lesson 12, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the full health-history summary of the patient you interviewed in Lesson 12 (card M2), from your notes.

Cards and texts · Week 4

Condition cards (fictional, Lesson 10): H1 – hypertension for 5 years; asthma as a child, none now; no diabetes. H2 – type 2 diabetes for 2 years; a kidney infection last spring.

Surgical cards (fictional, Lesson 11): S1 – appendix surgery in 2015, 3 days in the hospital; broke her left wrist in 2019, no surgery. S2 – C-section in 2020; knee injury playing football two years ago, recovery took 6 weeks.

5-part order card (Lesson 12): conditions → surgery → medicines → allergies → family.

student.title: Vital Signs and Measurements
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ hear, say and check numbers and units
  • ☐ read a vital-signs chart aloud
  • ☐ report a change between two readings

Words

Lesson Word Example
13 decimal point Thirty-seven point five.
13 degree Her temperature is 38 degrees.
13 kilogram (kg) He weighs 72 kilograms.
13 pound (lb) She weighs 160 pounds.
13 centimeter (cm) The cut is 2 centimeters long.
13 inch (in) He is 5 feet 4 inches tall.
13 percent (%) Oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
13 unit Always say the unit with the number.
14 vital signs Let me check your vital signs.
14 blood pressure (BP) Your blood pressure is 120 over 80.
14 pulse / heart rate (HR) His heart rate is 72.
14 respiratory rate (RR) Her respiratory rate is 16.
14 temperature (T) Your temperature is normal.
14 oxygen saturation (SpO2) SpO2 is 95 percent on room air.
14 beats per minute 72 beats per minute.
14 breaths per minute 16 breaths per minute.
15 reading The first reading was 118 over 76.
15 baseline His baseline heart rate is 74.
15 increase His heart rate has increased.
15 decrease Her oxygen saturation has decreased.

Useful phrases

  • Did you say thir-TEEN or THIR-ty?
  • Could you spell that, please? / Let me repeat that back.
  • The blood pressure was 138 over 86 at 9 a.m.
  • The temperature has gone up from 36.8 to 38.3. It's higher than this morning.

Practice: say these aloud. 13 · 30 · 15 · 50 · 98.6 °F · 37.5 °C · 120/80 · 72 kg · 160 lb · 98%

Homework: after Lesson 13, record the 10 numbers in the practice list, with units. After Lesson 14, record yourself reading charts V1 and V2. After Lesson 15, send your voice note.

Voice note: report how the vital signs changed from chart V1 to chart V2. Include every unit.

Cards and texts · Week 5

Mock charts (fictional, Lessons 14–15):

Chart Time BP HR RR T SpO2
V1 8 a.m. 118/76 74 16 36.8 °C 98%
V2 2 p.m. 142/90 96 22 38.3 °C 94%

Blank chart (Lesson 14):

Chart Time BP HR RR T SpO2

Report frame (Lesson 15): I'm reporting the vital signs for ___ in room ___. At ___ his / her temperature was ___. At ___ it was ___, so it has gone up / down. His / her heart rate has increased / decreased from ___ to ___. His / her oxygen saturation is ___ percent on room air. His / her blood pressure is ___ over ___.

student.title: Heart and Lungs · Midpoint
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about chest symptoms
  • ☐ ask about breathing and give breathing directions
  • ☐ do an interview, read a chart and give a 1-minute report on my own (midpoint check)

Words

Lesson Word Example
16 heartbeat I can feel my heartbeat.
16 circulation Exercise helps circulation.
16 artery Arteries carry blood from the heart.
16 vein Veins carry blood back to the heart.
16 chest pain Do you have chest pain now?
16 palpitations My heart is racing. I have palpitations.
16 swelling (edema) There is swelling in both ankles.
16 irregular Her heartbeat is irregular.
17 breath Take a deep breath.
17 breathe Breathe in slowly.
17 shortness of breath I get shortness of breath on the stairs.
17 cough I have had a cough for two days.
17 wheezing I hear wheezing when she breathes.
17 sputum (phlegm) Do you cough up any sputum?
17 inhale Inhale through your nose.
17 exhale Exhale slowly through your mouth.

Useful phrases

  • My heart is beating fast right now. Usually it beats slowly.
  • Does it happen when you walk or when you rest?
  • I have trouble breathing. / I get short of breath when I climb stairs.
  • Take a deep breath in… and breathe out slowly.
  • I'm going to get the nurse right away.

Midpoint check (Lesson 18): a 3-minute interview, reading a chart, and a 1-minute report. Your teacher will compare it with your Lesson 1 recording.

Homework: after Lesson 16, label a heart diagram. After Lesson 17, record 5 breathing sentences. After Lesson 18, send your voice note.

Voice note: record your midpoint report again, with your 2 improvements.

Cards and texts · Week 6

Chest cards (fictional, Lesson 16): C1 – tight chest when climbing stairs, goes away with rest, for 2 weeks. C2 – heart racing at night for 3 days; ankles swollen in the evening.

Midpoint report checklist (Lesson 18):

  • ☐ Name and age
  • ☐ Main symptoms
  • ☐ When they started
  • ☐ History and allergy
  • ☐ All 5 values with units and the time

student.title: Digestion, Urination and Nutrition
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about eating, drinking and swallowing
  • ☐ ask personal questions respectfully
  • ☐ combine a digestion and urinary interview

Words

Lesson Word Example
19 appetite I have a poor appetite this week.
19 diet My diet has a lot of bread.
19 nutrition Good nutrition helps recovery.
19 fluids Please drink plenty of fluids.
19 intake What is your daily fluid intake?
19 hydration Hydration is important in hot weather.
19 dehydration Diarrhea can cause dehydration.
19 swallow Food gets stuck when I swallow.
20 bowel movement When was your last bowel movement?
20 stool Was the stool hard or soft?
20 constipation I've had constipation for four days.
20 diarrhea He has had diarrhea since yesterday.
20 bloating I have bloating after meals.
20 cramps I have stomach cramps.
20 regular Are your bowel movements regular?
20 usual Is that usual for you?
21 urinate (pass urine) Does it burn when you urinate?
21 frequency Frequency means going very often.
21 urgency Urgency means you can't wait.
21 burning There is burning when I pass urine.

Useful phrases

  • I need to ask a few personal questions. These are routine questions we ask everyone. Is that OK?
  • How much water do you drink a day? How many meals do you eat?
  • When was your last bowel movement? Was it normal for you?
  • How often do you pass urine? Do you get up at night to go?

Homework: after Lesson 19, record a 60-second description of your own food and drink. After Lesson 20, record 5 respectful bowel questions. After Lesson 21, send your voice note.

Voice note: give your 30-second summary of the patient you interviewed in Lesson 21 (card U2), from your notes, then say 3 respectful questions you would ask any patient.

Cards and texts · Week 7

Intake cards (fictional, Lesson 19): F1 – 3 meals; poor appetite this week; 4 glasses of water and 3 cups of tea a day. F2 – 2 meals with a lot of bread; 1 bottle of soda a day; trouble swallowing pills.

Bowel cards (fictional, Lesson 20): B1 – last bowel movement 4 days ago (usually every day); hard stool; bloating; cramps 5/10. B2 – diarrhea 6 times since yesterday; cramps; drinking very little.

Urinary card (fictional, Lesson 21): U1 – burning when urinating for 2 days; goes every hour, 3 times a night; urgency; darker urine; drinks 2 glasses a day.

4-part order card (Lesson 21): food → fluids → bowels → urine.

student.title: Movement, Skin and Sensation
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ give polite movement directions and offer help
  • ☐ describe a wound without guessing what it is
  • ☐ ask about feeling, name, place and time

Words

Lesson Word Example
22 muscle My leg muscles are weak.
22 joint The knee is a joint.
22 mobility Her mobility is limited.
22 balance He has poor balance.
22 stiff My back is stiff in the morning.
22 cane She walks with a cane.
22 walker Please use your walker.
22 wheelchair Would you like a wheelchair?
23 wound The wound is on her left arm.
23 cut There is a 2 cm cut on his palm.
23 bruise There is a purple bruise on her leg.
23 redness I can see some redness.

Useful phrases

  • Could you lift your right arm for me? / Bend your knee, please.
  • May I help you stand up? / Let me get someone to help us.
  • There is a red area about 3 cm wide on the left forearm.
  • I can see some redness. I'll tell the nurse so she can check it.
  • Can you tell me your name? Do you know where you are? Can you tell me what day it is?

Homework: after Lesson 22, describe 3 mobility situations. After Lesson 23, record 4 wound descriptions. After Lesson 24, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the 1-minute factual summary of card N1, then 3 polite movement directions.

Cards and texts · Week 8

Direction verbs (Lesson 22): lift · bend · straighten · turn · squeeze · push

Wound cards (fictional, Lesson 23): W1 – cut on the right palm, 2 cm long, dressing dry and clean. W2 – purple bruise on the left shin, about 5 cm. W3 – red area around a scratch on the left forearm, 3 cm wide, warm, a small amount of yellow drainage.

Wound description frame (Lesson 23): There is a ___ on the ___ (where). It is about ___ cm (size). It is ___ (color). The dressing is ___ (dressing).

Sensation cards (fictional, Lesson 24): N1 – Rustam Nazarov, 70; tingling in both feet for a month; numbness in the left hand since this morning (new); alert; knows his name and where he is, not the day. N2 – Zarina Kamolova, 58; dizzy when standing; poor balance; uses a cane; alert and oriented.

Summary frame (Lesson 24): The patient reports… She / He is alert and…

student.title: Medicines
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ name medicine forms and routes
  • ☐ read a medicine label correctly
  • ☐ ask about medicines and check understanding with teach-back

Words

Lesson Word Example
25 tablet Take one tablet.
25 capsule Swallow the capsule with water.
25 liquid This medicine is a liquid.
25 injection The vaccine is an injection.
25 inhaler Use your inhaler when needed.
25 cream Apply the cream to the skin.
25 by mouth (oral, PO) This tablet is taken by mouth.
25 IV (intravenous) IV means into a vein.
26 dose What is the dose?
26 milligram (mg) Each tablet is 10 milligrams.
26 milliliter (mL) Take 10 milliliters.
26 once daily Take it once daily in the morning.
26 twice daily Apply it twice daily.
26 every 8 hours Take it every 8 hours.
26 as needed (PRN) Use it as needed for cough.
26 with food Take it with food.
27 side effect This medicine can make you sleepy. That's a side effect.
27 missed dose I had a missed dose yesterday.
27 refill You have two refills.
27 teach-back Let's do teach-back: tell me how you will take it.

Practice: read label L1 aloud (Cards and texts · Week 9).

Useful phrases

  • This medicine is taken by mouth. / You take it by mouth.
  • Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with food. (amount → route → how often)
  • I want to make sure I explained this clearly. Can you tell me how you will take this medicine?
  • That's a good question for your pharmacist or doctor.

Homework: after Lesson 25, make 8 picture flashcards. After Lesson 26, record 2 labels with exact units. After Lesson 27, send your voice note.

Voice note: explain label L2 to a patient, then ask for teach-back.

Cards and texts · Week 9

Labels (fictional, Lessons 26–27):

Label Medicine Directions
L1 CALMEXA 10 mg tablets Take 1 tablet by mouth once daily in the morning. Qty 30. Refills: 2.
L2 RESPIRA-X syrup 5 mg/5 mL Take 10 mL by mouth every 8 hours as needed for cough. Do not take more than 3 doses in 24 hours.
L3 DERMOSOL cream 1% Apply a thin layer to the affected skin twice daily. For external use only.

Label map (Lesson 26): name → strength → amount → route → how often.

student.title: Tests and Procedures
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ explain a sample instruction card
  • ☐ explain an imaging test from a card
  • ☐ explain a handwashing sequence and give a polite reminder

Words

Lesson Word Example
28 blood test You have a blood test tomorrow.
28 urine sample Please give a urine sample.
28 specimen The specimen goes to the lab.
28 laboratory (lab) The lab is on the second floor.
28 result The doctor will explain the result.
28 fasting This is a fasting blood test.
28 collect Collect the first urine of the morning.
28 container Use the clean container.
29 X-ray You need a chest X-ray.
29 CT scan The CT scan takes 10 minutes.
29 MRI Remove all metal before the MRI.
29 ultrasound A gel is used for the ultrasound.
29 imaging Imaging is on the first floor.
29 contrast (dye) Some scans use contrast.
29 procedure The procedure doesn't hurt.
29 consent form Please sign the consent form.
30 hand hygiene Hand hygiene stops infections.
30 gloves Put on gloves before you start.
30 mask Please wear a mask in this room.
30 isolation This room is in isolation.

Useful phrases

  • You have to / need to come at 8 a.m. You don't have to fast for this test.
  • The instructions say only water.
  • You're going to have an MRI tomorrow. It will take about 30 minutes.
  • The radiology team will check that with you.
  • Excuse me, before you go in, could you please clean your hands and put on a mask?
  • Clean your hands before touching the patient and after removing your gloves.

Homework: after Lesson 28, record one test-card explanation. After Lesson 29, make 4 imaging flashcards. After Lesson 30, send your voice note.

Voice note: explain card T1 or card I1, then give the isolation reminder.

Cards and texts · Week 10

Test cards (fictional, Lesson 28): T1 – blood test, fasting: no food or drink except water for 8 hours before; come to the lab at 8 a.m.; bring your ID. T2 – urine sample: first urine of the morning; use the clean container; write your name and the time on the label; bring it to the lab within 1 hour.

Imaging cards (fictional, Lesson 29): I1 – MRI of the knee, Tuesday 3:00 p.m., Radiology, 1st floor; takes 30–45 minutes; remove all metal (jewelry, watch); the machine is loud, earplugs are given; tell staff if you have metal in your body. I2 – abdominal ultrasound, Friday 9:30 a.m.; no food for 6 hours before; a gel is put on the skin; it does not hurt.

4-part frame (Lesson 29): what → when → how long → how to prepare.

Handwashing steps (Lesson 30): wet your hands → soap → rub for at least 20 seconds → rinse → dry → turn off the tap with the towel.

student.title: Patient Communication and Teamwork

This week I can:

  • ☐ respond kindly to a worried patient
  • ☐ give a short SBAR report
  • ☐ confirm a handoff and write a 3-sentence note

Words

31 respect We treat every patient with respect.
31 reassure I tried to reassure her.
32 handoff I'm giving the handoff to the night nurse.
32 report Let me give you a quick report.
32 situation S is for situation.
32 background B is for background.
32 assessment A is for assessment.
32 recommendation R is for recommendation.
32 update I'm calling with an update.
32 read-back Please do a read-back of the numbers.
33 confirm Let me confirm the room number.
33 reported The patient reported pain.
33 observed I observed swelling.
33 document Please document the time.

Useful phrases

  • I can see you're worried. / It sounds like… / Would you like…?
  • I'm calling about… in room… (S) → She was admitted… (B) → Her vital signs are… (A) → Could you come and see her, please? (R)
  • Let me confirm: room 5, headache since this morning, 6 out of 10.
  • "I feel dizzy" → The patient said she felt dizzy. / Patient reports dizziness.

Practice: SBAR. I'm calling about Mrs. Rahimova in room 8. She has had new shortness of breath since 3 p.m. She was admitted yesterday with a chest infection. Her respiratory rate is 26 and her oxygen saturation is 91 percent on room air. Could you come and see her, please?

Homework: after Lesson 31, record 3 caring responses to cards E1–E3. After Lesson 32, record one SBAR report from card SB2. After Lesson 33, send your voice note.

Voice note: give the SBAR report for card SB2, then read your 3-sentence note aloud.

Cards and texts · Week 11

Empathy cards (fictional, Lesson 31): E1 – worried about MRI results. E2 – does not want her son to hear her history. E3 – an older Uzbek speaker with very little English.

SBAR case cards (fictional, Lessons 32–33):

SB1 – Dilfuza Rahimova, 64, room 8 SB2 – Anvar Qodirov, 59, room 3
Situation New shortness of breath since 3 p.m. Shaky and sweaty; blood sugar 58 mg/dL at 11 a.m.
Background Admitted yesterday with a chest infection; history of asthma Type 2 diabetes; took insulin at 7 a.m.; ate very little breakfast
Assessment (supplied) RR 26, SpO2 91% on room air, HR 104, T 38.4 °C Alert; HR 102
Recommendation (supplied) Could you come and see her, please? Could you come and see him now, please?

SBAR frame (Lesson 32): S – I'm calling about ___ in room ___. She / He has had ___ since ___. B – She / He was admitted ___ with ___. She / He has a history of ___. A – Her / His ___ is ___ (values from the card only). R – Could you come and see her / him, please? Read-back: Can you repeat that back to me?

Note template (Lesson 33): 1. Patient reports ___ since ___. 2. ___ (what happened, with the time). 3. ___ (a value you observed, with the time); alert and oriented.

This week I can:

  • ☐ ask an instructor about an assignment
  • ☐ follow and question skills-lab instructions
  • ☐ complete the five-task final assessment

Words

Lesson Word Example
34 lecture The lecture starts at 9 a.m.
34 syllabus The dates are in the syllabus.
34 assignment The assignment is a care plan.
34 due date (deadline) The due date is Friday.
34 rubric The rubric shows how it is scored.
34 quiz We have a quiz on Tuesday.
34 chapter Nursing textbooks are divided into chapters.
34 office hours I'll come to your office hours.
35 clinical placement My clinical placement is at a hospital.
35 simulation Today we have a simulation.
35 skills lab We practice in the skills lab.
35 mannequin Take the vital signs on the mannequin.
35 demonstrate The instructor will demonstrate first.
35 preceptor My preceptor is an experienced nurse.
35 care plan Write a care plan for the case.
35 feedback I will give feedback at the end.

Useful phrases

  • Could you tell me when the assignment is due? / Do you know where I can find the rubric?
  • I'm sorry I missed Monday's lecture. Could I come to your office hours?
  • Could you show me again? / Could you repeat the second step?
  • If I don't understand, I'll ask.

Homework: after Lesson 34, record a question to your instructor about card A1. After Lesson 35, prepare and record your final 90-second introduction, and review the words you find hardest.

Final assessment (Lesson 36): five tasks: (1) your introduction, (2) a patient interview, (3) a measurement report, (4) a label explanation with teach-back, (5) a question to an instructor.

Final voice note: your new 90-second introduction. Listen to your Lesson 1 introduction first and hear how far you have come.

Cards and texts · Week 12

Mock syllabus page (Lesson 34): ShifoLife B1 Medical English · 12-week course. Teacher: Mrs. Karimova. Office hours: Tuesday 2–4 p.m., online, or by email. Lessons: Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 6:00–7:00 p.m. Week 3: read the Vocabulary Book, B1 Week 3; Word quiz 1 on Friday (10 questions, 15 minutes). Assignment 1: a 1-minute recorded patient report; due Friday of Week 5 at 11:59 p.m.; scored with the rubric in My progress. Late work loses 10% per day.

Assignment cards (fictional, Lesson 34): A1 – Doc, B1 Week 10: read the definitions and examples for Lessons 28–29; write one new sentence for each word; check your work with the 4-skill rubric in My progress; due Friday 11:59 p.m., send to your teacher by email. A2 – word quiz on B1 Weeks 9–10 next Tuesday in class; 20 multiple-choice questions; 30 minutes.

Skills-lab card SL1 (fictional, Lesson 35): Skills lab 2 · Vital signs on the mannequin. 1. Clean your hands. 2. Introduce yourself to the patient. 3. Check the patient's name and date of birth. 4. Take the blood pressure and pulse. 5. Write the results on the form. 6. Tell the instructor when you finish; feedback comes at the end.

student.title: Grammar Handbook
student.html:
How to use this handbook

This is the grammar companion to the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 books. Each lesson card names one grammar point; this handbook explains it in full. Teachers use it to prepare the 4-minute grammar slot. Students use it for homework and revision.

Most units follow this layout; reference units use tables instead:

  1. When we use it: the meanings, in short bullets.
  2. Structure: formulas for + (statement), − (negative) and ? (question), each with a healthcare example.
  3. Short answers and short forms.
  4. Keywords: the time words and signal words that go with it.
  5. Watch out!: the mistakes students make most, including typical mistakes of Uzbek speakers. ✗ = wrong, ✓ = right.
  6. Try it: 4 quick items, with the key underneath.

Symbols

Symbol Meaning Example
S subject The patient, she, I
V1 base form go, take, feel
V2 past form went, took, felt
V3 past participle gone, taken, felt
V-ing -ing form going, taking, feeling
(Q/W) question word (optional) what, where, when, how
+ / − / ? statement / negative / question

Part 1 · B1 Foundation

Unit 1 · Grammar words and the alphabet

Grammar words used in this handbook

Term What it is Example
Subject who or what does the action The nurse checks the chart.
Verb the action or state The nurse checks the chart.
Auxiliary verb a helper verb for questions, negatives and tenses: be, do, have, will Does it hurt?
Noun a person, thing or idea nurse, chart, pain
Pronoun a word instead of a noun she, it, them
Adjective describes a noun a sharp pain
Adverb describes a verb or adjective; often how, when, how often breathe slowly, always, very tired
Preposition place, time, direction in, on, at, under, before
Article a, an, the the patient

Tense names. Each tense has two names; both are correct. Simple = Indefinite · Continuous = Progressive · Perfect · Perfect Continuous. Each one exists in the Present, Past and Future: 12 tenses in total (see Reference table A).

The alphabet: 26 letters

  • 5 vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u.
  • 21 consonant letters. Y can work as a consonant (yes) or a vowel (happy, dizzy).

Learn the letter names in sound groups. It makes spelling names on the phone much easier.

Sound Letters
"ay" (as in day) A H J K
"ee" (as in see) B C D E G P T V Z
"eh" (as in bed) F L M N S X
"eye" I Y
"oh" O
"you" Q U W
"ar" R

In the USA, Z is "zee"; in the UK it is "zed".

Watch out!

  • A, E, I are the most confused: A = "ay", E = "ee", I = "eye".
  • G ("jee") and J ("jay") are often swapped.
  • W is "double-u". For two of the same letter together, say "double": Anna → A-double N-A; Rassul → R-A-double S-U-L.
  • Abbreviations are spelled letter by letter: MRI = "em-ar-eye", ECG = "ee-see-jee".

Try it. Spell aloud: (1) Karimova (2) Yusupov (3) ECG (4) Jasur.

Show the answers

(1) K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A (2) Y-U-S-U-P-O-V (3) E-C-G ("ee-see-jee") (4) J-A-S-U-R (J = "jay").

Unit 2 · Nouns: singular and plural

When we use it: one thing = singular (a tablet); two or more = plural (two tablets).

Rule Ending Examples
Most nouns + -s nurse → nurses · bed → beds · lung → lungs
Ends in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x + -es bus → buses · glass → glasses · dish → dishes · patch → patches · box → boxes
Some nouns in -o + -es potato → potatoes · tomato → tomatoes (but photo → photos)
Consonant + y y → -ies artery → arteries · injury → injuries · baby → babies
Vowel + y + -s day → days · X-ray → X-rays · boy → boys
Ends in -f / -fe f → -ves half → halves · knife → knives · life → lives · wife → wives
Irregular new form man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · mouse → mice
No change same form sheep · fish · deer · series · species
Latin / Greek (common in medicine) special diagnosis → diagnoses · bacterium → bacteria · vertebra → vertebrae · criterion → criteria · nucleus → nuclei

Watch out!

  • After a number, English always needs the plural. Uzbek speakers often keep the noun singular after a number: ✗ three tablet. ✓ three tablets, two days, 5 milligrams.
  • People is already plural: ✓ People are waiting. ✗ peoples.
  • Uncountable nouns have no plural: ✗ informations, advices, equipments (see Unit 17).
  • One child, two children; one foot, two feet: say these correctly in body and family vocabulary.

Try it. Make plural: (1) knee (2) diagnosis (3) child (4) injury.

Show the answers

(1) knees (2) diagnoses (3) children (4) injuries.

Unit 3 · Articles: a, an, the

When we use it

  • a / an = one, not a specific one; the first time we mention it: There's a patient in room 4.
  • the = a specific one that we both know; the second mention; something unique: The patient in room 4 is asleep. The heart pumps blood.
  • No article for plural or uncountable nouns in general: Nurses work long shifts. Blood carries oxygen.

A or an? It depends on the first sound, not the first letter.

an (vowel sound) a (consonant sound)
an apple, an injection a patient, a nurse
an hour (silent h) a hospital (h is heard)
an X-ray ("ex") a unit ("you")
an MRI ("em"), an ECG ("ee") a uniform, a European ("you")

Fixed phrases (no article): by mouth, at home, at work, go to bed, on duty. In the USA: in the hospital (UK: in hospital).

Watch out!

  • Uzbek has no articles, so learners drop them. ✗ She is nurse. ✓ She is a nurse. ✗ Patient is in room 5. ✓ The patient is in room 5.
  • Jobs always take a/an: I want to be a nurse. He is an anesthetist.
  • Don't use the with names: ✗ the Dr. Lee.

Try it. Add a, an or the: (1) I have ___ appointment. (2) She needs ___ MRI. (3) ___ pharmacy is on the first floor. (4) He works in ___ hospital in Ohio.

Show the answers

(1) an (2) an (3) The (4) a.

Unit 4 · Pronouns and possessives

Subject Object Possessive adjective Possessive pronoun Reflexive
I me my mine myself
you you your yours yourself
he him his his himself
she her her hers herself
it it its — itself
we us our ours ourselves
they them their theirs themselves

She gave him her card. The card is hers. She did it herself.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often mix up he and she, because Uzbek uses one word for he, she and it. In English you must choose. ✗ Mrs. Karimova says he has pain. ✓ She says she has pain. In a report, a wrong pronoun can mean the wrong patient.
  • its (possessive) vs it's (= it is): The heart and its valves. It's beating fast.
  • their (possessive) · there (place) · they're (= they are).
  • Use they for one person when you don't know or don't need the gender: If a patient feels dizzy, they should sit down.
  • Body parts take a possessive: ✓ Lift your arm. ✗ Lift the arm (sounds like an object, not their own arm).

Try it. (1) This is Mr. Saidov. ___ wife is here. (2) Mrs. Karimova says ___ head hurts. (3) Please give ___ (we) the chart. (4) The bag is ___ (she).

Show the answers

(1) His (2) her (3) us (4) hers.

Unit 5 · Numbers, dates and times

Ordinal numbers (first, second, third): add -th, except numbers ending in 1, 2 or 3 (1st, 22nd, 33rd); 11th, 12th and 13th take -th.

1st first 2nd second 3rd third 4th fourth 5th fifth
8th eighth 9th ninth 12th twelfth 20th twentieth 21st twenty-first

Spelling changes: eight → eighth, five → fifth, nine → ninth, twelve → twelfth, twenty → twentieth.

Saying numbers in healthcare

Written Say Note
13 / 30 thir-TEEN / THIR-ty stress tells them apart
37.5 thirty-seven point five
0.5 mg zero point five milligrams
1,200 mL one thousand two hundred milliliters
120/80 a hundred and twenty over eighty blood pressure
98% ninety-eight percent
03/12/1998 March twelfth, nineteen ninety-eight US order: month/day/year
2026 twenty twenty-six
10:15 ten fifteen / a quarter past ten
14:30 fourteen thirty (hospital) / two thirty p.m.

Prepositions of time: at 10:30, at night · on Monday, on March 12 · in March, in 2025, in the morning.

Watch out!

  • Decimal point vs comma. In Uzbekistan 37,5 is a decimal; in the USA a comma separates thousands. ✓ 37.5 (thirty-seven point five) · 1,200 (one thousand two hundred).
  • US dates: 04/07 is April 7, not 4 July. Always say the month as a word when you check.
  • Teen/ty: if in doubt, ask Did you say thirteen or thirty? or say the digits: "one-three".

Try it. Say aloud: (1) 15 (2) 38.2 °C (3) 11/30/2001 (4) 18:45.

Show the answers

(1) fif-TEEN (2) thirty-eight point two degrees (3) November thirtieth, two thousand one (4) eighteen forty-five / a quarter to seven p.m.

Unit 6 · To be (am, is, are · was, were · will be)

When we use it: to say what or who someone is, how they are, where they are, and their age.

Present Past Future
I am I was I will be
he / she / it is he / she / it was he / she / it will be
you / we / they are you / we / they were you / we / they will be

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + noun / adjective / place I am a nursing student. The patient is in room 5.
− S + am / is / are + not + … She is not dizzy. They are not in the ward.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + …? Is he awake? Where is the pharmacy?

Short answers: Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. ✗ Yes, she's. (no short form in a yes short answer)

Short forms: I'm · you're · he's / she's / it's · we're · they're. Negative: isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't, won't be. With I: ✓ I'm not ✗ I amn't.

Use one short form only: ✓ He's not or ✓ He isn't, never ✗ He'sn't.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often leave out am / is / are: ✗ I nurse. ✗ She very tired. ✓ I am a nurse. She is very tired.
  • Don't add be to other verbs: ✗ I am agree. I am live in Ohio. ✓ I agree. I live in Ohio.
  • Age uses be: ✓ I am 25. ✗ I have 25 years.
  • Feelings with adjectives use be: I am cold, hungry, afraid, worried.
  • I am to do means a plan or an order (You are to stay in bed), not the normal present. For now, use I do or I'm doing.
  • You will hear ain't (= am not / isn't / aren't) in informal US speech. Understand it; never use it at work.

Try it. (1) The doctor ___ busy now. (2) We ___ at work yesterday. (3) ___ you allergic to anything? (4) He ___ (not) in pain.

Show the answers

(1) is (2) were (3) Are (4) isn't / is not.

Unit 7 · Have / have got

When we use it: to talk about possession, family, conditions and symptoms. I have diabetes. She has a fever. I've got a cough.

Have (all English, especially American)

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + noun She has a rash.
− S + do / does + not + have + noun He doesn't have any allergies.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + have + …? Do* you have* any pain?

Have got (spoken, especially British; present only)

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + got + noun I've got a headache.
− S + have / has + not + got + noun She hasn't got a temperature.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + got + …? Has* he got* his insurance card?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't. (have) · Yes, I have. / No, he hasn't. (have got)

Short forms: I've got, she's got (here 's = has). With plain have, don't shorten: ✓ I have a cough ✗ I've a cough.

Past: had for everyone: She had surgery in 2015. Did you have a fever? (no had got)

Have as an action: have breakfast, have a shower, have surgery, have a test. Here have can be continuous: She's having an X-ray now. ✗ She's having diabetes.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She have a fever. ✓ She has a fever. ✗ Does she has…? ✓ Does she have…?
  • Uzbek speakers often build have as "at me is": ✗ At me is a pain. ✓ I have a pain.
  • In US clinics ask Do you have…? ✗ Have you any allergies? sounds old-fashioned.

Try it. (1) ___ you ___ any children? (2) He ___ (not) a temperature. (3) She ___ got a cough. (4) They ___ an appointment last week.

Show the answers

(1) Do … have (2) doesn't have / hasn't got (3) has (4) had.

Unit 8 · There is / there are and prepositions of place

When we use it: to say that something exists or is in a place: There is a cut on his hand. There are two wounds.

Formula Example
+ There is + singular / uncountable · There are + plural There is some drainage. There are three patients in the waiting area.
− There isn't a / any … · There aren't any … There isn't any swelling. There aren't any beds.
? Is there a / any …? · Are there any …? Is there* any redness? Are there* any visitors?

Short answers: Yes, there is. / No, there aren't. Short form: there's (= there is). Past: there was / there were.

Prepositions of place

Preposition Example
in pain in the abdomen (inside)
on a rash on the arm (surface)
at at the front desk
above / below the cut is just above the knee
next to / between the elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist
behind / in front of the kidneys are behind the intestines
on the left / right side of swelling on the left side of the neck

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often put the place first and leave out there is: ✗ In room 5 is a patient. ✓ There is a patient in room 5.
  • Match the noun: ✗ There is two wounds. ✓ There are two wounds.
  • Don't use it has for existence: ✗ It has a cut on his hand. ✓ There is a cut on his hand. / He has a cut on his hand.

Try it. (1) ___ any blood in the urine? (2) ___ two pills on the table. (3) The pain is ___ my lower back. (4) There ___ (not) any visitors yesterday.

Show the answers

(1) Is there (2) There are (3) in (4) weren't.

Unit 9 · Present Simple (Present Indefinite)

When we use it

  • Habits and repeated actions: She takes insulin every morning.
  • Schedules and timetables: Visiting hours start at 2 p.m.
  • Facts and general truths: The heart pumps blood.
  • States: I feel dizzy. He knows his medicines.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V1 (he / she / it + -s) I check my sugar daily. She checks her sugar daily.
− S + do / does + not + V1 I don't smoke. He doesn't drink alcohol.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + V1? Do* you take any vitamins? How often does* she use her inhaler?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

He / she / it spelling: take → takes · wash → washes · cry → cries · go → goes · do → does · have → has.

Pronouncing -s: "s" in takes, checks · "z" in feels, needs · "iz" in washes, uses.

Keywords: every (day, morning, week) · always · usually · often · sometimes · occasionally · rarely · seldom · never · once / twice a day · from time to time.

Word order: frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be: She always takes it at night. He is often dizzy.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She take insulin. ✓ She takes insulin.
  • Only one -s: ✗ Does she takes…? ✓ Does she take…?
  • ✗ He don't smoke. ✓ He doesn't smoke.

Try it. (1) My mother ___ (have) diabetes. (2) ___ he ___ (use) his inhaler every day? (3) I ___ (not / drink) coffee. (4) The kidneys ___ (filter) the blood.

Show the answers

(1) has (2) Does … use (3) don't drink (4) filter.

Unit 10 · Present Continuous (Present Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action happening now: The patient is sleeping.
  • A temporary situation around now: I'm studying English this year.
  • A fixed plan for the future: She's having surgery on Monday.
  • An annoying repeated habit, with always: He's always pulling at his IV.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + V-ing My heart is beating fast.
− S + am / is / are + not + V-ing She isn't eating today.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + V-ing? Are* you having* trouble breathing?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.

Here be is a helper. I am a nurse (here am is the main verb) vs I am working (am only builds the tense).

-ing spelling: take → taking · sit → sitting · lie → lying · breathe → breathing.

Keywords: now · right now · at the moment · currently · today · this week · these days · still.

State verbs are not normally continuous: know, want, need, believe, understand, like, hate, seem, belong. ✗ I am knowing. ✓ I know. Feel and hurt can be both: My back hurts / is hurting.

Simple or continuous? He takes insulin every day (habit) · He's taking his insulin now (at this moment).

Watch out!

  • Don't drop be: ✗ She sleeping. ✓ She is sleeping.
  • ✗ I am needing water. ✓ I need water.

Try it. (1) Be quiet: the baby ___ (sleep). (2) ___ you ___ (take) any medicine at the moment? (3) She ___ (not / breathe) normally. (4) I ___ (understand) the instructions.

Show the answers

(1) is sleeping (2) Are … taking (3) isn't breathing (4) understand.

Unit 11 · Past Simple (Past Indefinite)

When we use it: a finished action at a finished time in the past, with no link to now. She fell yesterday. He had surgery in 2015.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V2 (regular: -ed; irregular: see table D) The pain started on Sunday. I took a tablet.
− S + did + not + V1 She didn't vomit.
? (Q/W) + did + S + V1? When did it start? Did you fall?

Short answers: Yes, she did. / No, I didn't.

-ed spelling: start → started · stop → stopped · cry → cried · use → used.

Pronouncing -ed: "t" in stopped, checked · "d" in called, used · "id" in started, needed.

Keywords: yesterday · ago · last (night, week, year) · in 2019 · at 3 a.m. · on Monday · when.

Watch out!

  • After did, use V1: ✗ Did you took it? ✓ Did you take it? ✗ She didn't came. ✓ She didn't come.
  • Ago goes after the time: ✓ three days ago ✗ ago three days.
  • With a finished time, don't use the Present Perfect: ✗ I have taken it yesterday. ✓ I took it yesterday.

Try it. (1) The pain ___ (begin) two days ago. (2) ___ you ___ (eat) breakfast? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) well last night. (4) He ___ (break) his wrist in 2019.

Show the answers

(1) began (2) Did … eat (3) didn't sleep (4) broke.

Unit 12 · Present Perfect

When we use it

  • A past action with a result now: I'm full. I have eaten. (Compare: I ate pasta yesterday: past only.)
  • Experience in life (any time until now): Have* you ever had* surgery?
  • A situation from the past until now: I've had this cough for three days.
  • Something just finished: The doctor has just left.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + V3 She has taken her tablets.
− S + have / has + not + V3 We haven't finished yet.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + V3? Have* you checked* your sugar today?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's / she's (here 's = has), haven't, hasn't.

Keywords: just · already · yet (in − and ?) · ever · never · recently · so far · today · this week · for · since.

For or since? for + a length of time: for three days, for a week · since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since this morning.

Present Perfect or Past Simple? Ask about life with the Present Perfect; give the details with the Past Simple: Have you ever had surgery? – Yes, I had my appendix out in 2015.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present for since: ✗ I am here since Monday. ✓ I've been here since Monday.
  • ✗ for Monday ✓ since Monday · ✗ since three days ✓ for three days.
  • No finished time: ✗ I have seen the doctor yesterday. ✓ I saw the doctor yesterday.

Try it. (1) She ___ (have) a headache since this morning. (2) ___ you ever ___ (be) in hospital? (3) I ___ (not / take) my insulin yet. (4) He ___ (work) here for two years.

Show the answers

(1) has had (2) Have … been (3) haven't taken (4) has worked.

Unit 13 · Questions

Question words

Word Asks about Example
What thing, information What brings you in today?
Where place Where does it hurt?
When time When did it start?
Who person Who is your doctor?
Which a choice Which arm is it?
Why reason Why did you stop the tablets?
How way, condition How are you feeling?
How long duration How long have you had it?
How often frequency How often do you use your inhaler?
How much / How many amount / number How much water do you drink? How many tablets?
How bad / How severe degree How bad is the pain from 0 to 10?

Word order: Q-A-S-V. (Q/W) + Auxiliary + Subject + main Verb: When did the pain start? How long have you been here?

Subject questions (the question word is the subject) have no do/does/did: Who called the ambulance? ✗ Who did call…?

Indirect (polite) questions: Could you tell me / Do you know + (Q/W) + S + V (normal order, no do): Could you tell me where the pharmacy is? Do you know when it started? ✗ Could you tell me where is the pharmacy?

Open and closed questions. Closed (Do you have pain?) gets yes/no. Open (Tell me about the pain) gets the story. Start interviews with open questions.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often make a question with intonation only. In English, use the helper verb: ✗ You have pain? ✓ Do you have pain?
  • Keep the helper before the subject: ✗ Where it hurts? ✓ Where does it hurt?

Try it. Make questions: (1) (how long / you / have / this cough) (2) (where / the pain / be) (3) (who / take / your blood pressure) (4) Could you tell me (when / the doctor / come)?

When we use it

Form Use Example

will realistic hopes and fears I hope I'll pass. I'm afraid it will hurt.
going to a plan decided before now I'm going to apply to nursing school.
going to a prediction from what we see now She's very pale. She's going to faint.

Structure (will)

Formula Example
+ S + will + V1 The doctor will explain the results.
− S + will not (won't) + V1 It won't hurt.
? (Q/W) + will + S + V1? When will I get the results?

Short answers: Yes, it will. / No, it won't. · Short forms: I'll, you'll, she'll, won't.

Keywords: tomorrow · the day after tomorrow · next (week, month) · in two days · soon · later · tonight · this afternoon.

Modal Meaning Example

Formula Example

− S + modal + not + V1 You mustn't drink alcohol with this.

  • In nursing, should sounds like advice. Report the clinician's advice: The doctor says you should rest.

Unit 18 · Relative clauses: who, which, where

When we use it: to say which person, thing or place we mean, or to add information.

Word For Example

Defining (no commas): tells us which one. The nurse who looked after me was kind.

(1) who (2) where (3) which / that / (nothing) (4) who.

Unit 19 · Past Continuous (Past Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action in progress at a moment in the past: At 3 a.m. he was sleeping.
  • A longer action interrupted by a shorter one (Past Simple): She was walking to the bathroom when she fell.
  • Two actions in progress at the same time: While* the nurse was checking his pulse, he was talking* to his son.
  • The background of a story: It was raining and the ED was getting busy.

The action has no link to now and no result: it was simply in progress.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + was / were + V-ing They were waiting in the waiting area.
− S + was / were + not + V-ing She wasn't breathing normally.
? (Q/W) + was / were + S + V-ing? What were you doing when the pain started?

Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren't. Short forms: only in the negative: wasn't, weren't.

Keywords: while · as · when · at (3 a.m.) yesterday · all night · at that moment.

When or while? when + the short action (Past Simple); while / as + the long action (Past Continuous).

Watch out!

  • ✗ When I was fall… ✓ When I fell… (the short action is Past Simple)
  • State verbs stay simple: ✗ I was knowing him. ✓ I knew him.

Try it. (1) He ___ (carry) boxes when he ___ (feel) the pain. (2) What ___ you ___ (do) at 11 p.m.? (3) While I ___ (cook), I ___ (cut) my finger. (4) She ___ (not / sleep) when the nurse came in.

Show the answers

(1) was carrying … felt (2) were … doing (3) was cooking … cut (4) wasn't sleeping.

Unit 20 · Present Perfect Continuous

When we use it

  • An activity that started in the past and is still going on, with focus on how long: I've been coughing for a week.
  • A recent activity with a result you can see: Her eyes are red. She's been crying.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + been + V-ing He has been using his inhaler more than usual.
− S + have / has + not + been + V-ing I haven't been sleeping well.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + been + V-ing? How long have you been having this pain?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Keywords: for · since · how long · all day · all week · lately · recently.

Simple or continuous?

Present Perfect Continuous Present Perfect Simple
duration, the activity itself result, a number, a completed amount
I've been taking this tablet for a year. I've taken three tablets today.
She's been waiting since 9. She's waited three hours. (finished or counted)

State verbs stay simple: I've had this cough for a week. I've known her for years. For repeated symptoms the continuous is fine: I've been having headaches lately.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present here: ✗ I am coughing since Monday. ✓ I've been coughing since Monday.
  • Don't forget been: ✗ I have coughing. ✓ I have been coughing.

Try it. (1) How long ___ you ___ (feel) like this? (2) She ___ (wait) since 9 a.m. (3) I ___ (have) diabetes for ten years. (4) He ___ (take) four tablets so far today.

(1) have … been feeling (2) has been waiting (3) have had (4) has taken.

Unit 21 · Past Perfect and narrative tenses

When we use it

  • Past Perfect (had + V3): an action before another past moment: When the ambulance arrived, she had already stopped bleeding.
  • Past Perfect Continuous (had been + V-ing): an activity that continued up to a past moment: She had been feeling dizzy all morning before she fell.

Structure (Past Perfect)

Formula Example
+ S + had + V3 He had taken his insulin before lunch.
− S + had + not + V3 She hadn't eaten since breakfast.
? (Q/W) + had + S + V3? Had* you felt* dizzy before the fall?

Short answers: Yes, I had. / No, she hadn't. Short forms: I'd, she'd (here 'd = had), hadn't.

Keywords: before · after · by the time · already · when · until · by (10 a.m.).

Telling a story in order: three tenses together

Tense Job Example
Past Continuous background At 2 p.m. she was walking to the bathroom…
Past Simple main events …when she slipped and hit her head.
Past Perfect earlier events She hadn't eaten since breakfast, and she had been feeling dizzy all morning.

Watch out!

  • When before / after already show the order, the Past Simple is fine: She ate before she took the tablet.
  • ✗ She had fell. ✓ She had fallen. (use V3: see table D)

Show the answers

(1) had stopped (2) Had … taken (3) hadn't slept (4) had been working.

Unit 22 · The passive

When we use it: when the action matters more than who did it. Very common in reports, procedures, labels and textbooks.

Structure: a form of be + V3. Add by + person only if it matters.

Tense Passive Example
Present Simple am / is / are + V3 This tablet is taken by mouth.
Present Continuous am / is / are being + V3 The dressing is being changed.
Past Simple was / were + V3 The blood pressure was recorded at 10:00.
Present Perfect have / has been + V3 Has* the dressing been changed* today?
Future will be + V3 The results will be explained by the doctor.
Modal modal + be + V3 Consent must be obtained first.
Formula Example
+ S + be + V3 The sample was sent to the lab.
− S + be + not + V3 The site has not been marked.
? (Q/W) + be + S + V3? When was the patient admitted?

Watch out!

  • Use V3, not V2: ✗ The sample was took. ✓ The sample was taken.
  • Verbs with no object have no passive: ✗ It was happened. The patient was died. ✓ It happened. The patient died. (also arrive, occur, fall)
  • Speak actively to patients: You take it by mouth. Use the passive in notes and reports.

Unit 23 · Reported speech

When we use it: to tell someone what another person said, asked or told them to do. Essential for handoffs and notes.

Say or tell? say (something): He said he was dizzy. · tell + person: He told me he was dizzy. ✗ He said me.

Statements: move one tense back

Direct speech Reported speech
"I feel dizzy." She said she felt dizzy.
"I'm having chest pain." He said he was having chest pain.
"I took it yesterday." She said she had taken it the day before.
"I'll call you." He said he would call me.
"I can't sleep." She said she couldn't sleep.

Also change: today → that day · yesterday → the day before · tomorrow → the next day · here → there · I / my → he / his.

Questions: normal word order, no do: "Where is the toilet?" → He asked where the toilet was. · Yes/no questions use if / whether: She asked if she could eat.

Instructions: told / asked + person + (not) to + V1: The doctor told him not to drive. · Labels: The label says to take it with food.

In clinical notes the present is normal: Patient reports pain 6/10. Denies nausea. States she slept badly. For a safety concern, quote the exact words: The patient stated, "I don't see the point anymore."

Watch out!

  • ✗ He asked where is the toilet. ✓ He asked where the toilet was.
  • ✗ She told to wait. ✓ She told me to wait.

Try it. Report: (1) "I have a headache." (she) (2) "Did you take your insulin?" (the nurse asked him) (3) "Don't eat after midnight." (the doctor told her) (4) "I'll come back at 5." (he)

Show the answers

(1) She said she had a headache. (2) The nurse asked him if he had taken his insulin. (3) The doctor told her not to eat after midnight. (4) He said he would come back at 5.

Unit 24 · Conditionals: zero, first, second, third

Type Meaning If-clause Main clause Example
Zero facts, always true Present Simple Present Simple If blood sugar drops too low, people feel shaky.
First real, possible future Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction If the pain gets worse, I'll call the nurse. If you notice a fever, call the clinic.
Second unreal or unlikely, present or future Past Simple / Past Continuous would / could / might + V1 If you stopped smoking, your breathing would improve.
Third unreal past (it didn't happen) Past Perfect would / could / might + have + V3 If I had known about the allergy, I would have told the doctor.

Structure notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. If it comes first, use a comma: If it hurts, tell me. / Tell me if it hurts.
  • Negatives: If you don't take it, … · If I hadn't checked, … · … it wouldn't help.
  • Questions: What will you do if the patient refuses? What would you do if a patient shouted at you?
  • Unless = if not: Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
  • Second conditional with be: were for all persons in formal English: If I were you, I'd ask the pharmacist.

Watch out!

  • No will in the if-clause: ✗ If you will notice redness… ✓ If you notice redness…
  • No would in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known… ✓ If I had known…
  • First or second? First = it may really happen. Second = imagined: If I win the scholarship, I'll… (I applied) vs If I were the surgeon, I would… (imagined: I am a nursing student).

Try it. (1) If you ___ (feel) dizzy, sit down. (2) If she ___ (have) more time, she would study more. (3) If he ___ (call) earlier, we ___ (help) him. (4) Water ___ (boil) if you heat it to 100 °C.

Show the answers

(1) feel (2) had (3) had called … would have helped (4) boils.

Unit 25 · Question tags

When we use it: to check information you think is true. Very useful in medication reconciliation and handoffs.

Structure: positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. The tag uses the same helper verb (or do / does / did).

Sentence Tag
You take it twice a day, don't you?
You haven't eaten since midnight, have you?
She's allergic to penicillin, isn't she?
He took it this morning, didn't he?
You'll come back on Tuesday, won't you?
You can walk, can't you?
I'm next, aren't I? (special form)

Intonation: falling = you're confirming, you expect yes. Rising = a real question, you're not sure.

Answer the fact, not the tag: You don't smoke, do you? – No, I don't. (= I don't smoke)

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often use one tag for everything: ✗ You take it twice a day, isn't it? ✓ …, don't you?
  • Match the tense: ✗ He took it, doesn't he? ✓ …, didn't he?

Show the answers

(1) don't you (2) has she (3) wasn't it (4) won't you.

Unit 26 · Hedging and deduction

When we use it: to show how sure we are. Nurses report facts carefully and never sound more certain than they are.

Possibility: may, might, could + V1

  • This medicine may cause drowsiness. (labels, leaflets)
  • The change might be important. I'll tell the nurse.
  • Her symptoms could be related to the new tablet. (in a discussion with the team, not a diagnosis for the patient)

Deduction: how sure am I?

Certainty Present Past Example
sure it's true must + V1 / be must have + V3 You must be exhausted. She must have fallen.
possible may / might / could + V1 may / might / could have + V3 He might be in pain. She could have missed a dose.
sure it's not true can't + V1 / be can't have + V3 That can't be easy. He can't have taken it: the box is full.

Appearance verbs (observations, not conclusions): He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. She seems to be in pain. He looks pale.

Softening words: possibly, probably, likely, approximately, about, around, tends to.

  • No to after modals: ✗ He must to be tired. ✓ He must be tired.
  • maybe (adverb) vs may be (verb): Maybe it's the medicine. = *It may be* the medicine.
  • ✗ She seems is tired. ✓ She seems tired / seems to be tired.

(1) must (2) can't (3) may / might (4) appears.

Unit 28 · Discourse markers

When we use it: to show how ideas connect in lectures, presentations, essays and seminars.

Function Spoken / neutral Written / formal
Adding also, and, plus furthermore, moreover, in addition
Contrasting but, though however, in contrast, whereas, nevertheless, on the other hand
Cause because, since, as due to (+ noun), owing to

Grammar of linkers

  • However, Therefore, Consequently start a new sentence and take a comma: Hand hygiene prevents infection. However, it is often forgotten.
  • although, whereas, because join two clauses: Although she was in pain, she walked to the bathroom.
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite* the pain, she walked. Despite feeling* dizzy, she walked.
  • due to + noun: …due to time pressure (✗ due to people are busy).

Watch out!

  • ✗ Although she was tired, but she worked. Use one linker: ✓ Although she was tired, she worked.
  • ✗ despite of ✓ despite / in spite of.
  • Moreover in a conversation sounds like a lecture. Match the register.

(1) However (2) Despite / In spite of (3) consequently / as a result (4) Although.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.
