(1) However (2) Despite / In spite of (3) consequently / as a result (4) Although.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.

Try it. (1) She stopped ___ (smoke) last year. (2) The ___ (break) arm needs an X-ray. (3) The patient ___ (sit) by the window is Mr. Rakhimov. (4) The news was ___ (worry), so the family was ___ (worry).

Show the answers

(1) smoking (2) broken (3) sitting (4) worrying … worried.

Unit 31 · Cleft sentences and emphasis

When we use it: to put the most important information first, to prioritize in a summary, or to correct someone politely.

Pattern Structure Example
What-cleft What + S + V + is / was + focus What concerns me most is the new sore on her foot.
It-cleft It is / was + focus + that / who + rest It's* the evening doses that* he misses.
The thing / reason The thing that… / The reason (why)… + is (that) The reason* she stopped is that* the tablets are expensive.
All All + S + V + is All she needs is a little more time.

Correcting politely: It wasn't the morning dose she missed; it was the evening one.

Watch out!

  • No extra it: ✗ What concerns me most it is the sore. ✓ What concerns me most is the sore.
  • Keep the order: ✗ Is the evening dose that he misses. ✓ It's the evening dose that he misses.

Try it. Rewrite with emphasis: (1) The cost worries her. (What…) (2) He missed the Tuesday appointment. (It was…) (3) She needs a social worker. (What…) (4) She stopped because of the side effects. (The reason…)

Show the answers

(1) What worries her is the cost. (2) It was the Tuesday appointment that he missed. (3) What she needs is a social worker. (4) The reason (why) she stopped is (that) she had side effects.

Unit 32 · Tentative and diplomatic language

When we use it: to make suggestions to seniors, to disagree in a seminar, and to ask sensitive questions without pressure.

Function Phrases
Polite requests I was wondering whether… Would it be possible to…? Would you mind + V-ing?
Suggestions to the team Could we consider…? Would it be worth + V-ing…? It might be helpful to…
Sensitive questions I was wondering if you could tell me a bit about… What gets in the way of…?
Disagreeing I see it slightly differently. While I take your point,… I'm not sure I agree, because…
Not knowing I'm not sure, but I think… As far as I know,… I'd need to check.

Why the past tense sounds polite: I was wondering and I wanted to ask talk about now, but the past form adds distance and sounds less direct.

Softeners: a bit, slightly, perhaps, possibly, just (Could I just check…?).

But not for safety. When a patient may be harmed, be clear and firm (CUS): I'm concerned. I'm uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.

Watch out!

  • ✗ Would you mind to wait? ✓ Would you mind waiting?
  • Over-softening in an emergency causes delay: ✗ I was wondering whether you might possibly come… ✓ I need you to come now.

Try it. Make more tentative: (1) Book an interpreter. (2) You're wrong. (3) Can I ask about your alcohol use? (4) Review his pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) Could we consider booking an interpreter? (2) I see it slightly differently. (3) I was wondering if I could ask about your alcohol use. (4) Would it be worth reviewing his pain relief?

Unit 33 · Mixed and formal conditionals

Mixed conditionals

Type If-clause Main clause Example
past cause → present result Past Perfect would + V1 If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be in hospital now.
present situation → past result Past Simple would have + V3 If he weren't so afraid of needles, he would have had the test last week.

Formal inversion (leaflets, letters, academic writing): drop if and invert.

  • Should you notice any redness, contact the clinic. (= If you notice…)
  • Had I known about the allergy, I would have said so. (= If I had known…)
  • Were the patient to refuse, the team would discuss alternatives. (= If the patient refused…)

Other ways to say if

Word Meaning Example
unless if not Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
provided that / as long as only if You can go home as long as someone stays with you.
in case as a precaution (≠ if) Take your inhaler in case you need it.
otherwise if not, then… Keep the dressing dry; otherwise it may get infected.
supposing / what if imagining What if the results are positive?

Watch out!

  • in case ≠ if: Take your inhaler in case you get wheezy (take it with you now anyway) vs Use your inhaler if you get wheezy (only when it happens).
  • No would after if in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known…

Try it. (1) If I ___ (study) harder last year, I ___ (be) in nursing school now. (2) ___ you have any questions, please call. (3) Bring water ___ the wait is long. (4) You can drive ___ you don't feel drowsy.

Show the answers

(1) had studied … would be (2) Should (3) in case (4) as long as / provided that.

Unit 34 · Academic grammar: reporting verbs and the passive

When we use it: in summaries, care-plan rationales, essays and reflections.

Reporting verbs, from weak to strong

Strength Verbs Example
tentative suggests, indicates, implies The research suggests that lifestyle change can delay onset.
neutral states, reports, describes, notes The textbook states that…
strong shows, demonstrates, confirms, establishes The study demonstrates a clear link…
arguing argues, claims, maintains The author argues that…

The academic passive and impersonal structures

  • It is recommended that patients… It has been shown that…
  • Patients are advised to… Pressure injuries are associated with…
  • There is evidence* that… There is* a need for…

Tenses in academic writing

  • Present Simple for general facts and what a source says: Hand hygiene reduces infection. The author argues…
  • Past Simple for a specific study: The study found that…
  • Present Perfect for research up to now: Several studies have shown…

Style: no contractions (does not, not doesn't); avoid I think in essays (reflections are the exception: they use I); hedge claims (appears to, is likely to, may contribute to).

Watch out!

  • Too strong: ✗ This proves that… ✓ This suggests that…
  • Copying the source's sentence with small changes is plagiarism. Paraphrase fully and cite.

Try it. Make it academic: (1) Lots of studies show exercise helps. (2) Doctors say patients should check their feet. (3) I think the patient didn't understand. (4) This proves the leaflet works.

Show the answers

(1) Several studies have shown that exercise is beneficial. (2) Patients are advised to check their feet daily. (3) The patient appeared not to understand. (4) This suggests that the leaflet is effective.

Reference tables

A · All 12 tenses: structure (verb: take)

Present

Tense + − ?
Simple I take · she takes I don't take · she doesn't take Do you take? · Does she take?
Continuous I am taking · she is taking I'm not taking · she isn't taking Are you taking? · Is she taking?
Perfect I have taken · she has taken I haven't taken · she hasn't taken Have you taken? · Has she taken?
Perfect Continuous I have been taking I haven't been taking Have you been taking?

Past

Tense + − ?
Simple I took I didn't take Did you take?
Continuous I was taking · they were taking I wasn't taking · they weren't taking Were you taking?
Perfect I had taken I hadn't taken Had you taken?
Perfect Continuous I had been taking I hadn't been taking Had you been taking?

Future

Tense + − ?
Simple I will take I won't take Will you take?
Continuous I will be taking I won't be taking Will you be taking?
Perfect I will have taken I won't have taken Will you have taken?
Perfect Continuous I will have been taking I won't have been taking Will you have been taking?

The pattern: Continuous always has be + V-ing. Perfect always has have + V3. Perfect Continuous has both: have been + V-ing.

B · When we use each tense

Tense Main uses Example
Present Simple habits; schedules; facts; states She takes insulin every morning.
Present Continuous happening now; temporary; fixed plans; annoying habits (always) He's sleeping now.
Present Perfect past action with a result now; life experience; up to now (for / since) I've already taken it.
Present Perfect Continuous activity from the past until now, focus on duration; recent activity with a visible result I've been coughing for a week.
Past Simple finished action at a finished time; a sequence of events She fell yesterday.
Past Continuous in progress at a past moment; background; interrupted by a short action She was walking when she fell.
Past Perfect earlier than another past moment She had eaten before the test.
Past Perfect Continuous duration up to a past moment She had been feeling dizzy all morning.
Future Simple (will) decisions now; promises; predictions; realistic hopes and fears; facts about the future I'll call the nurse.
Future Continuous in progress at a future moment This time tomorrow you'll be having surgery.
Future Perfect finished by a future moment By Friday you'll have finished the antibiotics.
Future Perfect Continuous duration up to a future moment By June I'll have been studying for two years.

C · Time keywords

Simple Continuous Perfect Perfect Continuous
Present every…, always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom, never, once / twice a…, from time to time, generally now, right now, at the moment, at present, currently, these days, today, this week, still just, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, today, this week, for, since for, since, how long, all day, all week, lately, recently
Past yesterday, ago, last…, in (2019), at (3 a.m.), on (Monday), when while, as, when, at (3 a.m.) yesterday, all night, at that moment before, after, by (10 a.m.), by the time, already, when for, since, before, until, by the time, all morning
Future tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, next…, in (two days), soon, later, some day, tonight this time tomorrow, at (10) tomorrow, all day tomorrow by (Friday), by the time, before for, by (June), by the time

D · Irregular verbs for healthcare

V1 V2 V3 Example
be was / were been Have you been in hospital before?
become became become It became worse at night.
begin began begun The pain began on Sunday.
bleed bled bled The cut bled for 10 minutes.
break broke broken She broke her wrist.
bring brought brought Have you brought your medicines?
come came come He came in by ambulance.
cut cut cut I cut my hand on glass.
do did done Have you done the test?
drink drank drunk She hasn't drunk anything today.
drive drove driven Who drove you here?
eat ate eaten Have you eaten since midnight?
fall fell fallen He fell in the bathroom.
feel felt felt I felt dizzy.
forget forgot forgotten I forgot my insulin.
get got got (US: gotten) It's gotten worse.
give gave given The nurse gave him pain relief.
go went gone The swelling has gone down.
have had had She had surgery in 2018.
hold held held Hold your breath.
hurt hurt hurt My back hurt all night.
keep kept kept Keep the dressing dry.
know knew known I've known her for years.
leave left left The doctor has just left.
lie (down) lay lain She lay in bed all day.
lose lost lost He lost consciousness.
put put put Put the needle in the sharps container.
say said said She said she felt sick.
see saw seen Has the doctor seen you?
shake shook shaken Shake well before use.
sleep slept slept I haven't slept well.
swell swelled swollen My ankle is swollen.
take took taken Have you taken your tablets?
tell told told She told me about the pain.
throw (up) threw thrown He threw up twice.
understand understood understood Have you understood the instructions?
wake (up) woke woken I woke up at 3 a.m.
wear wore worn Please wear a mask.
write wrote written I've written it down.

Watch out: lie (lie, lay, lain) = be in a flat position: Lie down, please. · lay (lay, laid, laid) = put something down: Lay the patient on her side.

E · -ing and -ed forms at a glance

Form Meaning Example See
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb I was listening to music. Units 10, 19, 20
Gerund V-ing as a noun Walking every day helps. Avoid lifting. Unit 30
Participle I V-ing as an adjective (active) a bleeding wound, the patient sitting by the window Unit 30
Participle II (V3) V3 as an adjective (passive or finished) a broken leg, the prescribed dose Units 22, 30
-ing adjective the cause of a feeling confusing instructions Unit 30
-ed adjective the feeling a confused patient Unit 30

-ing spelling: take → taking (drop -e) · sit → sitting (double the consonant after one short vowel) · lie → lying, die → dying (ie → y) · see → seeing (keep -ee).

F · Conditionals at a glance

Type If-clause Main clause Meaning Example
Zero Present Simple Present Simple always true If you smile, you start to feel better.
First Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction real future If the pain gets worse, call us.
Second Past Simple would + V1 unreal now / unlikely future If I were you, I'd rest.
Third Past Perfect would have + V3 unreal past If I had known, I would have told you.
Mixed (past → now) Past Perfect would + V1 past cause, present result If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be here now.
Mixed (now → past) Past Simple would have + V3 present situation, past result If he weren't afraid of needles, he would have had the test.
Formal inversion Should / Had / Were + S… as above written, formal Should you notice redness, contact the clinic.

Two rules for every type: no will and no would in the if-clause. Comma after the if-clause when it comes first.

teacher.title: Vocabulary Book
teacher.html:
This book holds every new word from the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 courses, with a plain-English definition and an example of how it is used. The words follow the course order: level → week → lesson.

Each entry

Column What it shows
L the lesson where the word is taught
Word the word or phrase, with its abbreviation if there is one
Type the part of speech
Definition what it means, in simple English
Example how it is used in healthcare

Types: n. = noun · v. = verb · adj. = adjective · adv. = adverb · phr. = phrase · abbr. = abbreviation · prefix / suffix = word part · phr. v. = phrasal verb · prep. = preposition.

How to study a word

  1. Read the definition, then cover it and explain the word in your own English words.
  2. Say the example aloud twice.
  3. Make a new sentence about a patient, your family or your studies.
  4. Review the week's words before the third lesson of the week, and all the level's words before Lessons 18 and 36.

B1 Foundation

Week 1 · Healthcare Basics

L Word Type Definition Example
1 nursing school n. a college or program where people study to become nurses I plan to apply to nursing school next year.
1 registered nurse (RN) n. a nurse who has finished a nursing degree and passed the licensing exam My goal is to become a registered nurse.
1 patient n. a person who receives medical care The patient is waiting in room 4.
1 healthcare n. the work of keeping people healthy and treating illness I want to work in healthcare.
1 career n. the work a person does over many years of their life Nursing is a good career.
1 goal n. something you want to achieve My goal is to work in a hospital.
1 experience n. knowledge or skill you get from doing something I don't have hospital experience yet.
1 degree n. a qualification from a college or university A nursing degree takes two to four years.
2 physician n. a medical doctor The physician will see you soon.
2 nursing assistant n. a worker who helps patients wash, eat and move, under a nurse A nursing assistant helped him walk.
2 pharmacist n. a person trained to prepare and give out medicines Ask the pharmacist about side effects.
2 receptionist n. a person at the front desk who greets and checks in patients The receptionist checked my insurance card.
2 emergency department (ED) n. the hospital area for urgent and serious problems He was brought to the ED by ambulance.
2 unit n. one department or area of a hospital She works on the surgical unit.
2 pharmacy n. a place where medicines are prepared and sold The pharmacy is on the first floor.
2 shift n. a fixed period of work, e.g. day or night I work the night shift.
3 appointment n. an arranged time to see a doctor or nurse I have an appointment at ten thirty.
3 check in v. to tell the front desk that you have arrived Please check in at the front desk.
3 insurance card n. a card that shows who pays for your medical care Do you have your insurance card?
3 date of birth n. the day, month and year you were born Can you tell me your date of birth?

Week 2 · The Human Body

L Word Type Definition Example
4 abdomen n. the front part of the body between the chest and the hips The pain is in my abdomen.
4 chest n. the front of the body between the neck and the abdomen Put your hand on your chest.
4 shoulder n. the joint where the arm joins the body My left shoulder hurts.
4 elbow n. the joint in the middle of the arm The elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist.
4 wrist n. the joint between the hand and the arm She broke her wrist.
4 hip n. the joint where the leg joins the body His hip is stiff.
4 knee n. the joint in the middle of the leg Can you bend your knee?
4 ankle n. the joint between the foot and the leg Her ankle is swollen.
5 brain n. the organ in the head that controls the body and thinking The brain controls the body.
5 heart n. the organ that pumps blood around the body The heart pumps blood.
5 lungs n. the two organs in the chest that take in oxygen The lungs take in oxygen.
5 liver n. a large organ that cleans the blood and helps digestion The liver cleans the blood.
5 kidneys n. two organs that filter the blood and make urine The kidneys make urine.
5 intestines n. the long tube that takes in food and water after the stomach The intestines absorb food and water.
5 bladder n. the organ that stores urine The bladder stores urine.
5 pancreas n. an organ that makes insulin and helps digestion The pancreas produces insulin.
6 upper adj. nearer the head The pain is in my upper back.
6 lower adj. nearer the feet I have lower back pain.
6 anterior adj. at the front of the body Place the stethoscope on the anterior chest.
6 posterior adj. at the back of the body Listen to the posterior chest.

Week 3 · Symptoms and Pain

L Word Type Definition Example
7 symptom n. something a patient feels that may show illness What symptoms do you have?
7 fever n. a body temperature higher than normal She has had a fever since last night.
7 chills n. feeling cold and shaking, often with a fever He has chills at night.
7 nausea n. the feeling that you are going to vomit I have nausea after meals.
7 vomiting n. bringing food up from the stomach out of the mouth She has been vomiting since morning.
7 dizziness n. feeling that you or the room is spinning, or unsteady I have dizziness when I stand up.
7 fatigue n. being very tired with no energy Fatigue is common after surgery.
7 weakness n. lack of strength in the muscles He has weakness in both legs.
8 sharp adj. (pain) strong and sudden, like a cut It's a sharp pain on the right side.
8 dull adj. (pain) not strong but steady I have a dull ache in my back.
8 burning adj. (pain) hot, like a burn I get a burning pain after meals.
8 aching adj. (pain) continuous and not severe My legs are aching.
8 throbbing adj. (pain) beating like a pulse I have a throbbing headache.
8 constant adj. there all the time The pain is constant.
8 comes and goes phr. starts and stops again and again The pain comes and goes.
8 pain scale n. a scale from 0 to 10 for rating pain On the pain scale, it's a 6.
9 onset n. the start of a symptom or illness The onset was sudden.
9 duration n. how long something lasts What is the duration of the pain?
9 suddenly adv. very quickly and without warning It started suddenly.
9 gradually adv. slowly, a little at a time The swelling went down gradually.

Week 4 · Health History

L Word Type Definition Example
10 medical history n. a record of a person's past illnesses and treatments Let's go over your medical history.
10 condition n. an illness or health problem Do you have any medical conditions?
10 chronic adj. lasting a long time or coming back again and again Asthma is a chronic condition.
10 diabetes n. a condition in which blood sugar is too high My mother has diabetes.
10 hypertension n. high blood pressure He takes a tablet for hypertension.
10 asthma n. a condition that makes the airways narrow and breathing difficult She uses an inhaler for asthma.
10 infection n. an illness caused by germs such as bacteria or viruses She had a kidney infection last spring.
10 diagnosis n. the name of a patient's illness, decided by a clinician There is no diagnosis yet.
11 surgery n. treatment in which a surgeon operates on the body Have you ever had surgery?
11 operation n. a single act of surgery The operation took two hours.
11 procedure n. a medical action or test done in a set way It was a small procedure.
11 injury n. damage to the body, e.g. from a fall He had a knee injury.
11 fracture n. a broken bone The X-ray shows a fracture.
11 hospital stay n. the time a patient spends in hospital She had a three-day hospital stay.
11 recovery n. the process of getting well again Recovery took six weeks.
11 scar n. a mark left on the skin after a wound heals There is a small scar on my abdomen.
12 allergic to phr. having a bad body reaction to something I'm allergic to penicillin.
12 reaction n. the way the body responds to something What reaction did you have?
12 rash n. an area of red spots on the skin I got a rash on my arms.
12 family history n. illnesses that parents, brothers and sisters have had Is there a family history of diabetes?

Week 5 · Vital Signs and Measurements

L Word Type Definition Example
13 decimal point n. the dot in a number such as 37.5 Say the decimal point clearly: thirty-seven point five.
13 degree n. a unit for measuring temperature Her temperature is 38 degrees.
13 kilogram (kg) n. a metric unit of weight (1,000 grams) He weighs 72 kilograms.
13 pound (lb) n. a US unit of weight (about 0.45 kg) She weighs 160 pounds.
13 centimeter (cm) n. a metric unit of length (1/100 of a meter) The cut is 2 centimeters long.
13 inch (in) n. a US unit of length (about 2.5 cm) He is 5 feet 4 inches tall.
13 percent (%) n. a part of 100 Oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
13 unit n. a standard measure, such as mg, mL or kg Always say the unit with the number.
14 vital signs n. the main body measurements: temperature, pulse, breathing, blood pressure, oxygen I need to check your vital signs.
14 blood pressure (BP) n. the force of blood against the walls of the arteries Your blood pressure is 120 over 80.
14 pulse / heart rate (HR) n. the number of heartbeats per minute His heart rate is 72.
14 respiratory rate (RR) n. the number of breaths per minute Her respiratory rate is 16.
14 temperature (T) n. how hot the body is Your temperature is normal.
14 oxygen saturation (SpO2) n. the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is carrying oxygen SpO2 is 95 percent on room air.
14 beats per minute (bpm) phr. heartbeats counted in one minute 72 beats per minute.
14 breaths per minute phr. breaths counted in one minute 16 breaths per minute.
15 reading n. a number shown by a measuring device The first reading was 118 over 76.
15 baseline n. a first or usual measurement used for comparison His baseline heart rate is 74.
15 increase v. / n. to go up; a rise His heart rate has increased.
15 decrease v. / n. to go down; a fall Her oxygen saturation has decreased.

Week 6 · Heart and Lungs

L Word Type Definition Example
16 heartbeat n. one beat of the heart I can feel my heartbeat.
16 circulation n. the movement of blood around the body Exercise helps circulation.
16 artery n. a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart Arteries carry blood from the heart.
16 vein n. a blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart The nurse took blood from a vein.
16 chest pain n. pain anywhere in the chest Do you have chest pain now?
16 palpitations n. feeling your heart beat fast, hard or unevenly I have palpitations at night.
16 swelling (edema) n. a part of the body becoming larger because of fluid There is swelling in both ankles.
16 irregular adj. not even or steady Her heartbeat is irregular.
17 breath n. the air taken in or let out of the lungs Take a deep breath.
17 breathe v. to take air in and out of the lungs Breathe in slowly.
17 shortness of breath n. difficulty getting enough air I get shortness of breath on the stairs.
17 cough n. / v. a sudden noisy push of air from the lungs; to do this I have had a cough for two days.
17 wheezing n. a whistling sound when breathing I can hear wheezing.
17 sputum (phlegm) n. thick mucus coughed up from the lungs Do you cough up any sputum?
17 inhale v. to breathe in Inhale through your nose.
17 exhale v. to breathe out Exhale slowly through your mouth.

Week 7 · Digestion, Urination and Nutrition

L Word Type Definition Example
19 appetite n. the wish to eat I have a poor appetite this week.
19 diet n. the food a person usually eats My diet has a lot of bread.
19 nutrition n. the food the body needs to stay healthy Good nutrition helps recovery.
19 fluids n. drinks and other liquids Please drink plenty of fluids.
19 intake n. the amount taken into the body What is your daily fluid intake?
19 hydration n. having enough water in the body Hydration is important in hot weather.
19 dehydration n. not having enough water in the body Diarrhea can cause dehydration.
19 swallow v. to move food or drink from the mouth to the stomach Food gets stuck when I swallow.
20 bowel movement n. passing waste from the bowels When was your last bowel movement?
20 stool n. solid waste from the bowels Was the stool hard or soft?
20 constipation n. difficulty passing stool, or passing it rarely I've had constipation for four days.
20 diarrhea n. passing loose, watery stool often He has had diarrhea since yesterday.
20 bloating n. a full, tight feeling in the abdomen I have bloating after meals.
20 cramps n. sudden painful tightening of muscles, e.g. in the abdomen I have stomach cramps.
20 regular adj. happening at the usual times Are your bowel movements regular?
20 usual adj. normal for this person Is that usual for you?
21 urinate v. to pass urine Does it burn when you urinate?
21 frequency n. needing to pass urine very often She has frequency and urgency.
21 urgency n. a sudden strong need to pass urine Urgency means you can't wait.
21 burning n. a hot, painful feeling, e.g. when passing urine There is burning when I pass urine.

Week 8 · Movement, Skin and Sensation

L Word Type Definition Example
22 muscle n. body tissue that tightens to make movement My leg muscles are weak.
22 joint n. a place where two bones meet The knee is a joint.
22 mobility n. the ability to move around Her mobility is limited.
22 balance n. the ability to stay steady without falling He has poor balance.
22 stiff adj. hard to bend or move My back is stiff in the morning.
22 cane n. a stick that helps a person walk She walks with a cane.
22 walker n. a metal frame a person holds while walking Please use your walker.
22 wheelchair n. a chair with wheels for people who cannot walk well Would you like a wheelchair?
23 wound n. an injury where the skin is broken The wound is on her left arm.
23 cut n. a wound made by something sharp There is a 2 cm cut on his palm.
23 bruise n. a dark mark on the skin after a hit There is a purple bruise on her leg.
23 redness n. red color on the skin I can see some redness.
23 drainage n. fluid coming out of a wound There is a small amount of drainage.

Week 9 · Medicines

L Word Type Definition Example

25 capsule n. medicine inside a small soft or hard shell Swallow the capsule whole.
25 liquid n. medicine in a form you can pour This medicine is a liquid.
25 injection n. medicine put into the body with a needle Insulin is given by injection.
25 inhaler n. a device for breathing medicine into the lungs Use your inhaler when needed.
25 cream n. a soft medicine you put on the skin Apply the cream twice daily.
25 by mouth (oral, PO) phr. swallowed This tablet is taken by mouth.
25 IV (intravenous) adj. / abbr. into a vein He is getting fluids by IV.
26 dose n. the amount of medicine taken at one time What is the dose?
26 milligram (mg) n. a small unit of weight (1/1,000 of a gram) Each tablet is 10 milligrams.
26 milliliter (mL) n. a small unit of liquid (1/1,000 of a liter) Take 10 milliliters.
26 once daily phr. one time every day Take it once daily in the morning.
26 twice daily phr. two times every day Apply it twice daily.
26 every 8 hours phr. three times in 24 hours, with 8 hours between doses Take it every 8 hours.
26 as needed (PRN) phr. only when you need it Use it as needed for pain.
26 with food phr. together with a meal Take it with food.
27 side effect n. an unwanted effect of a medicine Sleepiness is a side effect.
27 missed dose n. a dose that was not taken at the right time Tell the nurse about any missed dose.
27 refill n. a new supply of the same prescription You have two refills.
27 teach-back n. asking the patient to explain instructions in their own words Let's do teach-back: how will you take it?

Week 10 · Tests and Procedures

L Word Type Definition Example
28 blood test n. a test of a small amount of blood You have a blood test tomorrow.
28 urine sample n. a small amount of urine collected for testing Please give a urine sample.
28 specimen n. a sample of blood, urine or tissue for testing The specimen goes to the lab.
28 laboratory (lab) n. a place where samples are tested The lab is on the second floor.
28 result n. what a test shows The doctor will explain the result.

28 container n. a box or cup that holds something Use the clean container.
29 X-ray n. a picture of the inside of the body, especially bones You need a chest X-ray.

29 MRI n. a detailed picture of the body made with a magnet Remove all metal before the MRI.
29 ultrasound n. a picture of the inside of the body made with sound waves A gel is used for the ultrasound.
29 imaging n. tests that make pictures of the inside of the body Imaging is on the first floor.
29 contrast (dye) n. a liquid that makes parts of the body clearer on a scan Some scans use contrast.
29 procedure (revision) n. a medical action or test done in a set way The procedure doesn't hurt.
29 consent form n. a document a patient signs to agree to treatment Please sign the consent form.
30 hand hygiene n. cleaning the hands to stop germs spreading Hand hygiene stops infections.
30 gloves n. thin coverings worn on the hands for protection Put on gloves before you start.
30 mask n. a covering over the nose and mouth Please wear a mask in this room.
30 isolation n. keeping a patient apart to stop infection spreading This patient is in isolation.

Week 11 · Patient Communication and Teamwork

L Word Type Definition Example
31 concern n. a worry Do you have any concerns?
31 worried adj. feeling that something bad may happen I can see you're worried.
31 uncomfortable adj. not feeling at ease, physically or emotionally Are you uncomfortable?
31 privacy n. being away from other people's attention Would you like some privacy?
31 confidential adj. to be kept secret and shared only with those who need it Your information is confidential.
31 interpreter n. a person who changes speech from one language into another Would you like an interpreter?
31 respect n. treating someone as important and valued We treat every patient with respect.
31 reassure v. to help someone feel less worried I tried to reassure her.
32 handoff n. passing care and information to the next nurse I'm giving the handoff to the night nurse.
32 report n. a short spoken or written summary Let me give you a quick report.
32 situation n. (SBAR) what is happening now S is for situation.
32 background n. (SBAR) the relevant history B is for background.
32 assessment n. (SBAR) what you have found A is for assessment.
32 recommendation n. (SBAR) what you are asking for R is for recommendation.
32 update n. new information I'm calling with an update.
32 read-back n. repeating information to check it is correct Please do a read-back of the numbers.
33 confirm v. to check that something is correct Let me confirm the room number.
33 reported adj. told by the patient Write down reported symptoms, such as pain.
33 observed adj. seen or measured by the nurse Observed signs include swelling and redness.
33 document v. to write in the patient's record Please document the time.

Week 12 · Nursing-School Readiness

L Word Type Definition Example
34 lecture n. a talk given to students on a subject The lecture starts at 9 a.m.
34 syllabus n. the plan of a course, with topics, dates and rules The dates are in the syllabus.
34 assignment n. a piece of work given to students The assignment is a care plan.
34 due date (deadline) n. the last day to hand in work The due date is Friday.
34 rubric n. a guide that shows how work will be scored Check the rubric before you write.
34 quiz n. a short test We have a quiz on Tuesday.
34 chapter n. one section of a book Nursing textbooks are divided into chapters.
34 office hours n. the times a teacher is available to meet students I'll come to your office hours.
35 clinical placement n. time a student spends working and learning in a hospital or clinic My clinical placement is at a hospital.
35 simulation n. practice with a realistic but not real situation Today we have a simulation.

35 demonstrate v. to show how to do something The instructor will demonstrate first.
35 preceptor n. an experienced nurse who guides a student on placement My preceptor is very supportive.
35 care plan n. a written plan of a patient's nursing care Write a care plan for the case.
35 feedback n. comments on how well you did I will give feedback at the end.

student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to B2 Clinical Medical English

In B1 you learned to talk about healthcare. In B2 you will run real patient conversations: full interviews, exact reports, urgent calls, SBAR handoffs and caring, sensitive talk. This book is yours: write in it and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level B2 Clinical
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My B1 final score
My goal for B2

What's new in B2

  • You lead. Every lesson starts with 60 seconds of free speaking, and in the last role-play you get a card you have never seen.
  • Every detail counts. Your teacher corrects these at once: numbers, units, left/right, times and the word not.
  • Report and refer. You collect facts and pass them on. You never diagnose or give medical advice. Learn these by heart:
  • I'll let the nurse know right away.
  • That's a question for your doctor or pharmacist.
  • I'm not able to advise on that, but I'll find someone who can.
  • I'm concerned about this change. Could you come and see the patient?
  • Hot Seat Interpreting. You will interpret longer Uzbek turns into English, in the first person, adding nothing.
  • Homework: 20 minutes a day. After Lesson A: words and listening. After Lesson B: speak and record. After Lesson C: a 90–120 second voice note.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 2 for B2; Part 1 to review). Every unit ends with a short practice and the answers.

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (B2 section). Read the definition, then say the example aloud.

All patients, charts and labels in this book are fictional. This course teaches English, not clinical skills.

student.title: Advanced Patient Interviews
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ open an interview and get the chief complaint without leading
  • ☐ take a structured symptom history (OLDCARTS)
  • ☐ interview for 5 minutes and summarize in 60 seconds
Lesson Word Example
1 intake Let's start your intake.
1 verify I need to verify your date of birth.
1 preferred language What is your preferred language?
1 chief complaint Her chief complaint is fatigue.
1 reason for visit What is the reason for your visit?
1 concern What concerns you most?
1 bothersome Which symptom is most bothersome?
1 clarify Can I clarify one thing?
1 leading question Is it sharp? is a leading question.
2 location Where exactly is the pain?
2 character How would you describe the pain?
2 aggravating factor Walking is an aggravating factor.
2 relieving factor Rest is a relieving factor.
2 timing Is it constant, or does it come and go?
2 associated symptoms Any associated symptoms, like nausea?
2 pertinent negative No diarrhea is a pertinent negative.
2 radiate Does the pain radiate anywhere?
3 social history Let's go over your social history.
3 occupation What is your occupation?
3 tobacco Do you use tobacco in any form?
3 alcohol How much alcohol do you drink in a week?

Useful phrases: What brings you in today? · Tell me more about that. · How would you describe it? · How long have you been having this pain? · He reports… He denies…

OLDCARTS: Onset · Location · Duration · Character · Aggravating · Relieving · Timing · Severity.

Voice note: a 60-second history summary, then 3 open questions you would ask next.

Cards and texts · Week 1

Intake script: Hello, I'm Dilnoza, a nursing student. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth? What language would you prefer to use today? What brings you in today? Tell me more about that.

Match and Speak (Lesson 1): make each question open. Do you have pain? · Is it bad? · Did it start today? · Are you worried?

Complaint cards (fictional): K1 – Feruza, 41: I've been really tired and my feet tingle (3 weeks). K2 – Akmal, 29: My stomach has been bad since the weekend (upper abdominal pain and nausea, 3 days).

OLDCARTS grid:

Part What the patient says
Onset
Location
Duration
Character
Aggravating factors
Relieving factors
Timing
Severity (0–10)
Associated symptoms
Pertinent negatives

Observer checks: Lesson 1 – open question first · identity confirmed (name and date of birth) · no leading questions · one-sentence summary. Lesson 2 – all 8 OLDCARTS parts · one pertinent negative asked · timing and severity repeated back · no leading questions. Lesson 3 – 6 history parts covered (chief complaint, symptom details, past history, medicines and allergies, family history, social history) · denies used correctly · numbers right · summary 60 seconds or less.

student.title: Neurological Assessment and Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about neurological symptoms and exact timing
  • ☐ describe mental status in neutral words
  • ☐ report a new change with side and time
Lesson Word Example
4 migraine She has had migraines since she was a teenager.
4 fainting Have you had any fainting?
4 seizure He had a seizure last year.
4 slurred speech Her speech is slurred.
4 blurred vision Do you have blurred vision?
4 double vision Any double vision?
4 vertigo The room spins: that's vertigo.
4 sensitivity to light Bright light makes the headache worse.
4 warning sign Sudden weakness is a warning sign.
5 awake He is awake and talking.
5 drowsy She is drowsy but wakes to voice.
5 agitated He is agitated and pulling at his IV.
5 oriented She is oriented to person, place and time.
5 disoriented He is disoriented to time.
5 attention She can't keep her attention on the question.
5 memory How is his memory today?
5 baseline Is this his baseline?
5 responds to He responds to his name.
6 strength His strength is equal on both sides.
6 grip Her left grip is weaker.
6 gait His gait is unsteady.
6 unequal Grip strength is unequal.

Useful phrases: When did you first notice it? · Have you noticed any changes in your vision? · He appears drowsy. · I'm calling about a new change: new weakness in his left hand since 4 p.m.

Remember: never say a diagnosis (stroke). Say what you see and when.

Voice note: a change report with side and both times, then describe a patient's mental status.

Cards and texts · Week 2

Neuro cards (fictional): N1 – Gulchehra, 34: throbbing headache on the left side for 2 days; sensitive to light; nausea; has had similar headaches before. N2 – Bobur, 48: the room spins when he turns his head, for 1 week; no change in hearing.

Neuro follow-up card: Vision: Have you noticed any changes in your vision? · Speech: Have you had any trouble speaking or finding words? · Weakness: Have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs? · Numbness: Do you have any numbness or tingling? Where?

Mental-status card M2 (fictional): Kamila, 25: alert, oriented ×3, anxious, answers all questions.

Says / observe sorting table:

The patient or family says I observe

Change card R1 (fictional): Nodir Saidov, 66, room 14. 2 p.m.: grip equal, speech clear. 4 p.m.: left grip weaker than right; says my left hand feels heavy; gait unsteady; speech clear; alert and oriented ×3.

Observer checks: Lesson 4 – exact onset · neuro follow-ups asked · sudden change escalated at once · no diagnosis named. Lesson 5 – neutral words only · says vs observed kept apart · baseline asked · all three orientation questions. Lesson 6 – side correct · both times given · says vs observed apart · clear request at the end.

student.title: Cardiovascular Conditions and Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about chest symptoms clearly
  • ☐ report blood-pressure readings with position and time
  • ☐ explain an ECG from a card and refer other questions
Lesson Word Example
7 pressure I feel pressure in my chest.
7 tightness My chest feels tight on the stairs.
7 discomfort Any chest discomfort?
7 exertion Does it happen with exertion?
7 at rest Does it happen at rest?
7 spread Does it spread to your arm or jaw?
7 sweating She started sweating.
7 cardiac history Any cardiac history in your family?
7 heart attack His father had a heart attack at 50.
8 systolic Systolic is the top number.
8 diastolic Diastolic is the bottom number.
8 hypotension Hypotension means low blood pressure.
8 orthostatic We'll check orthostatic readings.
8 cuff The cuff will feel tight.
8 lying Lying down: 132 over 80.
8 standing Standing: 104 over 66.
8 lightheaded She feels lightheaded when she stands.
9 electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG) You need an ECG.
9 echocardiogram An echocardiogram is an ultrasound of the heart.
9 electrode Small electrodes are placed on your chest.
9 rhythm The ECG shows the heart's rhythm.

Useful phrases: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? · The blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down. · The doctor will look at the results and explain them to you. · I'm getting the nurse right away.

Voice note: explain the ECG to a patient, then report a lying and standing blood pressure.

Cards and texts · Week 3

Uzbek Bridge (Lesson 7): say each line in English. Ko‘kragimda bosim bor, chap qo‘limga tarqalyapti. · Zinadan chiqqanimda ko‘kragim siqiladi, dam olsam o‘tib ketadi. · Terlab ketdim va ko‘nglim aynidi. · Otam ellik yoshida infarkt bo‘lgan.

Chest cards (fictional): C1 – Rustam, 58: chest tightness walking uphill for 2 weeks; stops with rest. C2 – Madina, 36: heart racing at rest in the evenings for 5 days; 4 cups of coffee a day.

Time-clause card: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? · Does it go away after you stop? · Does it come on whenever you climb stairs? · Does the discomfort spread anywhere?

Orthostatic chart (fictional): Oydin Nazarova, 70. 10:00 lying: BP 132/80, HR 76. 10:03 standing: BP 104/66, HR 98; says she feels lightheaded.

Test cards (fictional): ECG – about 5–10 minutes; lie still; 10 small stickers (electrodes) on the chest, arms and legs; painless; no preparation; the doctor reviews the results. Echocardiogram – ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel on the chest; you may be asked to turn onto your left side; painless.

Observer checks: Lesson 7 – exertion vs rest · spread asked · urgent case escalated · no diagnosis told to the patient. Lesson 8 – top and bottom numbers in order · position and time for each · she says for symptoms · read-back correct. Lesson 9 – only card facts used · passive used correctly · clinical question referred · calm, reassuring tone.

student.title: Respiratory Conditions and Urgent Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ take a detailed breathing history
  • ☐ report oxygen readings with device and flow, and explain isolation
  • ☐ call for help clearly and calmly
Lesson Word Example
10 trigger What seems to trigger it?
10 allergen Dust is an allergen for her.
10 flare-up She is having an asthma flare-up.
10 congestion I have chest congestion.
10 productive cough A productive cough brings up sputum.
10 dry cough A dry cough brings nothing up.
10 rescue inhaler How often do you use your rescue inhaler?
10 nebulizer He uses a nebulizer at home.
10 peak flow Her peak flow is lower today.
11 nasal cannula She is on oxygen via nasal cannula.
11 oxygen mask He needs an oxygen mask.
11 room air SpO2 is 95% on room air.
11 liters per minute Oxygen at 2 liters per minute.
11 effort Breathing effort has increased.
11 shallow Her breathing is shallow.
11 droplet precautions Droplet precautions: everyone wears a mask.
11 airborne precautions Airborne precautions need a special mask.
11 N95 respirator Staff wear an N95 respirator.
12 distress The patient is in respiratory distress.
12 deteriorating His breathing is deteriorating.
12 rapid response Call the rapid response team.
12 reassess We will reassess in 15 minutes.

Useful phrases: Have you been using your inhaler more than usual? · SpO2 94% on 2 liters via nasal cannula. · This is… in room 6. I need help now. · I'm here with you. Help is coming.

Voice note: an urgent call in 30 seconds, then explain droplet precautions to a visitor.

Cards and texts · Week 4

Match and Speak (Lesson 10): match each patient phrase to a word. Phrases: I'm coughing stuff up · tickly cough, nothing comes up · my chest feels blocked · my asthma attack · my blue inhaler · the cat makes it worse. Words: rescue inhaler · allergen, trigger · dry cough · flare-up · productive cough · congestion.

Breathing cards (fictional): Rb1 – Lola, 22, asthma: flare-up for 3 days; using her rescue inhaler 6 times a day (usually twice a week); trigger: dust at her new job; dry cough at night. Rb2 – Sobir, 61, smoker: productive cough with yellow sputum for 1 week; short of breath after one flight of stairs.

Observation card O1 (fictional): Komil, 68. 8 a.m.: SpO2 95% on room air, RR 18. 12 p.m.: SpO2 90% on room air, RR 26, shallow breathing. 12:15 p.m.: SpO2 94% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula (as ordered).

Door sign IS1 (fictional): DROPLET PRECAUTIONS · Everyone entering: wear a surgical mask · Clean your hands before you go in and when you leave · Patient: wear a mask if you leave the room · Visitors: please ask the nurse before entering.

Oxygen report frame: At [time], SpO2 [ ]% on room air / on [ ] L/min via [nasal cannula / mask] · RR [ ] · breathing [shallow / more effort] · the patient says…

Urgent card U1 (fictional): Nilufar Yusupova, 59, room 6, 3:10 p.m. Sudden difficulty breathing; says I can't breathe; RR 32; SpO2 86% on 2 L nasal cannula (94% at 2 p.m.); sitting upright; frightened.

Observer checks: Lesson 10 – frequency of inhaler use asked · trigger asked · sputum described · proxy handled correctly. Lesson 11 – device and flow named · room air used correctly · each time given · isolation explained from the sign only. Lesson 12 – location first · facts in under 30 seconds · old and new value given · calm words to the patient.

student.title: Diabetes and Endocrine
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask about diabetes symptoms and routines
  • ☐ report glucose values with the right unit and time
  • ☐ summarize endocrine symptoms without diagnosing
Lesson Word Example

13 blood sugar Have you checked your blood sugar today?
13 insulin When did you take your insulin?
13 hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia means low blood sugar.
13 hyperglycemia Hyperglycemia means high blood sugar.
13 type 1 She has type 1 diabetes.
13 type 2 He has type 2 diabetes.
13 thirsty I'm thirsty all the time.
13 shaky I feel shaky and sweaty.
14 fingerstick Let's do a fingerstick check.
14 continuous glucose monitor (CGM) Her CGM shows a trend.
14 mg/dL 130 mg/dL (US unit)
14 mmol/L 7.2 mmol/L (unit used in Uzbekistan)
14 fasting glucose His fasting glucose was 112.
14 before meals Check before meals.
14 after meals It goes up after meals.
14 trend The trend is going up.
15 thyroid The thyroid is in your neck.
15 hormone The thyroid makes hormones.
15 cold / heat intolerance She can't stand the cold.
15 unexplained weight change She gained 5 kg without trying.

Useful phrases: If your sugar is low, you may feel shaky. · Was that 70 or 17? · Was that in millimoles per liter? · His readings have been trending up. · She reports… The doctor has ordered a blood test.

Unit alert: US = mg/dL. Uzbekistan = mmol/L. Always say the unit; never convert in your head.

Voice note: a glucose trend report, then a neutral 45-second endocrine summary.

Cards and texts · Week 5

Uzbek Bridge (Lesson 13): say each line in English. Qandim tushib ketganda qo‘llarim titraydi. · Doim chanqayman, kechasi ko‘p marta hojatxonaga turaman. · Bugun ertalab insulin qilmadim. · Qandimni o‘lchasam, 250 chiqdi.

Diabetes cards (fictional): D1 – Shahlo, 45, type 1: shaky, sweaty and hungry one hour after insulin; skipped lunch. D2 – Farhod, 52, type 2: very thirsty, urinating often, tired for 2 weeks, blurred vision; sugar 280 mg/dL yesterday.

Low / high symptom card: Low sugar (hypoglycemia): shaky, sweaty, hungry, confused · High sugar (hyperglycemia): thirsty, urinating often, tired, blurred vision · If your sugar is low, you may feel…

Glucose log G1 (fictional, mg/dL):

Day Fasting Before lunch Before dinner Bedtime
Mon 112 145 160 180
Tue 118 150 172 196
Wed 125 158 190 210

Match and Speak (Lesson 15): match each patient phrase to a term. Phrases: I'm always cold · I put on weight without eating more · my neck looks bigger · I'm hot and shaky all the time. Terms: neck swelling · heat intolerance, tremor · cold intolerance · unexplained weight gain.

Thyroid card Th1 (fictional): Gulnoza Tursunova, 39. Cold all the time and tired for about 3 months; gained 5 kg without changing her diet; dry skin; no medicines. The doctor has ordered a blood test.

Observer checks: Lesson 13 – last meal and last insulin asked · numbers with units · confusion escalated · no advice given. Lesson 14 – every value read back · unit said · time of day given · trend direction correct. Lesson 15 – no diagnosis named · duration given · weight with unit · the doctor's plan reported, not invented.

student.title: GI and Renal · Midpoint
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ ask detailed stomach questions respectfully
  • ☐ read and total an intake-and-output chart
  • ☐ do the midpoint tasks on my own
Lesson Word Example
16 cramping I have cramping in my lower abdomen.
16 tenderness There is tenderness when pressed.
16 heartburn I get heartburn at night.
16 indigestion Spicy food gives me indigestion.
16 reflux Reflux is worse when lying flat.
16 change in bowel habit Any change in bowel habit?
16 black stools Black stools must be reported.
16 jaundice Jaundice means yellow skin or eyes.
16 quadrant The pain is in the lower right quadrant.
17 intake and output (I&O) Please record intake and output.
17 fluid balance Her fluid balance is positive.
17 oral intake Oral intake was 1,100 mL today.
17 IV fluids IV fluids at 100 mL per hour.
17 urine output Urine output was 450 mL this shift.
17 positive balance More in than out.
17 negative balance More out than in.
17 measured Report measured values, not guesses.

Recognize for the midpoint: urinary tract infection (UTI) · flank pain · catheter · dialysis.

Useful phrases: Where exactly is the pain? Can you point to it? · A total of 1,400 mL was recorded over 12 hours. · I need to ask a few personal questions. Is that OK?

Midpoint check (Lesson 18): a 5-minute interview, a vital-signs and fluid report, and a 1-minute SBAR.

Voice note: re-record your midpoint SBAR with 2 improvements.

Cards and texts · Week 6

GI cards (fictional): GI1 – Anvar, 44: burning upper abdominal pain after spicy food and at night for 3 weeks; sour taste; worse lying flat. GI2 – Sevara, 30: lower abdominal cramping; diarrhea 4 times a day for 3 days; mild fever.

I&O chart F1 (fictional, 7 a.m.–7 p.m.): Oral: 8 a.m. tea 200 mL; 12 p.m. water 300 mL; 4 p.m. juice 250 mL. IV fluids: 100 mL per hour for 12 hours. Output: urine 10 a.m. 250 mL, 2 p.m. 200 mL, 6 p.m. 150 mL; vomited 100 mL at 1 p.m.

Totals frame: Oral intake [ ] mL · IV fluids [ ] mL · Total intake [ ] mL · Urine output [ ] mL · Other output [ ] mL · Total output [ ] mL · Balance + / − [ ] mL over [ ] hours.

SBAR frame (Lesson 18 and every handoff): S – Situation: who you are, where you are, the patient's name and the change now · B – Background: the key facts from the card: age, why the patient is here, what happened and when, important medicines · A – Assessment: what you observed or measured, with values, units and times, and what has changed; no diagnosis · R – Request: what you need, using the supplied request; then close the loop.

Observer checks: Lesson 16 – quadrant identified · degree words used · bowel questions respectful · black stools escalated. Lesson 17 – every unit said · period stated (12 hours) · totals correct · missing data questioned. Lesson 18 report checklist – values with units and times · change stated · intake and output with period · SBAR in order · request at the end.

student.title: Emergency Department Communication
student.html:
This week I can:

  • ☐ take a short arrival history without promising who is seen first
  • ☐ tell the story of an injury in the right order
  • ☐ give an urgent SBAR and close the loop
Lesson Word Example
19 triage The triage nurse will see you first.

student.title: Grammar Handbook
student.html:
How to use this handbook

This is the grammar companion to the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 books. Each lesson card names one grammar point; this handbook explains it in full. Teachers use it to prepare the 4-minute grammar slot. Students use it for homework and revision.

Most units follow this layout; reference units use tables instead:

  1. When we use it: the meanings, in short bullets.
  2. Structure: formulas for + (statement), − (negative) and ? (question), each with a healthcare example.
  3. Short answers and short forms.
  4. Keywords: the time words and signal words that go with it.
  5. Watch out!: the mistakes students make most, including typical mistakes of Uzbek speakers. ✗ = wrong, ✓ = right.
  6. Try it: 4 quick items, with the key underneath.

Symbols

Symbol Meaning Example
S subject The patient, she, I
V1 base form go, take, feel
V2 past form went, took, felt
V3 past participle gone, taken, felt
V-ing -ing form going, taking, feeling
(Q/W) question word (optional) what, where, when, how
+ / − / ? statement / negative / question

Part 2 · B2 Clinical

Unit 19 · Past Continuous (Past Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action in progress at a moment in the past: At 3 a.m. he was sleeping.
  • A longer action interrupted by a shorter one (Past Simple): She was walking to the bathroom when she fell.
  • Two actions in progress at the same time: While* the nurse was checking his pulse, he was talking* to his son.
  • The background of a story: It was raining and the ED was getting busy.

The action has no link to now and no result: it was simply in progress.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + was / were + V-ing They were waiting in the waiting area.
− S + was / were + not + V-ing She wasn't breathing normally.
? (Q/W) + was / were + S + V-ing? What were you doing when the pain started?

Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren't. Short forms: only in the negative: wasn't, weren't.

Keywords: while · as · when · at (3 a.m.) yesterday · all night · at that moment.

When or while? when + the short action (Past Simple); while / as + the long action (Past Continuous).

Watch out!

  • ✗ When I was fall… ✓ When I fell… (the short action is Past Simple)
  • State verbs stay simple: ✗ I was knowing him. ✓ I knew him.

Try it. (1) He ___ (carry) boxes when he ___ (feel) the pain. (2) What ___ you ___ (do) at 11 p.m.? (3) While I ___ (cook), I ___ (cut) my finger. (4) She ___ (not / sleep) when the nurse came in.

Show the answers

(1) was carrying … felt (2) were … doing (3) was cooking … cut (4) wasn't sleeping.

Unit 20 · Present Perfect Continuous

When we use it

  • An activity that started in the past and is still going on, with focus on how long: I've been coughing for a week.
  • A recent activity with a result you can see: Her eyes are red. She's been crying.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + been + V-ing He has been using his inhaler more than usual.
− S + have / has + not + been + V-ing I haven't been sleeping well.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + been + V-ing? How long have you been having this pain?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Keywords: for · since · how long · all day · all week · lately · recently.

Simple or continuous?

Present Perfect Continuous Present Perfect Simple
duration, the activity itself result, a number, a completed amount
I've been taking this tablet for a year. I've taken three tablets today.
She's been waiting since 9. She's waited three hours. (finished or counted)

State verbs stay simple: I've had this cough for a week. I've known her for years. For repeated symptoms the continuous is fine: I've been having headaches lately.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present here: ✗ I am coughing since Monday. ✓ I've been coughing since Monday.
  • Don't forget been: ✗ I have coughing. ✓ I have been coughing.

Try it. (1) How long ___ you ___ (feel) like this? (2) She ___ (wait) since 9 a.m. (3) I ___ (have) diabetes for ten years. (4) He ___ (take) four tablets so far today.

Show the answers

(1) have … been feeling (2) has been waiting (3) have had (4) has taken.

Unit 21 · Past Perfect and narrative tenses

When we use it

  • Past Perfect (had + V3): an action before another past moment: When the ambulance arrived, she had already stopped bleeding.
  • Past Perfect Continuous (had been + V-ing): an activity that continued up to a past moment: She had been feeling dizzy all morning before she fell.

Structure (Past Perfect)

Formula Example
+ S + had + V3 He had taken his insulin before lunch.
− S + had + not + V3 She hadn't eaten since breakfast.
? (Q/W) + had + S + V3? Had* you felt* dizzy before the fall?

Short answers: Yes, I had. / No, she hadn't. Short forms: I'd, she'd (here 'd = had), hadn't.

Keywords: before · after · by the time · already · when · until · by (10 a.m.).

Telling a story in order: three tenses together

Tense Job Example
Past Continuous background At 2 p.m. she was walking to the bathroom…
Past Simple main events …when she slipped and hit her head.
Past Perfect earlier events She hadn't eaten since breakfast, and she had been feeling dizzy all morning.

Watch out!

  • When before / after already show the order, the Past Simple is fine: She ate before she took the tablet.
  • ✗ She had fell. ✓ She had fallen. (use V3: see table D)

Try it. (1) By the time the doctor came, the pain ___ (stop). (2) ___ he ___ (take) anything before he came in? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) for two days before the seizure. (4) He ___ (work) for 10 hours when he collapsed.

Show the answers

(1) had stopped (2) Had … taken (3) hadn't slept (4) had been working.

Unit 22 · The passive

When we use it: when the action matters more than who did it. Very common in reports, procedures, labels and textbooks.

Structure: a form of be + V3. Add by + person only if it matters.

Tense Passive Example
Present Simple am / is / are + V3 This tablet is taken by mouth.
Present Continuous am / is / are being + V3 The dressing is being changed.
Past Simple was / were + V3 The blood pressure was recorded at 10:00.
Present Perfect have / has been + V3 Has* the dressing been changed* today?
Future will be + V3 The results will be explained by the doctor.
Modal modal + be + V3 Consent must be obtained first.
Formula Example
+ S + be + V3 The sample was sent to the lab.
− S + be + not + V3 The site has not been marked.
? (Q/W) + be + S + V3? When was the patient admitted?

Watch out!

  • Use V3, not V2: ✗ The sample was took. ✓ The sample was taken.
  • Verbs with no object have no passive: ✗ It was happened. The patient was died. ✓ It happened. The patient died. (also arrive, occur, fall)
  • Speak actively to patients: You take it by mouth. Use the passive in notes and reports.

Try it. Make passive: (1) The nurse checks the ID band. (2) Someone took the sample at 8. (3) They will remove the stitches in 10 days. (4) Has anyone told the family?

Show the answers

(1) The ID band is checked. (2) The sample was taken at 8. (3) The stitches will be removed in 10 days. (4) Has the family been told?

Unit 23 · Reported speech

When we use it: to tell someone what another person said, asked or told them to do. Essential for handoffs and notes.

Say or tell? say (something): He said he was dizzy. · tell + person: He told me he was dizzy. ✗ He said me.

Statements: move one tense back

Direct speech Reported speech
"I feel dizzy." She said she felt dizzy.
"I'm having chest pain." He said he was having chest pain.
"I took it yesterday." She said she had taken it the day before.
"I'll call you." He said he would call me.
"I can't sleep." She said she couldn't sleep.

Also change: today → that day · yesterday → the day before · tomorrow → the next day · here → there · I / my → he / his.

Questions: normal word order, no do: "Where is the toilet?" → He asked where the toilet was. · Yes/no questions use if / whether: She asked if she could eat.

Instructions: told / asked + person + (not) to + V1: The doctor told him not to drive. · Labels: The label says to take it with food.

In clinical notes the present is normal: Patient reports pain 6/10. Denies nausea. States she slept badly. For a safety concern, quote the exact words: The patient stated, "I don't see the point anymore."

Watch out!

  • ✗ He asked where is the toilet. ✓ He asked where the toilet was.
  • ✗ She told to wait. ✓ She told me to wait.

Try it. Report: (1) "I have a headache." (she) (2) "Did you take your insulin?" (the nurse asked him) (3) "Don't eat after midnight." (the doctor told her) (4) "I'll come back at 5." (he)

Show the answers

(1) She said she had a headache. (2) The nurse asked him if he had taken his insulin. (3) The doctor told her not to eat after midnight. (4) He said he would come back at 5.

Unit 24 · Conditionals: zero, first, second, third

Type Meaning If-clause Main clause Example
Zero facts, always true Present Simple Present Simple If blood sugar drops too low, people feel shaky.
First real, possible future Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction If the pain gets worse, I'll call the nurse. If you notice a fever, call the clinic.
Second unreal or unlikely, present or future Past Simple / Past Continuous would / could / might + V1 If you stopped smoking, your breathing would improve.
Third unreal past (it didn't happen) Past Perfect would / could / might + have + V3 If I had known about the allergy, I would have told the doctor.

Structure notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. If it comes first, use a comma: If it hurts, tell me. / Tell me if it hurts.
  • Negatives: If you don't take it, … · If I hadn't checked, … · … it wouldn't help.
  • Questions: What will you do if the patient refuses? What would you do if a patient shouted at you?
  • Unless = if not: Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
  • Second conditional with be: were for all persons in formal English: If I were you, I'd ask the pharmacist.

Watch out!

  • No will in the if-clause: ✗ If you will notice redness… ✓ If you notice redness…
  • No would in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known… ✓ If I had known…
  • First or second? First = it may really happen. Second = imagined: If I win the scholarship, I'll… (I applied) vs If I were the surgeon, I would… (imagined: I am a nursing student).

Try it. (1) If you ___ (feel) dizzy, sit down. (2) If she ___ (have) more time, she would study more. (3) If he ___ (call) earlier, we ___ (help) him. (4) Water ___ (boil) if you heat it to 100 °C.

Show the answers

(1) feel (2) had (3) had called … would have helped (4) boils.

Unit 25 · Question tags

When we use it: to check information you think is true. Very useful in medication reconciliation and handoffs.

Structure: positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. The tag uses the same helper verb (or do / does / did).

Sentence Tag
You take it twice a day, don't you?
You haven't eaten since midnight, have you?
She's allergic to penicillin, isn't she?
He took it this morning, didn't he?
You'll come back on Tuesday, won't you?
You can walk, can't you?
I'm next, aren't I? (special form)

Intonation: falling = you're confirming, you expect yes. Rising = a real question, you're not sure.

Answer the fact, not the tag: You don't smoke, do you? – No, I don't. (= I don't smoke)

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often use one tag for everything: ✗ You take it twice a day, isn't it? ✓ …, don't you?
  • Match the tense: ✗ He took it, doesn't he? ✓ …, didn't he?

Try it. (1) You live alone, ___? (2) She hasn't had surgery, ___? (3) It was this morning, ___? (4) You'll call us, ___?

Show the answers

(1) don't you (2) has she (3) wasn't it (4) won't you.

Unit 26 · Hedging and deduction

When we use it: to show how sure we are. Nurses report facts carefully and never sound more certain than they are.

Possibility: may, might, could + V1

  • This medicine may cause drowsiness. (labels, leaflets)
  • The change might be important. I'll tell the nurse.
  • Her symptoms could be related to the new tablet. (in a discussion with the team, not a diagnosis for the patient)

Deduction: how sure am I?

Certainty Present Past Example
sure it's true must + V1 / be must have + V3 You must be exhausted. She must have fallen.
possible may / might / could + V1 may / might / could have + V3 He might be in pain. She could have missed a dose.
sure it's not true can't + V1 / be can't have + V3 That can't be easy. He can't have taken it: the box is full.

Appearance verbs (observations, not conclusions): He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. She seems to be in pain. He looks pale.

Softening words: possibly, probably, likely, approximately, about, around, tends to.

Watch out!

  • No to after modals: ✗ He must to be tired. ✓ He must be tired.
  • maybe (adverb) vs may be (verb): Maybe it's the medicine. = *It may be* the medicine.
  • ✗ She seems is tired. ✓ She seems tired / seems to be tired.

Try it. (1) You've worked 12 hours. You ___ be tired. (2) The box is full. She ___ have taken any tablets. (3) Her fever ___ come back tonight, so check it at 10 p.m. (4) He ___ (appear) confused.

Show the answers

(1) must (2) can't (3) may / might (4) appears.

Unit 27 · Other future forms

When we use it

Form Structure Use Example
Future Continuous will be + V-ing in progress at a future time At 10 tomorrow you'll be having your MRI.
Future Perfect will have + V3 finished before a future time By Friday you will have finished the antibiotics.
Future Perfect Continuous will have been + V-ing duration up to a future time By June I will have been studying English for two years.
be about to am / is / are about to + V1 very near future The doctor is about to see you.
be due to am / is / are due to + V1 scheduled The doctor is due to see you at 10.

Negatives and questions follow will: She won't have finished by then. Will you be working tomorrow night?

Keywords: by (Friday) · by the time · before · for (two years) · this time tomorrow · at (10) tomorrow.

The future seen from the past (reported speech): will → would, am going to → was going to: She said she would call. I was going to phone you, but…

Watch out!

  • ✗ By Friday you will finish. (when the point is already done by then) ✓ By Friday you will have finished.
  • After by the time use the present: ✗ by the time the doctor will arrive ✓ by the time the doctor arrives**.

Try it. (1) This time tomorrow she ___ (have) her operation. (2) By 2028 she ___ (graduate). (3) The ambulance ___ (about / arrive). (4) By March he ___ (work) here for a year.

Show the answers

(1) will be having (2) will have graduated (3) is about to arrive (4) will have been working.

Unit 1 · Grammar words and the alphabet

Grammar words used in this handbook

Term What it is Example

Tense names. Each tense has two names; both are correct. Simple = Indefinite · Continuous = Progressive · Perfect · Perfect Continuous. Each one exists in the Present, Past and Future: 12 tenses in total (see Reference table A).

The alphabet: 26 letters

  • 5 vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u.
  • 21 consonant letters. Y can work as a consonant (yes) or a vowel (happy, dizzy).

Learn the letter names in sound groups. It makes spelling names on the phone much easier.

Sound Letters
"ay" (as in day) A H J K
"ee" (as in see) B C D E G P T V Z
"eh" (as in bed) F L M N S X
"eye" I Y
"oh" O
"you" Q U W
"ar" R

In the USA, Z is "zee"; in the UK it is "zed".

Watch out!

  • A, E, I are the most confused: A = "ay", E = "ee", I = "eye".
  • G ("jee") and J ("jay") are often swapped.
  • W is "double-u". For two of the same letter together, say "double": Anna → A-double N-A; Rassul → R-A-double S-U-L.

Try it. Spell aloud: (1) Karimova (2) Yusupov (3) ECG (4) Jasur.

Show the answers

(1) K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A (2) Y-U-S-U-P-O-V (3) E-C-G ("ee-see-jee") (4) J-A-S-U-R (J = "jay").

Unit 2 · Nouns: singular and plural

When we use it: one thing = singular (a tablet); two or more = plural (two tablets).

Rule Ending Examples
Most nouns + -s nurse → nurses · bed → beds · lung → lungs
Ends in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x + -es bus → buses · glass → glasses · dish → dishes · patch → patches · box → boxes
Some nouns in -o + -es potato → potatoes · tomato → tomatoes (but photo → photos)
Consonant + y y → -ies artery → arteries · injury → injuries · baby → babies
Vowel + y + -s day → days · X-ray → X-rays · boy → boys
Ends in -f / -fe f → -ves half → halves · knife → knives · life → lives · wife → wives
Irregular new form man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · mouse → mice
No change same form sheep · fish · deer · series · species
Latin / Greek (common in medicine) special diagnosis → diagnoses · bacterium → bacteria · vertebra → vertebrae · criterion → criteria · nucleus → nuclei

Watch out!

  • After a number, English always needs the plural. Uzbek speakers often keep the noun singular after a number: ✗ three tablet. ✓ three tablets, two days, 5 milligrams.
  • People is already plural: ✓ People are waiting. ✗ peoples.
  • Uncountable nouns have no plural: ✗ informations, advices, equipments (see Unit 17).
  • One child, two children; one foot, two feet: say these correctly in body and family vocabulary.

Try it. Make plural: (1) knee (2) diagnosis (3) child (4) injury.

Show the answers

(1) knees (2) diagnoses (3) children (4) injuries.

Unit 3 · Articles: a, an, the

When we use it

  • a / an = one, not a specific one; the first time we mention it: There's a patient in room 4.
  • the = a specific one that we both know; the second mention; something unique: The patient in room 4 is asleep. The heart pumps blood.
  • No article for plural or uncountable nouns in general: Nurses work long shifts. Blood carries oxygen.

A or an? It depends on the first sound, not the first letter.

an (vowel sound) a (consonant sound)
an apple, an injection a patient, a nurse
an hour (silent h) a hospital (h is heard)
an X-ray ("ex") a unit ("you")
an MRI ("em"), an ECG ("ee") a uniform, a European ("you")

Fixed phrases (no article): by mouth, at home, at work, go to bed, on duty. In the USA: in the hospital (UK: in hospital).

Watch out!

  • Uzbek has no articles, so learners drop them. ✗ She is nurse. ✓ She is a nurse. ✗ Patient is in room 5. ✓ The patient is in room 5.
  • Jobs always take a/an: I want to be a nurse. He is an anesthetist.
  • Don't use the with names: ✗ the Dr. Lee.

Try it. Add a, an or the: (1) I have ___ appointment. (2) She needs ___ MRI. (3) ___ pharmacy is on the first floor. (4) He works in ___ hospital in Ohio.

Show the answers

(1) an (2) an (3) The (4) a.

Unit 4 · Pronouns and possessives

Subject Object Possessive adjective Possessive pronoun Reflexive
I me my mine myself
you you your yours yourself
he him his his himself
she her her hers herself
it it its — itself
we us our ours ourselves
they them their theirs themselves

She gave him her card. The card is hers. She did it herself.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often mix up he and she, because Uzbek uses one word for he, she and it. In English you must choose. ✗ Mrs. Karimova says he has pain. ✓ She says she has pain. In a report, a wrong pronoun can mean the wrong patient.
  • its (possessive) vs it's (= it is): The heart and its valves. It's beating fast.
  • their (possessive) · there (place) · they're (= they are).
  • Use they for one person when you don't know or don't need the gender: If a patient feels dizzy, they should sit down.
  • Body parts take a possessive: ✓ Lift your arm. ✗ Lift the arm (sounds like an object, not their own arm).

Try it. (1) This is Mr. Saidov. ___ wife is here. (2) Mrs. Karimova says ___ head hurts. (3) Please give ___ (we) the chart. (4) The bag is ___ (she).

Show the answers

(1) His (2) her (3) us (4) hers.

Ordinal numbers (first, second, third): add -th, except numbers ending in 1, 2 or 3 (1st, 22nd, 33rd); 11th, 12th and 13th take -th.

1st first 2nd second 3rd third 4th fourth 5th fifth
8th eighth 9th ninth 12th twelfth 20th twentieth 21st twenty-first

Spelling changes: eight → eighth, five → fifth, nine → ninth, twelve → twelfth, twenty → twentieth.

Saying numbers in healthcare

Written Say Note
