Prepositions of time: at 10:30, at night · on Monday, on March 12 · in March, in 2025, in the morning.

Watch out!

  • Decimal point vs comma. In Uzbekistan 37,5 is a decimal; in the USA a comma separates thousands. ✓ 37.5 (thirty-seven point five) · 1,200 (one thousand two hundred).
  • US dates: 04/07 is April 7, not 4 July. Always say the month as a word when you check.
  • Teen/ty: if in doubt, ask Did you say thirteen or thirty? or say the digits: "one-three".

Try it. Say aloud: (1) 15 (2) 38.2 °C (3) 11/30/2001 (4) 18:45.

Show the answers

(1) fif-TEEN (2) thirty-eight point two degrees (3) November thirtieth, two thousand one (4) eighteen forty-five / a quarter to seven p.m.

Unit 6 · To be (am, is, are · was, were · will be)

When we use it: to say what or who someone is, how they are, where they are, and their age.

Present Past Future
I am I was I will be
he / she / it is he / she / it was he / she / it will be
you / we / they are you / we / they were you / we / they will be

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + noun / adjective / place I am a nursing student. The patient is in room 5.
− S + am / is / are + not + … She is not dizzy. They are not in the ward.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + …? Is he awake? Where is the pharmacy?

Short answers: Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. ✗ Yes, she's. (no short form in a yes short answer)

Short forms: I'm · you're · he's / she's / it's · we're · they're. Negative: isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't, won't be. With I: ✓ I'm not ✗ I amn't.

Use one short form only: ✓ He's not or ✓ He isn't, never ✗ He'sn't.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often leave out am / is / are: ✗ I nurse. ✗ She very tired. ✓ I am a nurse. She is very tired.
  • Don't add be to other verbs: ✗ I am agree. I am live in Ohio. ✓ I agree. I live in Ohio.
  • Age uses be: ✓ I am 25. ✗ I have 25 years.
  • Feelings with adjectives use be: I am cold, hungry, afraid, worried.
  • I am to do means a plan or an order (You are to stay in bed), not the normal present. For now, use I do or I'm doing.
  • You will hear ain't (= am not / isn't / aren't) in informal US speech. Understand it; never use it at work.

Try it. (1) The doctor ___ busy now. (2) We ___ at work yesterday. (3) ___ you allergic to anything? (4) He ___ (not) in pain.

Show the answers

(1) is (2) were (3) Are (4) isn't / is not.

Unit 7 · Have / have got

When we use it: to talk about possession, family, conditions and symptoms. I have diabetes. She has a fever. I've got a cough.

Have (all English, especially American)

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + noun She has a rash.
− S + do / does + not + have + noun He doesn't have any allergies.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + have + …? Do* you have* any pain?

Have got (spoken, especially British; present only)

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + got + noun I've got a headache.
− S + have / has + not + got + noun She hasn't got a temperature.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + got + …? Has* he got* his insurance card?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't. (have) · Yes, I have. / No, he hasn't. (have got)

Short forms: I've got, she's got (here 's = has). With plain have, don't shorten: ✓ I have a cough ✗ I've a cough.

Past: had for everyone: She had surgery in 2015. Did you have a fever? (no had got)

Have as an action: have breakfast, have a shower, have surgery, have a test. Here have can be continuous: She's having an X-ray now. ✗ She's having diabetes.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She have a fever. ✓ She has a fever. ✗ Does she has…? ✓ Does she have…?
  • Uzbek speakers often build have as "at me is": ✗ At me is a pain. ✓ I have a pain.
  • In US clinics ask Do you have…? ✗ Have you any allergies? sounds old-fashioned.

Try it. (1) ___ you ___ any children? (2) He ___ (not) a temperature. (3) She ___ got a cough. (4) They ___ an appointment last week.

Show the answers

(1) Do … have (2) doesn't have / hasn't got (3) has (4) had.

Unit 8 · There is / there are and prepositions of place

When we use it: to say that something exists or is in a place: There is a cut on his hand. There are two wounds.

Formula Example
+ There is + singular / uncountable · There are + plural There is some drainage. There are three patients in the waiting area.
− There isn't a / any … · There aren't any … There isn't any swelling. There aren't any beds.
? Is there a / any …? · Are there any …? Is there* any redness? Are there* any visitors?

Short answers: Yes, there is. / No, there aren't. Short form: there's (= there is). Past: there was / there were.

Prepositions of place

Preposition Example
in pain in the abdomen (inside)
on a rash on the arm (surface)
at at the front desk
above / below the cut is just above the knee
next to / between the elbow is between the shoulder and the wrist
behind / in front of the kidneys are behind the intestines
on the left / right side of swelling on the left side of the neck

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often put the place first and leave out there is: ✗ In room 5 is a patient. ✓ There is a patient in room 5.
  • Match the noun: ✗ There is two wounds. ✓ There are two wounds.
  • Don't use it has for existence: ✗ It has a cut on his hand. ✓ There is a cut on his hand. / He has a cut on his hand.

Try it. (1) ___ any blood in the urine? (2) ___ two pills on the table. (3) The pain is ___ my lower back. (4) There ___ (not) any visitors yesterday.

Show the answers

(1) Is there (2) There are (3) in (4) weren't.

Unit 9 · Present Simple (Present Indefinite)

When we use it

  • Habits and repeated actions: She takes insulin every morning.
  • Schedules and timetables: Visiting hours start at 2 p.m.
  • Facts and general truths: The heart pumps blood.
  • States: I feel dizzy. He knows his medicines.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V1 (he / she / it + -s) I check my sugar daily. She checks her sugar daily.
− S + do / does + not + V1 I don't smoke. He doesn't drink alcohol.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + V1? Do* you take any vitamins? How often does* she use her inhaler?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

He / she / it spelling: take → takes · wash → washes · cry → cries · go → goes · do → does · have → has.

Pronouncing -s: "s" in takes, checks · "z" in feels, needs · "iz" in washes, uses.

Keywords: every (day, morning, week) · always · usually · often · sometimes · occasionally · rarely · seldom · never · once / twice a day · from time to time.

Word order: frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be: She always takes it at night. He is often dizzy.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She take insulin. ✓ She takes insulin.
  • Only one -s: ✗ Does she takes…? ✓ Does she take…?
  • ✗ He don't smoke. ✓ He doesn't smoke.

Try it. (1) My mother ___ (have) diabetes. (2) ___ he ___ (use) his inhaler every day? (3) I ___ (not / drink) coffee. (4) The kidneys ___ (filter) the blood.

Show the answers

(1) has (2) Does … use (3) don't drink (4) filter.

Unit 10 · Present Continuous (Present Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action happening now: The patient is sleeping.
  • A temporary situation around now: I'm studying English this year.
  • A fixed plan for the future: She's having surgery on Monday.
  • An annoying repeated habit, with always: He's always pulling at his IV.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + V-ing My heart is beating fast.
− S + am / is / are + not + V-ing She isn't eating today.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + V-ing? Are* you having* trouble breathing?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.

Here be is a helper. I am a nurse (here am is the main verb) vs I am working (am only builds the tense).

-ing spelling: take → taking · sit → sitting · lie → lying · breathe → breathing.

Keywords: now · right now · at the moment · currently · today · this week · these days · still.

State verbs are not normally continuous: know, want, need, believe, understand, like, hate, seem, belong. ✗ I am knowing. ✓ I know. Feel and hurt can be both: My back hurts / is hurting.

Simple or continuous? He takes insulin every day (habit) · He's taking his insulin now (at this moment).

Watch out!

  • Don't drop be: ✗ She sleeping. ✓ She is sleeping.
  • ✗ I am needing water. ✓ I need water.

Try it. (1) Be quiet: the baby ___ (sleep). (2) ___ you ___ (take) any medicine at the moment? (3) She ___ (not / breathe) normally. (4) I ___ (understand) the instructions.

Show the answers

(1) is sleeping (2) Are … taking (3) isn't breathing (4) understand.

Unit 11 · Past Simple (Past Indefinite)

When we use it: a finished action at a finished time in the past, with no link to now. She fell yesterday. He had surgery in 2015.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V2 (regular: -ed; irregular: see table D) The pain started on Sunday. I took a tablet.
− S + did + not + V1 She didn't vomit.
? (Q/W) + did + S + V1? When did it start? Did you fall?

Short answers: Yes, she did. / No, I didn't.

-ed spelling: start → started · stop → stopped · cry → cried · use → used.

Pronouncing -ed: "t" in stopped, checked · "d" in called, used · "id" in started, needed.

Keywords: yesterday · ago · last (night, week, year) · in 2019 · at 3 a.m. · on Monday · when.

Watch out!

  • After did, use V1: ✗ Did you took it? ✓ Did you take it? ✗ She didn't came. ✓ She didn't come.
  • Ago goes after the time: ✓ three days ago ✗ ago three days.
  • With a finished time, don't use the Present Perfect: ✗ I have taken it yesterday. ✓ I took it yesterday.

Try it. (1) The pain ___ (begin) two days ago. (2) ___ you ___ (eat) breakfast? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) well last night. (4) He ___ (break) his wrist in 2019.

Show the answers

(1) began (2) Did … eat (3) didn't sleep (4) broke.

Unit 12 · Present Perfect

When we use it

  • A past action with a result now: I'm full. I have eaten. (Compare: I ate pasta yesterday: past only.)
  • Experience in life (any time until now): Have* you ever had* surgery?
  • A situation from the past until now: I've had this cough for three days.
  • Something just finished: The doctor has just left.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + V3 She has taken her tablets.
− S + have / has + not + V3 We haven't finished yet.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + V3? Have* you checked* your sugar today?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's / she's (here 's = has), haven't, hasn't.

Keywords: just · already · yet (in − and ?) · ever · never · recently · so far · today · this week · for · since.

For or since? for + a length of time: for three days, for a week · since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since this morning.

Present Perfect or Past Simple? Ask about life with the Present Perfect; give the details with the Past Simple: Have you ever had surgery? – Yes, I had my appendix out in 2015.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present for since: ✗ I am here since Monday. ✓ I've been here since Monday.
  • ✗ for Monday ✓ since Monday · ✗ since three days ✓ for three days.
  • No finished time: ✗ I have seen the doctor yesterday. ✓ I saw the doctor yesterday.

Try it. (1) She ___ (have) a headache since this morning. (2) ___ you ever ___ (be) in hospital? (3) I ___ (not / take) my insulin yet. (4) He ___ (work) here for two years.

Show the answers

(1) has had (2) Have … been (3) haven't taken (4) has worked.

Unit 13 · Questions

Question words

Word Asks about Example
What thing, information What brings you in today?
Where place Where does it hurt?
When time When did it start?
Who person Who is your doctor?
Which a choice Which arm is it?
Why reason Why did you stop the tablets?
How way, condition How are you feeling?
How long duration How long have you had it?
How often frequency How often do you use your inhaler?

Word order: Q-A-S-V. (Q/W) + Auxiliary + Subject + main Verb: When did the pain start? How long have you been here?

Subject questions (the question word is the subject) have no do/does/did: Who called the ambulance? ✗ Who did call…?

Indirect (polite) questions: Could you tell me / Do you know + (Q/W) + S + V (normal order, no do): Could you tell me where the pharmacy is? Do you know when it started? ✗ Could you tell me where is the pharmacy?

Open and closed questions. Closed (Do you have pain?) gets yes/no. Open (Tell me about the pain) gets the story. Start interviews with open questions.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often make a question with intonation only. In English, use the helper verb: ✗ You have pain? ✓ Do you have pain?
  • Keep the helper before the subject: ✗ Where it hurts? ✓ Where does it hurt?

Try it. Make questions: (1) (how long / you / have / this cough) (2) (where / the pain / be) (3) (who / take / your blood pressure) (4) Could you tell me (when / the doctor / come)?

Show the answers

(1) How long have you had this cough? (2) Where is the pain? (3) Who took your blood pressure? (4) Could you tell me when the doctor is coming / will come?

Unit 14 · The future: will, going to, present continuous

When we use it

Form Use Example
will a decision now; a promise; an offer I'll get the nurse. I'll come back in 10 minutes.
will a prediction or a fact about the future The test will take about 30 minutes.
will realistic hopes and fears I hope I'll pass. I'm afraid it will hurt.
going to a plan decided before now I'm going to apply to nursing school.
going to a prediction from what we see now She's very pale. She's going to faint.
present continuous a fixed arrangement You're having an MRI tomorrow at 3.

Structure (will)

Formula Example
+ S + will + V1 The doctor will explain the results.
− S + will not (won't) + V1 It won't hurt.
? (Q/W) + will + S + V1? When will I get the results?

Structure (going to): S + am / is / are + going to + V1. He's going to stay overnight.

Short answers: Yes, it will. / No, it won't. · Short forms: I'll, you'll, she'll, won't.

Shall is used with I / we for offers and suggestions: Shall I call the nurse?

Keywords: tomorrow · the day after tomorrow · next (week, month) · in two days · soon · later · tonight · this afternoon.

Watch out!

  • No to after will: ✗ I will to call. ✓ I will call.
  • After when, before, after, if, until use the present, not will: ✗ When the doctor will come, I'll tell her. ✓ When the doctor comes, I'll tell her.

Try it. (1) Wait, I ___ (help) you. (2) Look at the IV bag: it ___ (run out) soon. (3) We ___ (meet) the surgeon at 9 tomorrow. (4) I'll call you when the results ___ (come).

Show the answers

(1) 'll help (2) 's going to run out (3) 're meeting (4) come.

Unit 15 · Modal verbs

Modal Meaning Example
can / can't ability; permission Can you move your fingers? You can't eat before the test.
could polite request; past ability Could you spell that, please? I couldn't sleep.
may formal permission; possibility May I help you stand up? It may cause drowsiness.
should / shouldn't advice, the right thing You should rest. You shouldn't drive today.
must / mustn't strong rule; mustn't = it is forbidden You must sign the form. You mustn't eat after midnight.
have to obligation (often from a rule) You have to fast for 8 hours.
don't have to / don't need to it is not necessary You don't have to fast for this test.
need to it is necessary I need to check your blood pressure.

Structure: S + modal + V1. No to, no -s, no do.

Formula Example
+ S + modal + V1 She should take it with food.
− S + modal + not + V1 You mustn't drink alcohol with this.
? (Q/W) + modal + S + V1? Can* I have* some water?

Have to and need to behave like normal verbs: Do* I have to fast? She doesn't need to* come back.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She cans walk. ✓ She can walk. · ✗ You must to sign. ✓ You must sign.
  • mustn't ≠ don't have to. You mustn't eat = eating is forbidden. You don't have to eat = you can if you want.
  • In nursing, should sounds like advice. Report the clinician's advice: The doctor says you should rest.

Try it. (1) ___ I open the window? (2) You ___ bring anything; we have everything. (3) You ___ smoke in the hospital. (4) She ___ (not / can) sleep last night.

Show the answers

(1) May / Can / Could (2) don't have to / don't need to (3) mustn't / can't (4) couldn't.

Unit 16 · Comparatives and describing change

Adjective Comparative Superlative
short: high, low, fast higher, lower, faster the highest
ends in one vowel + consonant: big, hot bigger, hotter the biggest
ends in -y: easy, heavy easier, heavier the easiest
long: painful, comfortable more painful the most painful
irregular: good, bad, far better, worse, further the best, the worst, the furthest

Comparing: higher than this morning · not as high as yesterday · the same as before.

Describing change

Up Down No change
go up, rise, increase go down, fall, drop, decrease stay the same, remain stable

His heart rate has gone up from 74 to 96. (start and end) · It increased by 22. (the difference) · There was a drop in oxygen saturation. (noun)

Watch out!

  • ✗ more higher ✓ higher · ✗ higher that ✓ higher than**.
  • ✗ from 74 until 96 ✓ from 74 to 96.
  • by = the amount of change; to = the new value.

Try it. (1) Her pain is ___ (bad) than yesterday. (2) This is the ___ (comfortable) chair. (3) The temperature rose ___ 36.8 ___ 38.3. (4) His weight dropped ___ 3 kg.

Show the answers

(1) worse (2) most comfortable (3) from … to (4) by.

Unit 17 · Countable and uncountable; how much / how many

Countable (a / an, plural) Uncountable (no a / an, no plural)
a tablet, two tablets water, blood, urine, sputum
a meal, three meals food, information, advice, equipment
a symptom, symptoms pain (in general), weight, sleep
a bottle, a glass, a cup medicine (the substance), insulin, oxygen

Amounts

With countable (plural) With uncountable
How many tablets? How much water?
a few days a little pain
many (questions, negatives) much (questions, negatives)
a lot of / lots of / some / any a lot of / lots of / some / any

some in + sentences and offers; any in − and ?: Would you like some water? Do you have any allergies? I don't take any medicines.

Making uncountables countable: a glass of water, a cup of tea, a piece of advice, 500 mL of fluid, a dose of insulin.

Pain can be both: Pain is common after surgery (general) / I have a sharp pain here (one specific pain).

Watch out!

  • ✗ informations, advices, equipments · ✗ an advice ✓ some advice / a piece of advice.
  • ✗ How much tablets? ✓ How many tablets?

Try it. (1) How ___ glasses of water do you drink? (2) How ___ alcohol do you drink a week? (3) I have ___ questions. (4) She ate only ___ food.

Show the answers

(1) many (2) much (3) a few / some (4) a little.

Unit 18 · Relative clauses: who, which, where

When we use it: to say which person, thing or place we mean, or to add information.

Word For Example
who people A pharmacist is someone who prepares medicines.
which things This is the tablet which helps your blood pressure.
that people or things (defining only) The nurse that helped me was kind.
where places The ED is the place where urgent patients go.
when times Morning is the time when I check my sugar.
whose possession The patient whose daughter called is in room 5.

Defining (no commas): tells us which one. The nurse who looked after me was kind.

Non-defining (commas): adds extra information; never that. Mr. Saidov, who is 66, has diabetes.

Leaving out who / which / that: possible when it is the object: The tablet (that) you took is for pain. Not possible when it is the subject: ✗ The nurse helped me was kind.

Watch out!

  • ✗ the man which ✓ the man who · ✗ the pharmacy who ✓ the pharmacy **which / where.
  • No extra pronoun: ✗ The patient who he has diabetes… ✓ The patient who has diabetes…
  • Uzbek speakers often put the description before the noun: ✗ the has-diabetes patient. English puts it after: the patient who has diabetes.

Try it. (1) A physician is a doctor ___ treats patients. (2) The lab is the place ___ samples are tested. (3) This is the inhaler ___ I use every day. (4) My mother, ___ is 60, has hypertension.

Show the answers

(1) who (2) where (3) which / that / (nothing) (4) who.

Part 3 · C1 Professional

Unit 28 · Discourse markers

When we use it: to show how ideas connect in lectures, presentations, essays and seminars.

Function Spoken / neutral Written / formal
Adding also, and, plus furthermore, moreover, in addition
Contrasting but, though however, in contrast, whereas, nevertheless, on the other hand
Cause because, since, as due to (+ noun), owing to
Result so therefore, consequently, as a result
Sequencing first, then, after that, finally firstly, secondly, subsequently, lastly
Example like, for example for instance, such as, to illustrate
Emphasis especially, the main thing is in particular, notably, the key point is
Conceding OK, but admittedly, while it is true that
Summarizing so, basically to sum up, in summary, overall

Grammar of linkers

  • However, Therefore, Consequently start a new sentence and take a comma: Hand hygiene prevents infection. However, it is often forgotten.
  • although, whereas, because join two clauses: Although she was in pain, she walked to the bathroom.
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite* the pain, she walked. Despite feeling* dizzy, she walked.
  • due to + noun: …due to time pressure (✗ due to people are busy).

Watch out!

  • ✗ Although she was tired, but she worked. Use one linker: ✓ Although she was tired, she worked.
  • ✗ despite of ✓ despite / in spite of.
  • Moreover in a conversation sounds like a lecture. Match the register.

Try it. (1) The test is painless. ___, it takes an hour. (2) ___ the noise, he slept well. (3) She missed her insulin; ___, her sugar rose. (4) ___ the leaflet is short, it is hard to read.

Show the answers

(1) However (2) Despite / In spite of (3) consequently / as a result (4) Although.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.

Try it. (1) She stopped ___ (smoke) last year. (2) The ___ (break) arm needs an X-ray. (3) The patient ___ (sit) by the window is Mr. Rakhimov. (4) The news was ___ (worry), so the family was ___ (worry).

Show the answers

(1) smoking (2) broken (3) sitting (4) worrying … worried.

Unit 31 · Cleft sentences and emphasis

When we use it: to put the most important information first, to prioritize in a summary, or to correct someone politely.

Pattern Structure Example
What-cleft What + S + V + is / was + focus What concerns me most is the new sore on her foot.
It-cleft It is / was + focus + that / who + rest It's* the evening doses that* he misses.
The thing / reason The thing that… / The reason (why)… + is (that) The reason* she stopped is that* the tablets are expensive.
All All + S + V + is All she needs is a little more time.

Correcting politely: It wasn't the morning dose she missed; it was the evening one.

Watch out!

  • No extra it: ✗ What concerns me most it is the sore. ✓ What concerns me most is the sore.
  • Keep the order: ✗ Is the evening dose that he misses. ✓ It's the evening dose that he misses.

Try it. Rewrite with emphasis: (1) The cost worries her. (What…) (2) He missed the Tuesday appointment. (It was…) (3) She needs a social worker. (What…) (4) She stopped because of the side effects. (The reason…)

Show the answers

(1) What worries her is the cost. (2) It was the Tuesday appointment that he missed. (3) What she needs is a social worker. (4) The reason (why) she stopped is (that) she had side effects.

Unit 32 · Tentative and diplomatic language

When we use it: to make suggestions to seniors, to disagree in a seminar, and to ask sensitive questions without pressure.

Function Phrases
Polite requests I was wondering whether… Would it be possible to…? Would you mind + V-ing?
Suggestions to the team Could we consider…? Would it be worth + V-ing…? It might be helpful to…
Sensitive questions I was wondering if you could tell me a bit about… What gets in the way of…?
Disagreeing I see it slightly differently. While I take your point,… I'm not sure I agree, because…
Not knowing I'm not sure, but I think… As far as I know,… I'd need to check.

Why the past tense sounds polite: I was wondering and I wanted to ask talk about now, but the past form adds distance and sounds less direct.

Softeners: a bit, slightly, perhaps, possibly, just (Could I just check…?).

But not for safety. When a patient may be harmed, be clear and firm (CUS): I'm concerned. I'm uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.

Watch out!

  • ✗ Would you mind to wait? ✓ Would you mind waiting?
  • Over-softening in an emergency causes delay: ✗ I was wondering whether you might possibly come… ✓ I need you to come now.

Try it. Make more tentative: (1) Book an interpreter. (2) You're wrong. (3) Can I ask about your alcohol use? (4) Review his pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) Could we consider booking an interpreter? (2) I see it slightly differently. (3) I was wondering if I could ask about your alcohol use. (4) Would it be worth reviewing his pain relief?

Unit 33 · Mixed and formal conditionals

Mixed conditionals

Type If-clause Main clause Example
past cause → present result Past Perfect would + V1 If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be in hospital now.
present situation → past result Past Simple would have + V3 If he weren't so afraid of needles, he would have had the test last week.

Formal inversion (leaflets, letters, academic writing): drop if and invert.

  • Should you notice any redness, contact the clinic. (= If you notice…)
  • Had I known about the allergy, I would have said so. (= If I had known…)
  • Were the patient to refuse, the team would discuss alternatives. (= If the patient refused…)

Other ways to say if

Word Meaning Example
unless if not Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
provided that / as long as only if You can go home as long as someone stays with you.
in case as a precaution (≠ if) Take your inhaler in case you need it.
otherwise if not, then… Keep the dressing dry; otherwise it may get infected.
supposing / what if imagining What if the results are positive?

Watch out!

  • in case ≠ if: Take your inhaler in case you get wheezy (take it with you now anyway) vs Use your inhaler if you get wheezy (only when it happens).
  • No would after if in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known…

Try it. (1) If I ___ (study) harder last year, I ___ (be) in nursing school now. (2) ___ you have any questions, please call. (3) Bring water ___ the wait is long. (4) You can drive ___ you don't feel drowsy.

Show the answers

(1) had studied … would be (2) Should (3) in case (4) as long as / provided that.

Unit 34 · Academic grammar: reporting verbs and the passive

When we use it: in summaries, care-plan rationales, essays and reflections.

Reporting verbs, from weak to strong

Strength Verbs Example
tentative suggests, indicates, implies The research suggests that lifestyle change can delay onset.
neutral states, reports, describes, notes The textbook states that…
strong shows, demonstrates, confirms, establishes The study demonstrates a clear link…
arguing argues, claims, maintains The author argues that…

The academic passive and impersonal structures

  • It is recommended that patients… It has been shown that…
  • Patients are advised to… Pressure injuries are associated with…
  • There is evidence* that… There is* a need for…

Tenses in academic writing

  • Present Simple for general facts and what a source says: Hand hygiene reduces infection. The author argues…
  • Past Simple for a specific study: The study found that…
  • Present Perfect for research up to now: Several studies have shown…

Style: no contractions (does not, not doesn't); avoid I think in essays (reflections are the exception: they use I); hedge claims (appears to, is likely to, may contribute to).

Watch out!

  • Too strong: ✗ This proves that… ✓ This suggests that…
  • Copying the source's sentence with small changes is plagiarism. Paraphrase fully and cite.

Try it. Make it academic: (1) Lots of studies show exercise helps. (2) Doctors say patients should check their feet. (3) I think the patient didn't understand. (4) This proves the leaflet works.

Show the answers

(1) Several studies have shown that exercise is beneficial. (2) Patients are advised to check their feet daily. (3) The patient appeared not to understand. (4) This suggests that the leaflet is effective.

Reference tables

A · All 12 tenses: structure (verb: take)

Present

Tense + − ?
Simple I take · she takes I don't take · she doesn't take Do you take? · Does she take?
Continuous I am taking · she is taking I'm not taking · she isn't taking Are you taking? · Is she taking?
Perfect I have taken · she has taken I haven't taken · she hasn't taken Have you taken? · Has she taken?
Perfect Continuous I have been taking I haven't been taking Have you been taking?

Past

Tense + − ?
Simple I took I didn't take Did you take?
Continuous I was taking · they were taking I wasn't taking · they weren't taking Were you taking?
Perfect I had taken I hadn't taken Had you taken?
Perfect Continuous I had been taking I hadn't been taking Had you been taking?

Future

Tense + − ?
Simple I will take I won't take Will you take?
Continuous I will be taking I won't be taking Will you be taking?
Perfect I will have taken I won't have taken Will you have taken?
Perfect Continuous I will have been taking I won't have been taking Will you have been taking?

The pattern: Continuous always has be + V-ing. Perfect always has have + V3. Perfect Continuous has both: have been + V-ing.

B · When we use each tense

Tense Main uses Example
Present Simple habits; schedules; facts; states She takes insulin every morning.
Present Continuous happening now; temporary; fixed plans; annoying habits (always) He's sleeping now.
Present Perfect past action with a result now; life experience; up to now (for / since) I've already taken it.
Present Perfect Continuous activity from the past until now, focus on duration; recent activity with a visible result I've been coughing for a week.
Past Simple finished action at a finished time; a sequence of events She fell yesterday.
Past Continuous in progress at a past moment; background; interrupted by a short action She was walking when she fell.
Past Perfect earlier than another past moment She had eaten before the test.
Past Perfect Continuous duration up to a past moment She had been feeling dizzy all morning.
Future Simple (will) decisions now; promises; predictions; realistic hopes and fears; facts about the future I'll call the nurse.
Future Continuous in progress at a future moment This time tomorrow you'll be having surgery.
Future Perfect finished by a future moment By Friday you'll have finished the antibiotics.
Future Perfect Continuous duration up to a future moment By June I'll have been studying for two years.

C · Time keywords

Simple Continuous Perfect Perfect Continuous
Present every…, always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom, never, once / twice a…, from time to time, generally now, right now, at the moment, at present, currently, these days, today, this week, still just, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, today, this week, for, since for, since, how long, all day, all week, lately, recently
Past yesterday, ago, last…, in (2019), at (3 a.m.), on (Monday), when while, as, when, at (3 a.m.) yesterday, all night, at that moment before, after, by (10 a.m.), by the time, already, when for, since, before, until, by the time, all morning
Future tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, next…, in (two days), soon, later, some day, tonight this time tomorrow, at (10) tomorrow, all day tomorrow by (Friday), by the time, before for, by (June), by the time

D · Irregular verbs for healthcare

V1 V2 V3 Example
be was / were been Have you been in hospital before?
become became become It became worse at night.
begin began begun The pain began on Sunday.
bleed bled bled The cut bled for 10 minutes.
break broke broken She broke her wrist.
bring brought brought Have you brought your medicines?
come came come He came in by ambulance.
cut cut cut I cut my hand on glass.
do did done Have you done the test?
drink drank drunk She hasn't drunk anything today.
drive drove driven Who drove you here?
eat ate eaten Have you eaten since midnight?
fall fell fallen He fell in the bathroom.
feel felt felt I felt dizzy.
forget forgot forgotten I forgot my insulin.
get got got (US: gotten) It's gotten worse.
give gave given The nurse gave him pain relief.
go went gone The swelling has gone down.
have had had She had surgery in 2018.
hold held held Hold your breath.
hurt hurt hurt My back hurt all night.
keep kept kept Keep the dressing dry.
know knew known I've known her for years.
leave left left The doctor has just left.
lie (down) lay lain She lay in bed all day.
lose lost lost He lost consciousness.
put put put Put the needle in the sharps container.
say said said She said she felt sick.
see saw seen Has the doctor seen you?
shake shook shaken Shake well before use.
sleep slept slept I haven't slept well.
swell swelled swollen My ankle is swollen.
take took taken Have you taken your tablets?
tell told told She told me about the pain.
throw (up) threw thrown He threw up twice.
understand understood understood Have you understood the instructions?
wake (up) woke woken I woke up at 3 a.m.
wear wore worn Please wear a mask.
write wrote written I've written it down.

Watch out: lie (lie, lay, lain) = be in a flat position: Lie down, please. · lay (lay, laid, laid) = put something down: Lay the patient on her side.

E · -ing and -ed forms at a glance

Form Meaning Example See
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb I was listening to music. Units 10, 19, 20
Gerund V-ing as a noun Walking every day helps. Avoid lifting. Unit 30
Participle I V-ing as an adjective (active) a bleeding wound, the patient sitting by the window Unit 30
Participle II (V3) V3 as an adjective (passive or finished) a broken leg, the prescribed dose Units 22, 30
-ing adjective the cause of a feeling confusing instructions Unit 30
-ed adjective the feeling a confused patient Unit 30

-ing spelling: take → taking (drop -e) · sit → sitting (double the consonant after one short vowel) · lie → lying, die → dying (ie → y) · see → seeing (keep -ee).

F · Conditionals at a glance

Type If-clause Main clause Meaning Example
Zero Present Simple Present Simple always true If you smile, you start to feel better.
First Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction real future If the pain gets worse, call us.
Second Past Simple would + V1 unreal now / unlikely future If I were you, I'd rest.
Third Past Perfect would have + V3 unreal past If I had known, I would have told you.
Mixed (past → now) Past Perfect would + V1 past cause, present result If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be here now.
Mixed (now → past) Past Simple would have + V3 present situation, past result If he weren't afraid of needles, he would have had the test.
Formal inversion Should / Had / Were + S… as above written, formal Should you notice redness, contact the clinic.

Two rules for every type: no will and no would in the if-clause. Comma after the if-clause when it comes first.

student.title: Vocabulary Book
student.html:
This book holds every new word from the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 courses, with a plain-English definition and an example of how it is used. The words follow the course order: level → week → lesson.

Each entry

Column What it shows
L the lesson where the word is taught
Word the word or phrase, with its abbreviation if there is one
Type the part of speech
Definition what it means, in simple English
Example how it is used in healthcare

Types: n. = noun · v. = verb · adj. = adjective · adv. = adverb · phr. = phrase · abbr. = abbreviation · prefix / suffix = word part · phr. v. = phrasal verb · prep. = preposition.

How to study a word

  1. Read the definition, then cover it and explain the word in your own English words.
  2. Say the example aloud twice.
  3. Make a new sentence about a patient, your family or your studies.
  4. Review the week's words before the third lesson of the week, and all the level's words before Lessons 18 and 36.

B2 Clinical

Week 1 · Advanced Patient Interviews

L Word Type Definition Example
1 intake n. the first set of questions when a patient arrives Let's start your intake.
1 verify v. to check that information is true or correct I need to verify your date of birth.
1 preferred language n. the language a patient wants to use What is your preferred language?
1 chief complaint n. the main problem that brings the patient in Her chief complaint is fatigue.
1 reason for visit n. why the patient has come What is the reason for your visit?
1 bothersome adj. causing worry or discomfort Which symptom is most bothersome?
1 clarify v. to make something clearer Can I clarify one thing?
1 leading question n. a question that suggests the answer "Is it sharp?" is a leading question.
2 location n. the place where something is Where exactly is the location of the pain?
2 character n. (pain) what it feels like How would you describe the character of the pain?
2 aggravating factor n. something that makes a symptom worse Walking is an aggravating factor.
2 relieving factor n. something that makes a symptom better Rest is a relieving factor.
2 timing n. when and how often a symptom happens Ask about timing: is it constant, or does it come and go?
2 associated symptoms n. other symptoms that happen together Any associated symptoms, like nausea?
2 pertinent negative n. an important symptom the patient does not have "No diarrhea" is a pertinent negative.
2 radiate v. (pain) to spread from one place to another Does the pain radiate to your back?
3 social history n. information about work, habits, home and lifestyle Let's go over your social history.
3 occupation n. a person's job What is your occupation?
3 tobacco n. the plant in cigarettes and other smoking products Do you use tobacco in any form?
3 alcohol n. the substance in drinks such as beer, wine and vodka How much alcohol do you drink in a week?

Week 2 · Neurological Assessment

L Word Type Definition Example
4 migraine n. a severe headache, often with nausea and sensitivity to light She has had migraines since she was a teenager.
4 fainting n. losing consciousness for a short time Have you had any fainting?
4 seizure n. a sudden attack of uncontrolled shaking or loss of awareness He had a seizure last year.
4 slurred speech n. words that are unclear or run together Her speech is slurred.
4 blurred vision n. seeing things unclearly Do you have blurred vision?
4 double vision n. seeing two of everything Any double vision?
4 vertigo n. a feeling that you or the room is spinning The room spins: that's vertigo.
4 sensitivity to light n. discomfort caused by bright light She has sensitivity to light with her headaches.
4 warning sign n. a sign that something serious may be happening Sudden weakness is a warning sign.
5 awake adj. not sleeping He is awake and talking.
5 drowsy adj. sleepy and hard to keep awake She is drowsy but wakes to voice.
5 agitated adj. restless, upset and unable to stay calm He is agitated and pulling at his IV.
5 oriented adj. knowing who you are, where you are and what day it is She is oriented to person, place and time.
5 disoriented adj. confused about who, where or when He is disoriented to time.
5 attention n. the ability to focus on something She can't keep her attention on the question.
5 memory n. the ability to remember How is his memory today?
5 responds to phr. reacts to something He responds to his name.
6 strength n. how strong a muscle is His strength is equal on both sides.
6 grip n. how strongly the hand can hold Her left grip is weaker.
6 gait n. the way a person walks His gait is unsteady.
6 unequal adj. not the same on both sides Grip strength is unequal.

Week 3 · Cardiovascular

L Word Type Definition Example
7 pressure n. (chest) a heavy, pushing feeling I feel pressure in my chest.
7 tightness n. a squeezing feeling I feel tightness in my chest on the stairs.
7 discomfort n. an unpleasant feeling that is not quite pain Any chest discomfort?
7 exertion n. physical effort Does it happen with exertion?
7 at rest phr. when not moving or exercising Does it happen at rest?
7 spread v. to move to other areas Does it spread to your arm or jaw?
7 sweating n. producing liquid from the skin She started sweating.
7 cardiac history n. past heart problems Any cardiac history in your family?

teacher.title: Introduction
teacher.html:
1. About this book

This is the teacher's book for B2 Clinical Medical English, the second of three ShifoLife levels (B1 → B2 → C1). It covers 12 weeks, 36 lessons of 60 minutes, three per week. A matching Student Edition holds the timetable, word lists and every card and text students use, without answer keys.

Who it is for: students who completed B1, or scored 18–27 on the placement check (printed in the B1 Teacher Edition, section 3). They can already take a basic history, read vital signs and a medicine label. B2 makes them run full patient conversations, report changes accurately and hand off with SBAR.

What it is not: clinical training. All patients, charts and labels are fictional. Students report and refer; they never diagnose, triage or change treatment.

How to use it: the method is the same as B1: the SHIFO Lesson Cycle, the Learn · Practice · Perform week and the Spark bank. Section 2 lists only what changes at B2.

Grammar companion: B2 grammar is explained in full in the Doc (Part 2, Units 19–27). Review Part 1 with any student who needs it.

Vocabulary companion: every new word in this book has an English definition, a word type and an example sentence in the Doc (B2 section, by week and lesson). Use it for Picture Reveal, Odd One Out and the weekly word review.

Copyright. © 2026 Shifo Life. All rights reserved. ShifoLife Medical English, the SHIFO Lesson Cycle and the Learn · Practice · Perform week are proprietary to Shifo Life. No part of this book may be copied, adapted or used to teach outside Shifo Life without written permission. Version 1.0 (draft for review).

2. The B2 level and what changes from B1

By Week 12 the student can run a 5-minute focused interview without a script, report numbers and changes with no errors, give a 1-minute SBAR, do discharge teach-back, respond to emotional and sensitive situations, and keep reported and observed information apart.

B1 B2
Student talk time 50% rising to 65% 60–70%
New words 8 per A/B lesson, 4 per C 8–9 per A/B lesson, 4 per C; max 22 a week
Start stage (S) Recall 3 words 60 seconds of free speaking on last lesson's topic, then 3 recycled words
Role-play rounds (F) Prompts → fewer prompts → new detail Prompts → no prompts → unseen card led by the student
Teacher's role Models first Models only when the student is stuck; otherwise plays patient, colleague or instructor
Correct at once Numbers, names, side, time, not Same, plus units and anything that changes the clinical meaning
Grammar band Present and past tenses, comparatives, modals Present perfect continuous, passive, reported speech, conditionals, question tags, hedging

The SHIFO timings are the same as in B1: A S 0–6 · H 6–24 · I 24–32 · F 32–50 · O 50–60. B S 0–6 · H 6–16 · I 16–30 · F 30–50 · O 50–60. C S 0–5 · H 5–12 · I 12–20 · F 20–50 · O 50–60.

New Spark for B2: Hot Seat Interpreting. The teacher speaks as an Uzbek patient in turns of 2–3 sentences. The student interprets each full turn into English, in the first person, without notes. Then reverse it with an English-speaking clinician. Score accuracy, completeness and no added words. Eight B1 Sparks appear in the lessons; use the ninth, Odd One Out, for the weekly word review.

Report and refer: phrases students use every week.

  • I'll let the nurse know right away.
  • That's a question for your doctor or pharmacist.
  • I'm not able to advise on that, but I'll find someone who can.
  • I'm concerned about this change. Could you come and see the patient?

SBAR frame (every handoff and urgent call):

  • S – Situation: who you are, where you are, the patient's name and the change now. This is Dilnoza, a nursing student in bay 3. I'm calling about Mrs. Qodirova. She is more drowsy.
  • B – Background: the key facts from the card: age, why the patient is here, what happened and when, important medicines.
  • A – Assessment: what you observed or measured, with values, units and times, and what has changed. No diagnosis.
  • R – Request: what you need, using the supplied request. Could you come and assess her now? Then close the loop: repeat back the reply.

Groups: keep B2 groups to 2–4 students. Each role-play has a third role, the observer, who fills a 4-point checklist printed on each lesson card.

3. B2 timetable: 36 lessons at a glance

Three lessons a week on fixed days with a day between them. Never move Lesson C before Lesson B.

# Wk Type Lesson Goal: the student can… Grammar (B2) Spark
1 1 A Intake and the chief complaint open an interview, confirm identity and language, and get the chief complaint without leading Open vs closed questions; Tell me more about… Match and Speak
2 1 B Detailed symptom history take a structured symptom history Present perfect continuous: How long have you been having…? Listen and Answer
3 1 C History review and summary run a 5-minute interview and give a 60-second summary Reporting verbs: reports, denies, states Mystery Patient
4 2 A Headache and neurological symptoms ask about neurological symptoms and timing When did you first notice…? past vs present perfect Picture Reveal
5 2 B Mental status and orientation describe mental status in neutral words appears, seems, is oriented to Error Hunt
6 2 C Reporting neurological changes report side, time and change without diagnosing Noun phrases: new left-sided weakness 60-Second Report
7 3 A Chest symptoms and cardiac history ask about chest symptoms clearly Time clauses: when, whenever, after; Does it spread? Uzbek Bridge
8 3 B Blood pressure and circulation report supplied cardiovascular readings Passive: was taken, was recorded Number Catch
9 3 C Cardiac tests explain test names from a card and refer other questions Present passive for procedures Listen and Answer
10 4 A Breathing history take a detailed breathing history Present perfect continuous; triggers Match and Speak
11 4 B Oxygen, observations and isolation report breathing observations and explain isolation on 2 L via nasal cannula; on room air Number Catch
12 4 C Urgent respiratory communication call for help clearly and calmly Short urgent sentences 60-Second Report
13 5 A Diabetes: words and symptoms ask about diabetes history and symptoms First conditional: If your sugar is low, you may feel… Uzbek Bridge
14 5 B Glucose monitoring and numbers report glucose values and times with no errors Trends: has been trending up Number Catch

35 12 B Integrated patient simulation complete a multi-step patient simulation Sequencing review Mystery Patient
36 12 C Final assessment complete five tasks without help Review Assessment

4. Assessment: Lessons 1, 18 and 36

The four skills are the same as in B1, scored 0–3, but the bar is higher. A student moves to C1 with 10 or more out of 12 at Lesson 36 and no skill below 2.

Skill 1 2 3 (B2 standard)
Vocabulary use Uses B2 words only when prompted Uses most B2 words correctly Chooses the precise term and the plain-English version for each listener
Clear speech Understood with effort Clear; stress sometimes off on long words Clear at natural speed; stresses key facts in a report
Listening and clarifying Gets the main point only Gets details; usually checks Catches every detail, checks numbers, and summarizes back
Accurate details Several errors in numbers, units, side or time One error, self-corrected No errors; keeps reported and observed facts apart

Score 0 when the skill is not yet shown.

When Tasks Recording kept
Lesson 1 (baseline) 3-minute intake interview with unseen card K3 (Lesson 1, Round 3); compare with the student's B1 final score or placement result Interview
Lesson 18 (midpoint) 5-minute focused interview (unseen card); fluid-balance and vital-sign report; 1-minute SBAR All three
Lesson 36 (final) Five tasks: advanced interview; measurement report; SBAR; discharge teach-back; instructor question All five, compared with Lessons 1 and 18

Every lesson: note 5 target words and 1 speaking goal in the student's book. Every Lesson C: one voice note of 90–120 seconds.

Completion: attend at least 32 of 36 lessons and reach the score above for the ShifoLife B2 Clinical Medical English certificate of completion. It is a course certificate, not a CEFR or clinical qualification.

teacher.title: Advanced Patient Interviews
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can open an interview professionally, take a structured symptom history, and summarize a full history in 60 seconds.

Prepare: complaint cards K1–K3; the OLDCARTS grid (Student Edition, Week 1 cards); pain card PC1 and history card H1 (below).

Lesson 1 · A Learn · Intake and the chief complaint
Goal Open an interview, confirm identity and language, and get the chief complaint without leading.
New words (9) intake, verify, preferred language, chief complaint, reason for visit, concern, bothersome, clarify, leading question
Recycle (B1) appointment, date of birth, interpreter
Grammar Open vs closed questions; Tell me more about… How would you describe…?
Spark Match and Speak (closed → open)
Assessment Baseline: record the Round 3 interview.
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds of free speaking: What changed for you during B1? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Leading: Is it a sharp pain? Open: How would you describe the pain? Model the intake script below.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak; the student turns closed questions into open ones.
32–50 F Round 1: card K1 with the script in view. Round 2: card K2 without notes; the student sums up the chief complaint in one sentence. Round 3 (unseen): card K3, the patient prefers Uzbek. The student offers a professional interpreter; while waiting for the interpreter, the student practices interpreting her first line (practice only). When the interpreter (the teacher) arrives, the student runs a 3-minute intake interview through them. Record it.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 open questions + 1 one-sentence summary. Set homework.

Intake script: Hello, I'm Dilnoza, a nursing student. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth? What language would you prefer to use today? What brings you in today? Tell me more about that.

Match and Speak: Do you have pain? → Tell me about any pain you've had. · Is it bad? → How would you describe it? · Did it start today? → When did it start? · Are you worried? → What concerns you most?

Complaint cards (fictional): K1 – Feruza, 41: I've been really tired and my feet tingle (3 weeks). K2 – Akmal, 29: My stomach has been bad since the weekend (upper abdominal pain and nausea, 3 days). K3 (unseen) – Hafiza, 67, prefers Uzbek: Oyog‘larim shishib ketyapti (→ My legs are swelling).

Observer checks: open question first · identity confirmed (name and date of birth) · no leading questions · one-sentence summary.

Stretch: add What do you think is causing it? Support: script card stays in view in Round 2.

Homework: record a 90-second interview opening with card K2.

Lesson 2 · B Practice · Detailed symptom history
Goal Take a structured symptom history.
New words (8) location, character, aggravating factor, relieving factor, timing, associated symptoms, pertinent negative, radiate
Recycle chief complaint, onset, duration
Grammar Present perfect continuous for ongoing (How long have you been having this pain?); present perfect simple for counts (How many times have you vomited?)
Spark Listen and Answer (fill the OLDCARTS grid)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the student gives the K2 chief complaint from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words with the OLDCARTS grid: Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating, Relieving, Timing, Severity. Pertinent negative = an important no (no diarrhea).
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads the narrative twice, the student fills the grid. Grammar in 4 minutes.
30–50 F Round 1: interview with the grid in view. Round 2: the teacher changes details mid-interview; the student repeats back exact timing and severity. Round 3 (unseen): pain card PC1 (below); the student leads with no grid.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 3 OLDCARTS questions in natural English. Set homework.

Narrative (teacher reads): It started on Sunday night, suddenly, in the middle of my stomach. Now it's moved to the lower right side. It's a sharp, constant pain, about seven out of ten. Walking makes it worse; lying still helps a little. I've also felt sick and I haven't wanted to eat. No diarrhea.

Grid key: Onset – Sunday night, sudden · Location – center, now lower right · Duration – since Sunday · Character – sharp · Aggravating – walking · Relieving – lying still · Timing – constant · Severity – 7/10 · Associated – nausea, poor appetite · Pertinent negative – no diarrhea.

Pain card PC1 (unseen, fictional): Jasur Tojiyev, 45, painter. Pain in his right shoulder for 5 days; it started the day after he painted a ceiling; aching, 5/10; worse when he lifts his arm above his head or lies on that side; rest and a warm shower help a little; worse at night; it does not spread; no numbness or weakness in the arm. Grid key: Onset – 5 days ago, after painting a ceiling · Location – right shoulder · Duration – 5 days · Character – aching · Aggravating – lifting the arm overhead, lying on it · Relieving – rest, warm shower · Timing – worse at night · Severity – 5/10 · Pertinent negatives – does not spread; no numbness or weakness.

Observer checks: all 8 OLDCARTS parts · one pertinent negative asked · timing and severity repeated back · no leading questions.

Stretch: ask Have you had anything like this before? Support: grid in view in Round 2.

Homework: write 6 follow-up questions and record them.

Lesson 3 · C Perform · History review and summary
Goal Run a 5-minute interview and give a 60-second summary.
New words (4) social history, occupation, tobacco, alcohol
Recycle pertinent negative, aggravating factor, chief complaint
Grammar Reporting verbs for summaries: He reports… He denies… He states that…
Spark Mystery Patient
Perform task Recorded 5-minute interview and 60-second summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the student explains OLDCARTS to an imaginary new classmate.
5–12 H 4 new words. Respectful wording: Do you use tobacco in any form? How much alcohol do you drink in a week?
12–20 I Model summary (below). Focus on denies for pertinent negatives.
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient; card H1 is hidden and the student has 5 minutes to cover all 6 history parts (chief complaint, symptom details, past history, medicines and allergies, family history, social history). Round 2: the student plays H1 and the teacher interviews, making 2 errors; the student spots them. Then the performance: record the interview and the 60-second summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

History card H1 (hidden, fictional): Davron Ergashev, 55, taxi driver. Cough for 3 weeks, worse at night. Smokes 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years; no alcohol. History: hypertension; one blood-pressure tablet daily; no allergies. Father had lung problems. Lives with his wife and two sons. Denies fever and weight loss.

Model summary: Mr. Ergashev is a 55-year-old taxi driver with a history of hypertension. He reports a cough for three weeks, worse at night. He has smoked about 15 cigarettes a day for 30 years. He denies fever and weight loss. He takes one blood-pressure tablet daily and has no allergies.

Observer checks: 6 history parts covered · denies used correctly · numbers right · summary 60 seconds or less.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the H1 summary, then 3 open questions you would ask next.

teacher.title: Neurological Assessment and Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about neurological symptoms with exact timing, describe mental status in neutral words, and report a new neurological change.

Prepare: 4 pictures (person holding their head, someone shielding eyes from light, someone fainting, blurred text); neuro cards N1–N3; mental-status cards M1–M2; change cards R1–R2.

Never name a diagnosis. Students say new weakness in the left arm, never stroke. The clinician decides.

Lesson 4 · A Learn · Headache and neurological symptoms
Goal Ask about neurological symptoms and timing.
New words (9) migraine, fainting, seizure, slurred speech, blurred vision, double vision, vertigo, sensitivity to light, warning sign
Recycle onset, radiate, associated symptoms
Grammar When did you first notice…? (past simple for a moment) vs Have you noticed any changes in…? (present perfect up to now)
Spark Picture Reveal
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the H1 summary from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Bridge: I passed out → fainting; my words came out wrong → slurred speech; the room is spinning → vertigo.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Model 4 neuro follow-ups: vision, speech, weakness, numbness.
32–50 F Spark (5 min): Picture Reveal. Round 1: card N1 with OLDCARTS and neuro follow-ups. Round 2: card N2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): card N3, a sudden change; the student says I'm going to get the nurse right away and does not continue the interview.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 When did you first notice…? + 1 Have you noticed…? Set homework.

Neuro cards (fictional): N1 – Gulchehra, 34: throbbing headache on the left side for 2 days; sensitive to light; nausea; has had similar headaches before. N2 – Bobur, 48: the room spins when he turns his head, for 1 week; no change in hearing. N3 (unseen) – Sharofat, 72: sudden slurred speech and weakness in her right arm, starting 20 minutes ago.

Observer checks: exact onset · neuro follow-ups asked · sudden change escalated at once · no diagnosis named.

Stretch: recognize the phrase the worst headache of my life: a patient who says it is escalated at once. Support: the neuro follow-up card (Student Edition, Week 2 cards).

Homework: record 5 neuro questions and their N1 answers.

Lesson 5 · B Practice · Mental status and orientation
Goal Describe mental status in neutral words.
New words (9) awake, drowsy, agitated, oriented, disoriented, attention, memory, baseline, responds to
Recycle confused, alert, fainting
Grammar He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. He is oriented to person and place, not time. She is able / unable to…
Spark Error Hunt
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe card N3 and what you did. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Oriented ×3 = knows person, place and time. Baseline = what is normal for this patient. Words to avoid: crazy, senile, demented.
16–30 I Listening: the teacher reads card M1 aloud; the student sorts facts into the patient says and I observe. Spark: Error Hunt (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student asks orientation questions to teacher-patient M1 and describes him. Round 2: M2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): a family member says He's not himself today; the student asks how he usually is (baseline).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: describe M1 in 2 neutral sentences. Set homework.

Mental-status cards (fictional): M1 – Tulkin Rahimov, 80: drowsy but wakes when spoken to; knows his name only; says I'm at home (he is in hospital). His daughter says he is usually fully oriented. M2 – Kamila, 25: alert, oriented ×3, anxious, answers all questions.

Error Hunt: Mr. Rahimov is alert and oriented to person and place. His daughter says this is his baseline. Key: drowsy, not alert; oriented to person only; his daughter says this is not his baseline.

Observer checks: neutral words only · says vs observed kept apart · baseline asked · all three orientation questions.

Stretch: add How is his memory compared with last week? Support: the says / observe sorting table (Student Edition, Week 2 cards).

Homework: describe 2 mental-status cards in writing, then read them aloud.

Lesson 6 · C Perform · Reporting neurological changes
Goal Report side, time and change without diagnosing.
New words (4) strength, grip, gait, unequal
Recycle baseline, drowsy, slurred speech
Grammar Compact noun phrases: new left-sided weakness; unequal grip strength; unsteady gait since 4 p.m.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 45-second change report for card R1
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: describe card M1 in neutral words.
5–12 H 4 new words. Practice left/right at speed: the teacher points, the student says left grip, right grip.
12–20 I Model the report below. Grammar: long sentence → noun phrase.
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on R1. Round 1: report with the model in view. Round 2: no notes; the teacher interrupts: Which side? What time? Round 3 (unseen): card R2 (below), a change in speech, not strength. Then the performance: record the R1 report.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Change card R1 (fictional): Nodir Saidov, 66, room 14. 2 p.m.: grip equal, speech clear. 4 p.m.: left grip weaker than right; says my left hand feels heavy; gait unsteady; speech clear; alert and oriented ×3.

Model report: I'm calling about Mr. Saidov in room 14. Since 4 p.m. he has had new weakness in his left hand: his left grip is weaker than his right. At 2 p.m. his grip was equal. He says his left hand feels heavy, and his gait is unsteady. He is alert and oriented, and his speech is clear. I'm concerned about this new change. Could you come and see him now?

Change card R2 (unseen, fictional): Saida Normatova, 70, room 8. 9 a.m.: speech clear; grip equal; alert and oriented ×3. 11 a.m.: speech slurred; her daughter says She sounds different; grip equal; coughs when she drinks water; alert; oriented to person and place, not time. Model report: I'm calling about Mrs. Normatova in room 8. Since 11 a.m. her speech has been slurred. At 9 a.m. it was clear. Her daughter says she sounds different. Her grip is equal. She coughs when she drinks water. She is alert and oriented to person and place, but not time. I'm concerned about this new change. Could you come and see her now?

Observer checks: side correct · both times given · says vs observed apart · clear request at the end.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the R1 report, then describe card M1.

teacher.title: Cardiovascular Conditions and Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about chest symptoms clearly, report blood-pressure readings with position and time, and explain a cardiac test from a card.

Prepare: chest cards C1–C3; orthostatic chart and chart BP2 (below); ECG and echocardiogram test cards (below).

Lesson 7 · A Learn · Chest symptoms and cardiac history
Goal Ask about chest symptoms clearly.
New words (9) pressure, tightness, discomfort, exertion, at rest, spread, sweating, cardiac history, heart attack
Recycle palpitations, radiate, swelling
Grammar Time clauses: Does it happen when you walk or when you rest? Does it go away after you stop? Does the discomfort spread anywhere?
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the R1 report from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Many patients say discomfort or pressure, not pain: ask about all three.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card C1; the student asks exertion vs rest, spread, associated symptoms. Round 2: C2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): C3, pressure right now; the student stops and says I'm getting the nurse right away. Please stay in bed.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 time-clause questions. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge:

Uzbek Model English
Ko‘kragimda bosim bor, chap qo‘limga tarqalyapti. I feel pressure in my chest, and it spreads to my left arm.
Zinadan chiqqanimda ko‘kragim siqiladi, dam olsam o‘tib ketadi. My chest gets tight when I climb stairs, and it goes away when I rest.
Terlab ketdim va ko‘nglim aynidi. I started sweating and felt sick.
Otam ellik yoshida infarkt bo‘lgan. My father had a heart attack at fifty.

Chest cards (fictional): C1 – Rustam, 58: chest tightness walking uphill for 2 weeks; stops with rest. C2 – Madina, 36: heart racing at rest in the evenings for 5 days; 4 cups of coffee a day. C3 (unseen) – Hamid, 63: chest pressure for 15 minutes, spreading to his jaw, sweating, now.

Observer checks: exertion vs rest · spread asked · urgent case escalated · no diagnosis told to the patient.

Stretch: ask about family cardiac history with ages. Support: time-clause card (Student Edition, Week 3 cards).

Homework: record 8 chest-symptom questions.

Lesson 8 · B Practice · Blood pressure and circulation
Goal Report supplied cardiovascular readings with position and time.
New words (8) systolic, diastolic, hypotension, orthostatic, cuff, lying, standing, lightheaded
Recycle hypertension, pulse, baseline
Grammar Passive: The blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down and was recorded again at 10:03 standing.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe chest card C1. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 8 words. Systolic = the top number; diastolic = the bottom number. Spark: Number Catch: 118/76 · 180/76 · 90/60 · 160/100 · 104/66.
16–30 I Model the report below. Grammar in 4 minutes: active → passive in reports.
30–50 F Round 1: report the orthostatic chart. Round 2: the teacher asks for exact values, position and time. Round 3 (unseen): chart BP2 (below); the student reports with no model.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 readings with position and time. Set homework.

Orthostatic chart (fictional): Oydin Nazarova, 70. 10:00 lying: BP 132/80, HR 76. 10:03 standing: BP 104/66, HR 98; says she feels lightheaded.

Model report: Mrs. Nazarova's blood pressure was taken at 10:00 lying down: 132 over 80, heart rate 76. At 10:03, standing, it was 104 over 66 and her heart rate was 98. She says she feels lightheaded when she stands.

Chart BP2 (unseen, fictional): Bekzod Hamroyev, 66. 14:00 lying: BP 128/78, HR 72. 14:03 standing: BP 100/62, HR 94; says I feel dizzy. I need to sit down. Model report: Mr. Hamroyev's blood pressure was taken at 14:00 lying down: 128 over 78, heart rate 72. At 14:03, standing, it was 100 over 62 and his heart rate was 94. His systolic pressure dropped from 128 to 100. He says he feels dizzy and needs to sit down.

Observer checks: top and bottom numbers in order · position and time for each · she says for symptoms · read-back correct.

Stretch: describe the change in one sentence with dropped from… to…. Support: chart in view.

Homework: record the orthostatic report.

Lesson 9 · C Perform · Cardiac tests
Goal Explain test names from a card and refer other questions.
New words (4) electrocardiogram (ECG / EKG), echocardiogram, electrode, rhythm
Recycle systolic, exertion, discomfort
Grammar Present passive for procedures: Small stickers called electrodes are placed on your chest. The doctor will explain the results.
Spark Listen and Answer
Perform task Recorded ECG explanation with one referral
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: the orthostatic report from memory.
5–12 H 4 new words. US hospitals often say EKG; both are correct.
12–20 I Spark: Listen and Answer: the teacher reads the echocardiogram card. Questions: What is it? How long does it take? What is put on the chest? Key: an ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel.
20–50 F Round 1: the student explains the ECG card to a nervous teacher-patient. Round 2: the echocardiogram card. Round 3: the patient asks Is my heart damaged?; the student refers: The doctor will look at the results and explain them to you. Then the performance: record Round 1 with the referral.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Test cards (fictional): ECG – about 5–10 minutes; lie still; 10 small stickers (electrodes) on the chest, arms and legs; painless; no preparation; the doctor reviews the results. Echocardiogram – ultrasound of the heart; 30–60 minutes; gel on the chest; you may be asked to turn onto your left side; painless.

Observer checks: only card facts used · passive used correctly · clinical question referred · calm, reassuring tone.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): explain the ECG to a patient, then report the orthostatic chart.

teacher.title: Respiratory Conditions and Urgent Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can take a detailed breathing history, report oxygen observations with device and flow, explain isolation precautions, and call for help clearly in an emergency.

Prepare: breathing cards Rb1–Rb3; observation card O1; pictures of a nasal cannula, an oxygen mask and an N95 respirator; door sign IS1 (below); urgent cards U1–U2.

Lesson 10 · A Learn · Breathing history
Goal Take a detailed breathing history.
New words (9) trigger, allergen, flare-up, congestion, productive cough, dry cough, rescue inhaler, nebulizer, peak flow
Recycle wheezing, sputum, shortness of breath
Grammar Present perfect continuous: Have you been using your inhaler more than usual? What seems to trigger it?
Spark Match and Speak (everyday ↔ clinical)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: explain the ECG card. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Productive = brings up sputum; dry = nothing comes up.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark (4 min): Match and Speak (below).
32–50 F Round 1: card Rb1. Round 2: card Rb2, no notes. Round 3 (unseen): Rb3, a parent speaking for a child; the student asks the parent, not the child.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 trigger questions. Set homework.

Match and Speak: I'm coughing stuff up ↔ productive cough · tickly cough, nothing comes up ↔ dry cough · my chest feels blocked ↔ congestion · my asthma attack ↔ flare-up · my blue inhaler ↔ rescue inhaler · the cat makes it worse ↔ allergen, trigger.

Breathing cards (fictional): Rb1 – Lola, 22, asthma: flare-up for 3 days; using her rescue inhaler 6 times a day (usually twice a week); trigger: dust at her new job; dry cough at night. Rb2 – Sobir, 61, smoker: productive cough with yellow sputum for 1 week; short of breath after one flight of stairs. Rb3 (unseen) – a mother: My son is 6. He's breathing fast and wheezing since this morning.

Observer checks: frequency of inhaler use asked · trigger asked · sputum described · proxy handled correctly.

Stretch: compare usual vs now: How often do you usually need it? Support: Match and Speak card in view.

Homework: record a full breathing interview with Rb2.

Lesson 11 · B Practice · Oxygen, observations and isolation
Goal Report breathing observations precisely and explain isolation precautions.
New words (9) nasal cannula, oxygen mask, room air, liters per minute, effort, shallow, droplet precautions, airborne precautions, N95 respirator
Recycle oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, isolation
Grammar Prepositions in reports: SpO2 94% on 2 liters per minute via nasal cannula; 90% on room air.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: describe Lola's flare-up. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words with pictures. Spark: Number Catch: SpO2 89 / 98 · 2 L / 12 L · RR 28 / 18 · 4 L/min.
16–30 I Model reading card O1. Grammar in 4 minutes: on and via.
30–50 F Round 1: the student reads O1 and confirms every number and device. Round 2: the student reports the change from 8 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. Round 3: the student explains door sign IS1 to a patient and a visitor (the teacher plays both).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 oxygen reading with device and flow. Set homework.

Observation card O1 (fictional): Komil, 68. 8 a.m.: SpO2 95% on room air, RR 18. 12 p.m.: SpO2 90% on room air, RR 26, shallow breathing. 12:15 p.m.: SpO2 94% on 2 L/min via nasal cannula (as ordered).

Door sign IS1 (fictional): DROPLET PRECAUTIONS · Everyone entering: wear a surgical mask · Clean your hands before you go in and when you leave · Patient: wear a mask if you leave the room · Visitors: please ask the nurse before entering.

Isolation model: Your door sign says droplet precautions. That means everyone who comes in wears a mask, and we may ask visitors to keep their distance. Please wear a mask if you leave the room.

Observer checks: device and flow named · room air used correctly · each time given · isolation explained from the sign only.

Stretch: explain the difference between droplet and airborne precautions in plain English. Support: the oxygen report frame (Student Edition, Week 4 cards).

Homework: record 5 observation sentences.

Lesson 12 · C Perform · Urgent respiratory communication
Goal Call for help clearly and calmly.
New words (4) distress, deteriorating, rapid response, reassess
Recycle shallow, room air, nasal cannula
Grammar Short urgent sentences: I need help in room 6 now. Calm imperatives to the patient: Stay sitting up. Breathe slowly with me.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded 30-second urgent call plus words of reassurance to the patient
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 60 seconds: report card O1.
5–12 H 4 new words. A rapid response team is called by hospital protocol; students learn the words to call for help.
12–20 I Model the urgent call and the reassurance (below). Spark: 60-Second Report on U1.
20–50 F Round 1: the call with the model in view. Round 2: no notes, 30 seconds. Round 3 (unseen): urgent card U2 (below); the student calls for help first, then reassures. Then the performance: record the U1 call and reassurance.
50–60 O Play the recording back. Two errors, then retry. Set the weekly voice note.

Urgent card U1 (fictional): Nilufar Yusupova, 59, room 6, 3:10 p.m. Sudden difficulty breathing; says I can't breathe; RR 32; SpO2 86% on 2 L nasal cannula (94% at 2 p.m.); sitting upright; frightened.

Model call: This is Dilnoza in room 6. I need help now. Mrs. Yusupova has sudden difficulty breathing. Her oxygen saturation is 86 percent on 2 liters; at 2 p.m. it was 94. Her respiratory rate is 32. Please come now. To the patient: I'm here with you. Help is coming. Stay sitting up and breathe slowly with me.

Urgent card U2 (unseen, fictional): Erkin Sobirov, 72, room 11, 6:40 a.m. Breathing fast and noisy; says I can't get my breath; RR 30; SpO2 88% on room air (96% at 4 a.m.); lips look pale; sitting on the edge of the bed; very anxious. Model call: This is Dilnoza in room 11. I need help now. Mr. Sobirov has sudden difficulty breathing. His oxygen saturation is 88 percent on room air; at 4 a.m. it was 96. His respiratory rate is 30. Please come now. To the patient: I'm here with you. Help is coming. Stay sitting up and breathe slowly with me.

Observer checks: location first · facts in under 30 seconds · old and new value given · calm words to the patient.

Weekly voice note (90–120 seconds): the U1 call, then the droplet-precautions explanation.

teacher.title: Diabetes and Endocrine
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can ask about diabetes symptoms and routines, report glucose values with the right unit and time, and summarize endocrine symptoms without diagnosing.

Why this week matters: diabetes is common among Uzbek patients. Spend extra care on numbers and units.

Prepare: diabetes cards D1–D3; glucose log G1; thyroid cards Th1–Th2.

Lesson 13 · A Learn · Diabetes: words and symptoms
Goal Ask about diabetes history and symptoms.
New words (9) glucose, blood sugar, insulin, hypoglycemia (low sugar), hyperglycemia (high sugar), type 1, type 2, thirsty, shaky
Recycle diabetes, pancreas, sweating
Grammar First conditional: If your sugar is low, you may feel shaky and sweaty. Have you checked your blood sugar today?
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 60 seconds: the U1 urgent call from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 9 words. Sounds: hypo-gly-CEE-mia, hyper-gly-CEE-mia. Low sugar: shaky, sweaty, hungry, confused. High sugar: thirsty, urinating often, tired, blurred vision.
24–32 I Grammar in 4 minutes. Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
