Show the answers

(1) Is there (2) There are (3) in (4) weren't.

Unit 9 · Present Simple (Present Indefinite)

When we use it

  • Habits and repeated actions: She takes insulin every morning.
  • Schedules and timetables: Visiting hours start at 2 p.m.
  • Facts and general truths: The heart pumps blood.
  • States: I feel dizzy. He knows his medicines.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V1 (he / she / it + -s) I check my sugar daily. She checks her sugar daily.
− S + do / does + not + V1 I don't smoke. He doesn't drink alcohol.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + V1? Do* you take any vitamins? How often does* she use her inhaler?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

He / she / it spelling: take → takes · wash → washes · cry → cries · go → goes · do → does · have → has.

Pronouncing -s: "s" in takes, checks · "z" in feels, needs · "iz" in washes, uses.

Keywords: every (day, morning, week) · always · usually · often · sometimes · occasionally · rarely · seldom · never · once / twice a day · from time to time.

Word order: frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be: She always takes it at night. He is often dizzy.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She take insulin. ✓ She takes insulin.
  • Only one -s: ✗ Does she takes…? ✓ Does she take…?
  • ✗ He don't smoke. ✓ He doesn't smoke.

Try it. (1) My mother ___ (have) diabetes. (2) ___ he ___ (use) his inhaler every day? (3) I ___ (not / drink) coffee. (4) The kidneys ___ (filter) the blood.

Show the answers

(1) has (2) Does … use (3) don't drink (4) filter.

Unit 10 · Present Continuous (Present Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action happening now: The patient is sleeping.
  • A temporary situation around now: I'm studying English this year.
  • A fixed plan for the future: She's having surgery on Monday.
  • An annoying repeated habit, with always: He's always pulling at his IV.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + V-ing My heart is beating fast.
− S + am / is / are + not + V-ing She isn't eating today.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + V-ing? Are* you having* trouble breathing?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.

Here be is a helper. I am a nurse (here am is the main verb) vs I am working (am only builds the tense).

-ing spelling: take → taking · sit → sitting · lie → lying · breathe → breathing.

Keywords: now · right now · at the moment · currently · today · this week · these days · still.

State verbs are not normally continuous: know, want, need, believe, understand, like, hate, seem, belong. ✗ I am knowing. ✓ I know. Feel and hurt can be both: My back hurts / is hurting.

Simple or continuous? He takes insulin every day (habit) · He's taking his insulin now (at this moment).

Watch out!

  • Don't drop be: ✗ She sleeping. ✓ She is sleeping.
  • ✗ I am needing water. ✓ I need water.

Try it. (1) Be quiet: the baby ___ (sleep). (2) ___ you ___ (take) any medicine at the moment? (3) She ___ (not / breathe) normally. (4) I ___ (understand) the instructions.

Show the answers

(1) is sleeping (2) Are … taking (3) isn't breathing (4) understand.

Unit 11 · Past Simple (Past Indefinite)

When we use it: a finished action at a finished time in the past, with no link to now. She fell yesterday. He had surgery in 2015.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V2 (regular: -ed; irregular: see table D) The pain started on Sunday. I took a tablet.
− S + did + not + V1 She didn't vomit.
? (Q/W) + did + S + V1? When did it start? Did you fall?

Short answers: Yes, she did. / No, I didn't.

-ed spelling: start → started · stop → stopped · cry → cried · use → used.

Pronouncing -ed: "t" in stopped, checked · "d" in called, used · "id" in started, needed.

Keywords: yesterday · ago · last (night, week, year) · in 2019 · at 3 a.m. · on Monday · when.

Watch out!

  • After did, use V1: ✗ Did you took it? ✓ Did you take it? ✗ She didn't came. ✓ She didn't come.
  • Ago goes after the time: ✓ three days ago ✗ ago three days.
  • With a finished time, don't use the Present Perfect: ✗ I have taken it yesterday. ✓ I took it yesterday.

Try it. (1) The pain ___ (begin) two days ago. (2) ___ you ___ (eat) breakfast? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) well last night. (4) He ___ (break) his wrist in 2019.

Show the answers

(1) began (2) Did … eat (3) didn't sleep (4) broke.

Unit 12 · Present Perfect

When we use it

  • A past action with a result now: I'm full. I have eaten. (Compare: I ate pasta yesterday: past only.)
  • Experience in life (any time until now): Have* you ever had* surgery?
  • A situation from the past until now: I've had this cough for three days.
  • Something just finished: The doctor has just left.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + V3 She has taken her tablets.
− S + have / has + not + V3 We haven't finished yet.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + V3? Have* you checked* your sugar today?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's / she's (here 's = has), haven't, hasn't.

Keywords: just · already · yet (in − and ?) · ever · never · recently · so far · today · this week · for · since.

For or since? for + a length of time: for three days, for a week · since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since this morning.

Present Perfect or Past Simple? Ask about life with the Present Perfect; give the details with the Past Simple: Have you ever had surgery? – Yes, I had my appendix out in 2015.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present for since: ✗ I am here since Monday. ✓ I've been here since Monday.
  • ✗ for Monday ✓ since Monday · ✗ since three days ✓ for three days.
  • No finished time: ✗ I have seen the doctor yesterday. ✓ I saw the doctor yesterday.

Try it. (1) She ___ (have) a headache since this morning. (2) ___ you ever ___ (be) in hospital? (3) I ___ (not / take) my insulin yet. (4) He ___ (work) here for two years.

Show the answers

(1) has had (2) Have … been (3) haven't taken (4) has worked.

Unit 18 · Relative clauses: who, which, where

When we use it: to say which person, thing or place we mean, or to add information.

Word For Example
who people A pharmacist is someone who prepares medicines.
which things This is the tablet which helps your blood pressure.
that people or things (defining only) The nurse that helped me was kind.
where places The ED is the place where urgent patients go.

Defining (no commas): tells us which one. The nurse who looked after me was kind.

Non-defining (commas): adds extra information; never that. Mr. Saidov, who is 66, has diabetes.

Leaving out who / which / that: possible when it is the object: The tablet (that) you took is for pain. Not possible when it is the subject: ✗ The nurse helped me was kind.

Watch out!

  • ✗ the man which ✓ the man who · ✗ the pharmacy who ✓ the pharmacy **which / where.
  • No extra pronoun: ✗ The patient who he has diabetes… ✓ The patient who has diabetes…
  • Uzbek speakers often put the description before the noun: ✗ the has-diabetes patient. English puts it after: the patient who has diabetes.

(1) who (2) where (3) which / that / (nothing) (4) who.

Unit 28 · Discourse markers

When we use it: to show how ideas connect in lectures, presentations, essays and seminars.

Function Spoken / neutral Written / formal
Adding also, and, plus furthermore, moreover, in addition

Grammar of linkers

  • However, Therefore, Consequently start a new sentence and take a comma: Hand hygiene prevents infection. However, it is often forgotten.
  • although, whereas, because join two clauses: Although she was in pain, she walked to the bathroom.
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite* the pain, she walked. Despite feeling* dizzy, she walked.
  • due to + noun: …due to time pressure (✗ due to people are busy).

Watch out!

  • ✗ Although she was tired, but she worked. Use one linker: ✓ Although she was tired, she worked.
  • ✗ despite of ✓ despite / in spite of.
  • Moreover in a conversation sounds like a lecture. Match the register.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.

Show the answers

(1) smoking (2) broken (3) sitting (4) worrying … worried.

Unit 31 · Cleft sentences and emphasis

When we use it: to put the most important information first, to prioritize in a summary, or to correct someone politely.

Pattern Structure Example
What-cleft What + S + V + is / was + focus What concerns me most is the new sore on her foot.
It-cleft It is / was + focus + that / who + rest It's* the evening doses that* he misses.
The thing / reason The thing that… / The reason (why)… + is (that) The reason* she stopped is that* the tablets are expensive.
All All + S + V + is All she needs is a little more time.

Correcting politely: It wasn't the morning dose she missed; it was the evening one.

Watch out!

  • No extra it: ✗ What concerns me most it is the sore. ✓ What concerns me most is the sore.
  • Keep the order: ✗ Is the evening dose that he misses. ✓ It's the evening dose that he misses.

Unit 32 · Tentative and diplomatic language

When we use it: to make suggestions to seniors, to disagree in a seminar, and to ask sensitive questions without pressure.

Function Phrases
Polite requests I was wondering whether… Would it be possible to…? Would you mind + V-ing?
Suggestions to the team Could we consider…? Would it be worth + V-ing…? It might be helpful to…
Sensitive questions I was wondering if you could tell me a bit about… What gets in the way of…?
Disagreeing I see it slightly differently. While I take your point,… I'm not sure I agree, because…
Not knowing I'm not sure, but I think… As far as I know,… I'd need to check.

Why the past tense sounds polite: I was wondering and I wanted to ask talk about now, but the past form adds distance and sounds less direct.

Softeners: a bit, slightly, perhaps, possibly, just (Could I just check…?).

But not for safety. When a patient may be harmed, be clear and firm (CUS): I'm concerned. I'm uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.

Watch out!

  • ✗ Would you mind to wait? ✓ Would you mind waiting?
  • Over-softening in an emergency causes delay: ✗ I was wondering whether you might possibly come… ✓ I need you to come now.

Try it. Make more tentative: (1) Book an interpreter. (2) You're wrong. (3) Can I ask about your alcohol use? (4) Review his pain relief.

Unit 33 · Mixed and formal conditionals

Mixed conditionals

Type If-clause Main clause Example
past cause → present result Past Perfect would + V1 If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be in hospital now.
present situation → past result Past Simple would have + V3 If he weren't so afraid of needles, he would have had the test last week.

Formal inversion (leaflets, letters, academic writing): drop if and invert.

  • Should you notice any redness, contact the clinic. (= If you notice…)
  • Had I known about the allergy, I would have said so. (= If I had known…)
  • Were the patient to refuse, the team would discuss alternatives. (= If the patient refused…)

Other ways to say if

Word Meaning Example

supposing / what if imagining What if the results are positive?

Watch out!

  • in case ≠ if: Take your inhaler in case you get wheezy (take it with you now anyway) vs Use your inhaler if you get wheezy (only when it happens).

Unit 34 · Academic grammar: reporting verbs and the passive

When we use it: in summaries, care-plan rationales, essays and reflections.

Reporting verbs, from weak to strong

Strength Verbs Example
tentative suggests, indicates, implies The research suggests that lifestyle change can delay onset.
neutral states, reports, describes, notes The textbook states that…
strong shows, demonstrates, confirms, establishes The study demonstrates a clear link…
arguing argues, claims, maintains The author argues that…

The academic passive and impersonal structures

  • It is recommended that patients… It has been shown that…
  • Patients are advised to… Pressure injuries are associated with…
  • There is evidence* that… There is* a need for…

Tenses in academic writing

  • Present Simple for general facts and what a source says: Hand hygiene reduces infection. The author argues…
  • Past Simple for a specific study: The study found that…
  • Present Perfect for research up to now: Several studies have shown…

Style: no contractions (does not, not doesn't); avoid I think in essays (reflections are the exception: they use I); hedge claims (appears to, is likely to, may contribute to).

Watch out!

  • Too strong: ✗ This proves that… ✓ This suggests that…
  • Copying the source's sentence with small changes is plagiarism. Paraphrase fully and cite.

Mixed (now → past) Past Simple would have + V3 present situation, past result If he weren't afraid of needles, he would have had the test.

Two rules for every type: no will and no would in the if-clause. Comma after the if-clause when it comes first.

teacher.title: Vocabulary Book
teacher.html:
This book holds every new word from the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 courses, with a plain-English definition and an example of how it is used. The words follow the course order: level → week → lesson.

Each entry

Column What it shows
L the lesson where the word is taught
Word the word or phrase, with its abbreviation if there is one
Type the part of speech
Definition what it means, in simple English
Example how it is used in healthcare

Types: n. = noun · v. = verb · adj. = adjective · adv. = adverb · phr. = phrase · abbr. = abbreviation · prefix / suffix = word part · phr. v. = phrasal verb · prep. = preposition.

How to study a word

  1. Read the definition, then cover it and explain the word in your own English words.
  2. Say the example aloud twice.
  3. Make a new sentence about a patient, your family or your studies.
  4. Review the week's words before the third lesson of the week, and all the level's words before Lessons 18 and 36.

B2 Clinical

Week 1 · Advanced Patient Interviews

L Word Type Definition Example
1 intake n. the first set of questions when a patient arrives Let's start your intake.
1 verify v. to check that information is true or correct I need to verify your date of birth.

Week 4 · Respiratory and Urgent Communication

L Word Type Definition Example

11 shallow adj. (breathing) not deep Her breathing is shallow.

11 N95 respirator n. a close-fitting mask that filters tiny particles Staff wear an N95 respirator.
12 distress n. serious difficulty or suffering The patient is in respiratory distress.

Week 5 · Diabetes and Endocrine

L Word Type Definition Example

14 fasting glucose n. blood sugar measured before eating His fasting glucose was 112.
14 before meals phr. just before eating Check your sugar before meals.

14 trend n. the general direction of change The trend is going up.
15 thyroid n. a gland in the neck that makes hormones The thyroid is in your neck.

Week 6 · GI and Renal

16 heartburn n. a burning feeling in the chest from stomach acid I get heartburn at night.
16 indigestion n. discomfort in the stomach after eating Spicy food gives me indigestion.

17 intake and output (I&O) n. a record of all fluid in and all fluid out Please record intake and output.

Week 7 · Emergency Department

L Word Type Definition Example
19 triage n. deciding the order in which patients are seen, by urgency The triage nurse will see you first.
19 arrival n. the moment someone comes in What time was his arrival?

Week 8 · Surgical and Postoperative Care

L Word Type Definition Example

student.title: Introduction
student.html:
Welcome to C1 Professional Medical English

C1 prepares you for life inside a US nursing program: following lectures, reading textbooks, presenting cases, writing care plans and reflections, handling difficult conversations, speaking up in the team, and interpreting between Uzbek and English. This book is yours: write in it and bring it to every lesson.

My details
Name
Level C1 Professional
Teacher
Class days and time
Start date
My B2 final score
My nursing school / target date

What's new in C1

  • Reading and writing every week. One short written task a week: a summary, a care plan, a report or a reflection. Log them at the end of this book.
  • Register matters. You'll learn to say the same thing to a doctor, a patient, a family member and in Uzbek (Register Switch).
  • Make your own examples. At C1 you write your own example sentence for each new word: it's how words stay with you.
  • Interpreting at a professional level. Week 11 trains you as a medical interpreter: accuracy, completeness, ethics.
  • Final OSCE. Lesson 36 is a five-station exam, just like nursing school.
  • Homework: 20–25 minutes a day. Lectures or reading after Lesson A; speaking and recording after Lesson B; your written task and voice note after Lesson C.

Grammar help: look up any grammar point in the Doc (Part 3 for C1; the reference tables cover all 12 tenses).

Word help: every word in your week tables has an English definition and an example in the Doc (C1 section). Read the definition and example, then write your own sentence in the table.

All patients, documents and cases in this book are fictional. This course teaches English, not clinical skills.

student.html:
• ☐ I can follow a lecture's structure.

2 Cornell notes, cue column, abbreviation, symbol, condense, reconstruct, key term, main idea, supporting detail
3 elaborate, query, synthesize, takeaway

Key language: Firstly… In contrast… Consequently… To sum up… · Note symbols: ↑ ↓ → ∴ ≈ · pt, hx, dx, tx, sx, w/, w/o, q2h · I was wondering whether you could expand on… Could you clarify what you meant by…?

Written task: a 60-word lecture summary. Voice note: your own 1-minute mini-lecture with 5 signposts.

Cards and texts · Week 1

Cornell notes template (Lessons 2–3):

Cue column (key terms, questions) Notes (main ideas, supporting details, symbols)
Summary (2–3 lines):

Symbol sheet:

Symbol or abbreviation Meaning
↑ / ↓ increase, high / decrease, low
→ / ← leads to, causes / caused by
∴ therefore
≈ about, approximately
+ and, plus
> / < more than / less than
pt patient
hx history
dx diagnosis
tx treatment
sx symptoms
w/ / w/o with / without
q2h every 2 hours
def definition

Mini-lecture ML1, hand hygiene (read after you listen; Lesson 1 Round 1): Today I'd like to talk about hand hygiene, and I'll cover three points: why it matters, when to do it, and why people forget. Firstly, why does it matter? Hands are the most common way germs move between patients. Consequently, hand hygiene is one of the simplest ways to prevent infection in hospital. Secondly, when should you do it? To illustrate, think of five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean procedure, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings. Thirdly, why do people forget? In contrast to what we might expect, it's usually not lack of knowledge but time pressure and habit. So, to sum up: hands carry germs, there are five key moments, and the main barrier is habit, not knowledge.

Key language: Research suggests… X is associated with… X is characterized by… · Roots: cardi, gastr, nephr, hepat, neur, derm, oste, pneum / pulmon · Paraphrase by changing words, word forms and structure; copying a sentence with a few new words is still plagiarism.

Written task: a 50-word textbook summary. Voice note: one fact told to a doctor, a patient, a family member, and in Uzbek.

Cards and texts · Week 2

Reading text RT1, Type 2 diabetes: an overview (Lessons 4–6): Type 2 diabetes is a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose. Its etiology involves both genetic and lifestyle risk factors, including obesity and physical inactivity. The underlying pathophysiology is insulin resistance: the body's cells do not respond normally to insulin. Clinical manifestations may include thirst, frequent urination and fatigue, although many patients have no symptoms at diagnosis. Research suggests that lifestyle interventions, such as increased activity and dietary change, can delay its onset in high-risk individuals. Long-term complications are associated with damage to the eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels. The rationale for regular monitoring is therefore to detect these changes early.

student.html:

Lesson New words My example sentences

8 notable for, significant for, unremarkable, otherwise well, ongoing, worsening, x-day history, onset of, associated with

Presentation frame: identifying data → presenting complaint → HPI → PMH → medicines and allergies → social history → findings → plan.

Key language: Mrs. X is a 64-year-old woman with a history of… who presents with a 3-day history of… · I didn't assess that, but I can find out. I'd defer to the physician on that.

Written task: a 120-word case summary. Voice note: a 3-minute case presentation.

Cards and texts · Week 3

Jumbled case cards CP2 (fictional; cut them up and sort them into frame order, Lesson 7):

  1. smokes 10 cigarettes a day
  2. cough and shortness of breath for 5 days, worse at night
  3. no allergies
  4. plan as documented: chest X-ray and nebulizer as ordered
  5. Islom Rakhimov, 47, construction worker
  6. SpO2 93% on room air, RR 24; wheeze heard on the physician's examination

Compression drill (Lesson 8): say each sentence in presentation style. She started having pain 3 days ago and it's getting worse. · He has had diabetes for 10 years. · The chest X-ray didn't show anything important. · Apart from that she is healthy. · The main thing in his history is asthma. · She feels sick, and it comes with the headache.

Leaflet paragraph LF1 (fictional): Patients with hypertension should adhere to their prescribed antihypertensive regimen and monitor their blood pressure regularly. Sodium intake should be limited to reduce cardiovascular risk.

Leaflet LF2, Starting insulin at home (fictional; Lessons 14, 15 and 32):

  • Keep unopened pens in the fridge. The pen you are using can stay at room temperature for up to 28 days.
  • Inject into the abdomen or thigh, and rotate sites.
  • Check your sugar before breakfast and before dinner.
  • If it is under 70 mg/dL, take 4 glucose tablets and check again in 15 minutes.

  • Put used needles in the sharps container.

student.title: Difficult Conversations

Lesson New words My example sentences

20 absorb, understanding, family meeting, decision-maker, palliative care, comfort, uncertainty, spiritual care, chaplain
21 reflective listening, therapeutic silence, compassionate, self-care

NURSE: Name: It sounds like you're frightened. · Understand: I can understand why you'd feel that way. · Respect: You've been so strong. · Support: I'll be here. · Explore: Tell me more about what worries you most.

Key language: What's your understanding of what's happening? Some people like to hear everything themselves; others prefer their family to be involved. What would you like? · To Am I going to die?: That's a really important question, and I don't want to guess. I'll make sure the doctor talks with you about it today.

Written task: a 120-word note of a patient's concerns. Voice note: a NURSE-based response, then a handoff.

Cards and texts · Week 7

Card DN-A (fictional; Lessons 19–20): Mrs. Feruza Alimova, 52. An hour ago the doctor told her that her biopsy shows cancer and explained the plan. She is tearful: I keep thinking about my children.

Patient lines PL1–PL5 (fictional; Lesson 19): match each line to the best response, then name the NURSE type.

Line The patient says Response
PL1 I just keep shaking. I don't even know what I'm feeling. a. You've done so much for your family.
PL2 Anyone would be upset, wouldn't they? Or am I overreacting? b. Take your time. Tell me more about what's on your mind.
PL3 I looked after my husband for ten years, and now this. c. It sounds like this has been a real shock.
PL4 I'm scared of going through this alone. d. You won't be on your own. I'll be here, and the team will be with you.
PL5 There's something else bothering me, but it's hard to say. e. I can understand why you'd feel this way. It's a lot to take in.

Family dialogue (Lesson 20), listening questions: Who does the patient want informed? What two kinds of support are requested? Who should each request go to?

The five steps: Listen → Acknowledge → Apologize for the experience → Act → Follow up with a time.

Key language: I'm sorry this happened. Let me find out what happened. · I can see you're very upset. I want to help you. I can't help while you're shouting. · Never: Calm down! That's not my job. · Safety first: if you feel threatened, step away and call for help.

Stage Ask yourself Sentence starter
1 Description What happened? During a role-play,…
2 Feelings What did I think and feel? At the time I felt…

Final voice note: your 2-minute introduction as a future nurse.

Cards and texts · Week 12

Q1 (language practice, Lesson 34): A patient with diabetes makes the following statements about foot care. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. I will check my feet every day. B. I will walk barefoot at home to let my feet breathe. C. I will tell my nurse about any cuts. D. I will dry carefully between my toes.

Stem bank ST1–ST20 (language practice, not nursing content). ST1–ST5: Lesson 34 Round 1 · ST6–ST10: Round 3, timed · ST11–ST20: homework. Underline the key words, say what the question really asks, then choose.

ST1. A patient using insulin at home checks her sugar before breakfast. It is 62 mg/dL. According to leaflet LF2, what should she do first? A. Inject her morning insulin. B. Take 4 glucose tablets. C. Eat breakfast and check again tomorrow. D. Wait 2 hours and check again.

ST2. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I shake the inhaler before I use it." B. "I breathe out fully before I press." C. "I press twice quickly, then breathe in." D. "I rinse my mouth after my steroid inhaler."

ST3. According to lecture ML2, which patients have a higher risk of pressure injuries? Select all that apply. A. a patient after surgery who cannot move easily B. a very ill older adult C. a patient with poor nutrition and moist skin D. a young adult who walks every day

ST4. Lecture ML1 lists five moments for hand hygiene. They include all of the following except: A. before touching a patient B. after touching the patient's surroundings C. after contact with body fluids D. after reading the patient's chart at the desk

ST5. Which statement by a patient indicates understanding of leaflet LF2? A. "I'll keep the pen I'm using in the freezer." B. "I'll inject into the same spot every day." C. "I'll put used needles in the sharps container." D. "I'll check my feet once a month."

ST6. A patient asks a nursing student, "Am I going to die?" What is the most appropriate response? A. "No, everything will be fine." B. "That's an important question. Can you tell me what's making you think about it? I'll make sure the doctor talks with you today." C. "You should ask the doctor, not me." D. "Let's talk about something happier."

ST7. A student sees a colleague about to give room 4's medicine to the patient in room 6. What is the student's initial action? A. Report it at the end of the shift. B. Speak up now and ask to check the ID band together. C. Tell the patient not to take any medicine today. D. Say nothing, because the colleague is senior.

ST8. During a history, Mrs. Tursunova mentions several problems. Which one should the student report as the priority? A. knee pain when she walks B. a new sore on her big toe that she did not notice for a week C. the clinic is far from her home D. she finds sweets hard to refuse at weddings

ST9. A professional interpreter should do all of the following except: A. interpret everything that is said B. speak in the first person C. give the patient advice about treatment D. use a transparency statement to ask for a repetition

ST10. A nursing student is learning to respond to complaints. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I'm sorry this happened." B. "Let me find out what happened." C. "It was the night nurse's fault." D. "I'll come back by 5 p.m. with an update."

ST11. Which actions are part of the nurse's role in informed consent in the USA? Select all that apply. A. witnessing the patient's signature B. checking that the patient understands C. explaining the risks of the procedure instead of the provider D. telling the provider if the patient does not understand

ST12. A relative phones and asks for a patient's test results. What is the most appropriate response? A. Read the results to the caller quickly. B. "I'm sorry, I can't share any information over the phone." C. Give the results if the caller knows the patient's date of birth. D. "The results are fine; don't worry."

ST13. Mrs. Ahmedova ran out of her blood-pressure tablets a week ago. Her BP is 178/102. What is the most appropriate action for a nursing student? A. Give her a tablet from another patient's supply. B. Report the reading to the nurse and the physician. C. Tell her the reading is normal. D. Advise her to take two tablets tonight.

ST14. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I wait 30 seconds before a second puff." B. "I hold my breath for 10 seconds." C. "I don't need to rinse my mouth after a steroid inhaler." D. "I attach the spacer before I press."

ST15. A relative becomes threatening. The student should do all of the following except: A. step back to a safe distance B. leave the room C. call the charge nurse or security D. stand close and argue until he calms down

ST16. After teaching, which statement indicates that the patient understands what an HbA1c test measures? A. "It shows my sugar right now." B. "It shows my average blood sugar over about 3 months." C. "It measures my blood pressure." D. "It shows whether I have an infection."

ST17. Which sentences are written correctly for an incident report (IR1)? Select all that apply. A. "At 03:10 the patient was found on the floor beside his bed." B. "The patient fell because the night nurse forgot the bed rails." C. "He stated, 'I wanted to go to the toilet.'" D. "He was silly to get up alone."

ST18. A patient's son starts adding his own opinions while he interprets. What is the nurse's initial action? A. Continue, because the family knows best. B. Offer a professional interpreter. C. Ask the patient to speak English. D. End the visit.

ST19. Mr. Mirzaev often forgets his evening doses. Which question is most appropriate? A. "Why are you non-compliant?" B. "What gets in the way of taking your evening medicines?" C. "You should have taken them, shouldn't you?" D. "Do you want to get worse?"

ST20. Lecture ML2 lists three ways to prevent pressure injuries. They include all of the following except: A. changing the patient's position regularly B. keeping the skin clean and dry C. checking the skin every day D. keeping the patient in one position all night

student.title: Grammar Handbook
student.html:
How to use this handbook

This is the grammar companion to the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 books. Each lesson card names one grammar point; this handbook explains it in full. Teachers use it to prepare the 4-minute grammar slot. Students use it for homework and revision.

Most units follow this layout; reference units use tables instead:

  1. When we use it: the meanings, in short bullets.
  2. Structure: formulas for + (statement), − (negative) and ? (question), each with a healthcare example.
  3. Short answers and short forms.
  4. Keywords: the time words and signal words that go with it.
  5. Watch out!: the mistakes students make most, including typical mistakes of Uzbek speakers. ✗ = wrong, ✓ = right.
  6. Try it: 4 quick items, with the key underneath.

Symbols

Symbol Meaning Example
S subject The patient, she, I
V1 base form go, take, feel
V2 past form went, took, felt
V3 past participle gone, taken, felt
V-ing -ing form going, taking, feeling
(Q/W) question word (optional) what, where, when, how
+ / − / ? statement / negative / question

Part 3 · C1 Professional

Unit 28 · Discourse markers

When we use it: to show how ideas connect in lectures, presentations, essays and seminars.

Function Spoken / neutral Written / formal
Adding also, and, plus furthermore, moreover, in addition
Contrasting but, though however, in contrast, whereas, nevertheless, on the other hand
Cause because, since, as due to (+ noun), owing to
Result so therefore, consequently, as a result
Sequencing first, then, after that, finally firstly, secondly, subsequently, lastly
Example like, for example for instance, such as, to illustrate
Emphasis especially, the main thing is in particular, notably, the key point is
Conceding OK, but admittedly, while it is true that
Summarizing so, basically to sum up, in summary, overall

Grammar of linkers

  • However, Therefore, Consequently start a new sentence and take a comma: Hand hygiene prevents infection. However, it is often forgotten.
  • although, whereas, because join two clauses: Although she was in pain, she walked to the bathroom.
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite* the pain, she walked. Despite feeling* dizzy, she walked.
  • due to + noun: …due to time pressure (✗ due to people are busy).

Watch out!

  • ✗ Although she was tired, but she worked. Use one linker: ✓ Although she was tired, she worked.
  • ✗ despite of ✓ despite / in spite of.
  • Moreover in a conversation sounds like a lecture. Match the register.

Try it. (1) The test is painless. ___, it takes an hour. (2) ___ the noise, he slept well. (3) She missed her insulin; ___, her sugar rose. (4) ___ the leaflet is short, it is hard to read.

Show the answers

(1) However (2) Despite / In spite of (3) consequently / as a result (4) Although.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.

Try it. (1) She stopped ___ (smoke) last year. (2) The ___ (break) arm needs an X-ray. (3) The patient ___ (sit) by the window is Mr. Rakhimov. (4) The news was ___ (worry), so the family was ___ (worry).

Show the answers

(1) smoking (2) broken (3) sitting (4) worrying … worried.

Unit 31 · Cleft sentences and emphasis

When we use it: to put the most important information first, to prioritize in a summary, or to correct someone politely.

Pattern Structure Example
What-cleft What + S + V + is / was + focus What concerns me most is the new sore on her foot.
It-cleft It is / was + focus + that / who + rest It's* the evening doses that* he misses.
The thing / reason The thing that… / The reason (why)… + is (that) The reason* she stopped is that* the tablets are expensive.
All All + S + V + is All she needs is a little more time.

Correcting politely: It wasn't the morning dose she missed; it was the evening one.

Watch out!

  • No extra it: ✗ What concerns me most it is the sore. ✓ What concerns me most is the sore.
  • Keep the order: ✗ Is the evening dose that he misses. ✓ It's the evening dose that he misses.

Try it. Rewrite with emphasis: (1) The cost worries her. (What…) (2) He missed the Tuesday appointment. (It was…) (3) She needs a social worker. (What…) (4) She stopped because of the side effects. (The reason…)

Show the answers

(1) What worries her is the cost. (2) It was the Tuesday appointment that he missed. (3) What she needs is a social worker. (4) The reason (why) she stopped is (that) she had side effects.

Unit 32 · Tentative and diplomatic language

When we use it: to make suggestions to seniors, to disagree in a seminar, and to ask sensitive questions without pressure.

Function Phrases
Polite requests I was wondering whether… Would it be possible to…? Would you mind + V-ing?
Suggestions to the team Could we consider…? Would it be worth + V-ing…? It might be helpful to…
Sensitive questions I was wondering if you could tell me a bit about… What gets in the way of…?
Disagreeing I see it slightly differently. While I take your point,… I'm not sure I agree, because…
Not knowing I'm not sure, but I think… As far as I know,… I'd need to check.

Why the past tense sounds polite: I was wondering and I wanted to ask talk about now, but the past form adds distance and sounds less direct.

Softeners: a bit, slightly, perhaps, possibly, just (Could I just check…?).

But not for safety. When a patient may be harmed, be clear and firm (CUS): I'm concerned. I'm uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.

Watch out!

  • ✗ Would you mind to wait? ✓ Would you mind waiting?
  • Over-softening in an emergency causes delay: ✗ I was wondering whether you might possibly come… ✓ I need you to come now.

Try it. Make more tentative: (1) Book an interpreter. (2) You're wrong. (3) Can I ask about your alcohol use? (4) Review his pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) Could we consider booking an interpreter? (2) I see it slightly differently. (3) I was wondering if I could ask about your alcohol use. (4) Would it be worth reviewing his pain relief?

Mixed conditionals

Type If-clause Main clause Example
past cause → present result Past Perfect would + V1 If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be in hospital now.
present situation → past result Past Simple would have + V3 If he weren't so afraid of needles, he would have had the test last week.

Formal inversion (leaflets, letters, academic writing): drop if and invert.

  • Should you notice any redness, contact the clinic. (= If you notice…)
  • Had I known about the allergy, I would have said so. (= If I had known…)
  • Were the patient to refuse, the team would discuss alternatives. (= If the patient refused…)

Other ways to say if

Word Meaning Example

Watch out!

  • in case ≠ if: Take your inhaler in case you get wheezy (take it with you now anyway) vs Use your inhaler if you get wheezy (only when it happens).

Try it. (1) If I ___ (study) harder last year, I ___ (be) in nursing school now. (2) ___ you have any questions, please call. (3) Bring water ___ the wait is long. (4) You can drive ___ you don't feel drowsy.

Show the answers

(1) had studied … would be (2) Should (3) in case (4) as long as / provided that.

Unit 34 · Academic grammar: reporting verbs and the passive

When we use it: in summaries, care-plan rationales, essays and reflections.

Reporting verbs, from weak to strong

Strength Verbs Example
tentative suggests, indicates, implies The research suggests that lifestyle change can delay onset.
neutral states, reports, describes, notes The textbook states that…
strong shows, demonstrates, confirms, establishes The study demonstrates a clear link…
arguing argues, claims, maintains The author argues that…

The academic passive and impersonal structures

  • It is recommended that patients… It has been shown that…
  • Patients are advised to… Pressure injuries are associated with…
  • There is evidence* that… There is* a need for…

Tenses in academic writing

  • Present Simple for general facts and what a source says: Hand hygiene reduces infection. The author argues…
  • Past Simple for a specific study: The study found that…
  • Present Perfect for research up to now: Several studies have shown…

Style: no contractions (does not, not doesn't); avoid I think in essays (reflections are the exception: they use I); hedge claims (appears to, is likely to, may contribute to).

Watch out!

  • Too strong: ✗ This proves that… ✓ This suggests that…
  • Copying the source's sentence with small changes is plagiarism. Paraphrase fully and cite.

Try it. Make it academic: (1) Lots of studies show exercise helps. (2) Doctors say patients should check their feet. (3) I think the patient didn't understand. (4) This proves the leaflet works.

Show the answers

(1) Several studies have shown that exercise is beneficial. (2) Patients are advised to check their feet daily. (3) The patient appeared not to understand. (4) This suggests that the leaflet is effective.

Unit 2 · Nouns: singular and plural

When we use it: one thing = singular (a tablet); two or more = plural (two tablets).

Rule Ending Examples
Most nouns + -s nurse → nurses · bed → beds · lung → lungs
Ends in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x + -es bus → buses · glass → glasses · dish → dishes · patch → patches · box → boxes
Some nouns in -o + -es potato → potatoes · tomato → tomatoes (but photo → photos)
Consonant + y y → -ies artery → arteries · injury → injuries · baby → babies
Vowel + y + -s day → days · X-ray → X-rays · boy → boys
Ends in -f / -fe f → -ves half → halves · knife → knives · life → lives · wife → wives
Irregular new form man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · mouse → mice
No change same form sheep · fish · deer · series · species

Watch out!

  • After a number, English always needs the plural. Uzbek speakers often keep the noun singular after a number: ✗ three tablet. ✓ three tablets, two days, 5 milligrams.

  • Uncountable nouns have no plural: ✗ informations, advices, equipments (see Unit 17).
  • One child, two children; one foot, two feet: say these correctly in body and family vocabulary.

Try it. Make plural: (1) knee (2) diagnosis (3) child (4) injury.

(1) knees (2) diagnoses (3) children (4) injuries.

Unit 3 · Articles: a, an, the

When we use it

  • a / an = one, not a specific one; the first time we mention it: There's a patient in room 4.
  • the = a specific one that we both know; the second mention; something unique: The patient in room 4 is asleep. The heart pumps blood.
  • No article for plural or uncountable nouns in general: Nurses work long shifts. Blood carries oxygen.

A or an? It depends on the first sound, not the first letter.

an (vowel sound) a (consonant sound)
an apple, an injection a patient, a nurse
an hour (silent h) a hospital (h is heard)
an X-ray ("ex") a unit ("you")
an MRI ("em"), an ECG ("ee") a uniform, a European ("you")

Fixed phrases (no article): by mouth, at home, at work, go to bed, on duty. In the USA: in the hospital (UK: in hospital).

Watch out!

  • Uzbek has no articles, so learners drop them. ✗ She is nurse. ✓ She is a nurse. ✗ Patient is in room 5. ✓ The patient is in room 5.
  • Jobs always take a/an: I want to be a nurse. He is an anesthetist.
  • Don't use the with names: ✗ the Dr. Lee.

(1) an (2) an (3) The (4) a.

Unit 6 · To be (am, is, are · was, were · will be)

When we use it: to say what or who someone is, how they are, where they are, and their age.

Present Past Future

Structure

Formula Example

Short answers: Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. ✗ Yes, she's. (no short form in a yes short answer)

When we use it: to talk about possession, family, conditions and symptoms. I have diabetes. She has a fever. I've got a cough.

Unit 9 · Present Simple (Present Indefinite)

When we use it

  • Habits and repeated actions: She takes insulin every morning.
  • Schedules and timetables: Visiting hours start at 2 p.m.

  • States: I feel dizzy. He knows his medicines.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V1 (he / she / it + -s) I check my sugar daily. She checks her sugar daily.
− S + do / does + not + V1 I don't smoke. He doesn't drink alcohol.

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

He / she / it spelling: take → takes · wash → washes · cry → cries · go → goes · do → does · have → has.

Pronouncing -s: "s" in takes, checks · "z" in feels, needs · "iz" in washes, uses.

Keywords: every (day, morning, week) · always · usually · often · sometimes · occasionally · rarely · seldom · never · once / twice a day · from time to time.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She take insulin. ✓ She takes insulin.
  • Only one -s: ✗ Does she takes…? ✓ Does she take…?
  • ✗ He don't smoke. ✓ He doesn't smoke.

(1) has (2) Does … use (3) don't drink (4) filter.

Unit 10 · Present Continuous (Present Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action happening now: The patient is sleeping.
  • A temporary situation around now: I'm studying English this year.
  • A fixed plan for the future: She's having surgery on Monday.
  • An annoying repeated habit, with always: He's always pulling at his IV.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + V-ing My heart is beating fast.
− S + am / is / are + not + V-ing She isn't eating today.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + V-ing? Are* you having* trouble breathing?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.

Here be is a helper. I am a nurse (here am is the main verb) vs I am working (am only builds the tense).

-ing spelling: take → taking · sit → sitting · lie → lying · breathe → breathing.

Keywords: now · right now · at the moment · currently · today · this week · these days · still.

State verbs are not normally continuous: know, want, need, believe, understand, like, hate, seem, belong. ✗ I am knowing. ✓ I know. Feel and hurt can be both: My back hurts / is hurting.

  • Don't drop be: ✗ She sleeping. ✓ She is sleeping.
  • ✗ I am needing water. ✓ I need water.

Unit 11 · Past Simple (Past Indefinite)

When we use it: a finished action at a finished time in the past, with no link to now. She fell yesterday. He had surgery in 2015.

Formula Example
+ S + V2 (regular: -ed; irregular: see table D) The pain started on Sunday. I took a tablet.

-ed spelling: start → started · stop → stopped · cry → cried · use → used.

Pronouncing -ed: "t" in stopped, checked · "d" in called, used · "id" in started, needed.

Keywords: yesterday · ago · last (night, week, year) · in 2019 · at 3 a.m. · on Monday · when.

  • After did, use V1: ✗ Did you took it? ✓ Did you take it? ✗ She didn't came. ✓ She didn't come.

Unit 12 · Present Perfect

When we use it

  • A past action with a result now: I'm full. I have eaten. (Compare: I ate pasta yesterday: past only.)
  • Experience in life (any time until now): Have* you ever had* surgery?
  • A situation from the past until now: I've had this cough for three days.
  • Something just finished: The doctor has just left.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + V3 She has taken her tablets.
− S + have / has + not + V3 We haven't finished yet.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + V3? Have* you checked* your sugar today?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's / she's (here 's = has), haven't, hasn't.

Keywords: just · already · yet (in − and ?) · ever · never · recently · so far · today · this week · for · since.

For or since? for + a length of time: for three days, for a week · since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since this morning.

Present Perfect or Past Simple? Ask about life with the Present Perfect; give the details with the Past Simple: Have you ever had surgery? – Yes, I had my appendix out in 2015.

  • Uzbek uses the present for since: ✗ I am here since Monday. ✓ I've been here since Monday.

  • No finished time: ✗ I have seen the doctor yesterday. ✓ I saw the doctor yesterday.

Why reason Why did you stop the tablets?
How way, condition How are you feeling?
How long duration How long have you had it?
How often frequency How often do you use your inhaler?

How bad / How severe degree How bad is the pain from 0 to 10?

Word order: Q-A-S-V. (Q/W) + Auxiliary + Subject + main Verb: When did the pain start? How long have you been here?

Subject questions (the question word is the subject) have no do/does/did: Who called the ambulance? ✗ Who did call…?

Indirect (polite) questions: Could you tell me / Do you know + (Q/W) + S + V (normal order, no do): Could you tell me where the pharmacy is? Do you know when it started? ✗ Could you tell me where is the pharmacy?

Open and closed questions. Closed (Do you have pain?) gets yes/no. Open (Tell me about the pain) gets the story. Start interviews with open questions.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often make a question with intonation only. In English, use the helper verb: ✗ You have pain? ✓ Do you have pain?
  • Keep the helper before the subject: ✗ Where it hurts? ✓ Where does it hurt?

When we use it

Form Use Example

will a prediction or a fact about the future The test will take about 30 minutes.
will realistic hopes and fears I hope I'll pass. I'm afraid it will hurt.

going to a prediction from what we see now She's very pale. She's going to faint.
present continuous a fixed arrangement You're having an MRI tomorrow at 3.

Structure (will)

Formula Example
+ S + will + V1 The doctor will explain the results.
− S + will not (won't) + V1 It won't hurt.
? (Q/W) + will + S + V1? When will I get the results?

Short answers: Yes, it will. / No, it won't. · Short forms: I'll, you'll, she'll, won't.

Watch out!

  • No to after will: ✗ I will to call. ✓ I will call.

Unit 15 · Modal verbs

Modal Meaning Example

could polite request; past ability Could you spell that, please? I couldn't sleep.
may formal permission; possibility May I help you stand up? It may cause drowsiness.

Formula Example
+ S + modal + V1 She should take it with food.
− S + modal + not + V1 You mustn't drink alcohol with this.

Have to and need to behave like normal verbs: Do* I have to fast? She doesn't need to* come back.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She cans walk. ✓ She can walk. · ✗ You must to sign. ✓ You must sign.
  • mustn't ≠ don't have to. You mustn't eat = eating is forbidden. You don't have to eat = you can if you want.
  • In nursing, should sounds like advice. Report the clinician's advice: The doctor says you should rest.

Unit 18 · Relative clauses: who, which, where

When we use it: to say which person, thing or place we mean, or to add information.

Word For Example
who people A pharmacist is someone who prepares medicines.
which things This is the tablet which helps your blood pressure.
that people or things (defining only) The nurse that helped me was kind.
where places The ED is the place where urgent patients go.
when times Morning is the time when I check my sugar.
whose possession The patient whose daughter called is in room 5.

Defining (no commas): tells us which one. The nurse who looked after me was kind.

Non-defining (commas): adds extra information; never that. Mr. Saidov, who is 66, has diabetes.

Leaving out who / which / that: possible when it is the object: The tablet (that) you took is for pain. Not possible when it is the subject: ✗ The nurse helped me was kind.

Watch out!

  • ✗ the man which ✓ the man who · ✗ the pharmacy who ✓ the pharmacy **which / where.
  • No extra pronoun: ✗ The patient who he has diabetes… ✓ The patient who has diabetes…
  • Uzbek speakers often put the description before the noun: ✗ the has-diabetes patient. English puts it after: the patient who has diabetes.

Show the answers

(1) who (2) where (3) which / that / (nothing) (4) who.

Part 2 · B2 Clinical

Unit 19 · Past Continuous (Past Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action in progress at a moment in the past: At 3 a.m. he was sleeping.
  • A longer action interrupted by a shorter one (Past Simple): She was walking to the bathroom when she fell.
  • Two actions in progress at the same time: While* the nurse was checking his pulse, he was talking* to his son.
  • The background of a story: It was raining and the ED was getting busy.

The action has no link to now and no result: it was simply in progress.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + was / were + V-ing They were waiting in the waiting area.
− S + was / were + not + V-ing She wasn't breathing normally.
? (Q/W) + was / were + S + V-ing? What were you doing when the pain started?

Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren't. Short forms: only in the negative: wasn't, weren't.

Keywords: while · as · when · at (3 a.m.) yesterday · all night · at that moment.

When or while? when + the short action (Past Simple); while / as + the long action (Past Continuous).

Watch out!

  • ✗ When I was fall… ✓ When I fell… (the short action is Past Simple)
  • State verbs stay simple: ✗ I was knowing him. ✓ I knew him.

Try it. (1) He ___ (carry) boxes when he ___ (feel) the pain. (2) What ___ you ___ (do) at 11 p.m.? (3) While I ___ (cook), I ___ (cut) my finger. (4) She ___ (not / sleep) when the nurse came in.

Show the answers

(1) was carrying … felt (2) were … doing (3) was cooking … cut (4) wasn't sleeping.

Unit 20 · Present Perfect Continuous

When we use it

  • An activity that started in the past and is still going on, with focus on how long: I've been coughing for a week.
  • A recent activity with a result you can see: Her eyes are red. She's been crying.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + been + V-ing He has been using his inhaler more than usual.
− S + have / has + not + been + V-ing I haven't been sleeping well.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + been + V-ing? How long have you been having this pain?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Keywords: for · since · how long · all day · all week · lately · recently.

Simple or continuous?

Present Perfect Continuous Present Perfect Simple
duration, the activity itself result, a number, a completed amount
I've been taking this tablet for a year. I've taken three tablets today.
She's been waiting since 9. She's waited three hours. (finished or counted)

State verbs stay simple: I've had this cough for a week. I've known her for years. For repeated symptoms the continuous is fine: I've been having headaches lately.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present here: ✗ I am coughing since Monday. ✓ I've been coughing since Monday.
  • Don't forget been: ✗ I have coughing. ✓ I have been coughing.

Try it. (1) How long ___ you ___ (feel) like this? (2) She ___ (wait) since 9 a.m. (3) I ___ (have) diabetes for ten years. (4) He ___ (take) four tablets so far today.

Show the answers

(1) have … been feeling (2) has been waiting (3) have had (4) has taken.

Unit 21 · Past Perfect and narrative tenses

When we use it

  • Past Perfect (had + V3): an action before another past moment: When the ambulance arrived, she had already stopped bleeding.
  • Past Perfect Continuous (had been + V-ing): an activity that continued up to a past moment: She had been feeling dizzy all morning before she fell.

Structure (Past Perfect)

Formula Example
+ S + had + V3 He had taken his insulin before lunch.
− S + had + not + V3 She hadn't eaten since breakfast.
? (Q/W) + had + S + V3? Had* you felt* dizzy before the fall?

Short answers: Yes, I had. / No, she hadn't. Short forms: I'd, she'd (here 'd = had), hadn't.

Keywords: before · after · by the time · already · when · until · by (10 a.m.).

Telling a story in order: three tenses together

Tense Job Example
Past Continuous background At 2 p.m. she was walking to the bathroom…
Past Simple main events …when she slipped and hit her head.
Past Perfect earlier events She hadn't eaten since breakfast, and she had been feeling dizzy all morning.

Watch out!

  • When before / after already show the order, the Past Simple is fine: She ate before she took the tablet.
  • ✗ She had fell. ✓ She had fallen. (use V3: see table D)

Try it. (1) By the time the doctor came, the pain ___ (stop). (2) ___ he ___ (take) anything before he came in? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) for two days before the seizure. (4) He ___ (work) for 10 hours when he collapsed.

Show the answers

(1) had stopped (2) Had … taken (3) hadn't slept (4) had been working.

Unit 22 · The passive

When we use it: when the action matters more than who did it. Very common in reports, procedures, labels and textbooks.

Structure: a form of be + V3. Add by + person only if it matters.

Tense Passive Example
Present Simple am / is / are + V3 This tablet is taken by mouth.
Present Continuous am / is / are being + V3 The dressing is being changed.
Past Simple was / were + V3 The blood pressure was recorded at 10:00.
Present Perfect have / has been + V3 Has* the dressing been changed* today?
Future will be + V3 The results will be explained by the doctor.
Modal modal + be + V3 Consent must be obtained first.
Formula Example
+ S + be + V3 The sample was sent to the lab.
− S + be + not + V3 The site has not been marked.
? (Q/W) + be + S + V3? When was the patient admitted?

Watch out!

  • Use V3, not V2: ✗ The sample was took. ✓ The sample was taken.
  • Verbs with no object have no passive: ✗ It was happened. The patient was died. ✓ It happened. The patient died. (also arrive, occur, fall)
  • Speak actively to patients: You take it by mouth. Use the passive in notes and reports.

Try it. Make passive: (1) The nurse checks the ID band. (2) Someone took the sample at 8. (3) They will remove the stitches in 10 days. (4) Has anyone told the family?

Show the answers

(1) The ID band is checked. (2) The sample was taken at 8. (3) The stitches will be removed in 10 days. (4) Has the family been told?

Unit 23 · Reported speech

When we use it: to tell someone what another person said, asked or told them to do. Essential for handoffs and notes.

Say or tell? say (something): He said he was dizzy. · tell + person: He told me he was dizzy. ✗ He said me.

Statements: move one tense back

Direct speech Reported speech
"I feel dizzy." She said she felt dizzy.
"I'm having chest pain." He said he was having chest pain.
"I took it yesterday." She said she had taken it the day before.
"I'll call you." He said he would call me.
"I can't sleep." She said she couldn't sleep.

Also change: today → that day · yesterday → the day before · tomorrow → the next day · here → there · I / my → he / his.

Questions: normal word order, no do: "Where is the toilet?" → He asked where the toilet was. · Yes/no questions use if / whether: She asked if she could eat.

Instructions: told / asked + person + (not) to + V1: The doctor told him not to drive. · Labels: The label says to take it with food.

In clinical notes the present is normal: Patient reports pain 6/10. Denies nausea. States she slept badly. For a safety concern, quote the exact words: The patient stated, "I don't see the point anymore."

Watch out!

  • ✗ He asked where is the toilet. ✓ He asked where the toilet was.
  • ✗ She told to wait. ✓ She told me to wait.

Try it. Report: (1) "I have a headache." (she) (2) "Did you take your insulin?" (the nurse asked him) (3) "Don't eat after midnight." (the doctor told her) (4) "I'll come back at 5." (he)

Show the answers

(1) She said she had a headache. (2) The nurse asked him if he had taken his insulin. (3) The doctor told her not to eat after midnight. (4) He said he would come back at 5.

Unit 24 · Conditionals: zero, first, second, third

Type Meaning If-clause Main clause Example
Zero facts, always true Present Simple Present Simple If blood sugar drops too low, people feel shaky.
First real, possible future Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction If the pain gets worse, I'll call the nurse. If you notice a fever, call the clinic.
Second unreal or unlikely, present or future Past Simple / Past Continuous would / could / might + V1 If you stopped smoking, your breathing would improve.
Third unreal past (it didn't happen) Past Perfect would / could / might + have + V3 If I had known about the allergy, I would have told the doctor.

Structure notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. If it comes first, use a comma: If it hurts, tell me. / Tell me if it hurts.
  • Negatives: If you don't take it, … · If I hadn't checked, … · … it wouldn't help.
  • Questions: What will you do if the patient refuses? What would you do if a patient shouted at you?
  • Unless = if not: Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
  • Second conditional with be: were for all persons in formal English: If I were you, I'd ask the pharmacist.

Watch out!

  • No will in the if-clause: ✗ If you will notice redness… ✓ If you notice redness…
  • No would in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known… ✓ If I had known…
  • First or second? First = it may really happen. Second = imagined: If I win the scholarship, I'll… (I applied) vs If I were the surgeon, I would… (imagined: I am a nursing student).

Try it. (1) If you ___ (feel) dizzy, sit down. (2) If she ___ (have) more time, she would study more. (3) If he ___ (call) earlier, we ___ (help) him. (4) Water ___ (boil) if you heat it to 100 °C.

Show the answers

(1) feel (2) had (3) had called … would have helped (4) boils.

Unit 25 · Question tags

When we use it: to check information you think is true. Very useful in medication reconciliation and handoffs.

Structure: positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. The tag uses the same helper verb (or do / does / did).

Sentence Tag
You take it twice a day, don't you?
You haven't eaten since midnight, have you?
She's allergic to penicillin, isn't she?
He took it this morning, didn't he?
You'll come back on Tuesday, won't you?
You can walk, can't you?
I'm next, aren't I? (special form)

Intonation: falling = you're confirming, you expect yes. Rising = a real question, you're not sure.

Answer the fact, not the tag: You don't smoke, do you? – No, I don't. (= I don't smoke)

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often use one tag for everything: ✗ You take it twice a day, isn't it? ✓ …, don't you?
  • Match the tense: ✗ He took it, doesn't he? ✓ …, didn't he?

Try it. (1) You live alone, ___? (2) She hasn't had surgery, ___? (3) It was this morning, ___? (4) You'll call us, ___?

Show the answers

(1) don't you (2) has she (3) wasn't it (4) won't you.

Unit 26 · Hedging and deduction

When we use it: to show how sure we are. Nurses report facts carefully and never sound more certain than they are.

Possibility: may, might, could + V1

  • This medicine may cause drowsiness. (labels, leaflets)
  • The change might be important. I'll tell the nurse.
  • Her symptoms could be related to the new tablet. (in a discussion with the team, not a diagnosis for the patient)

Deduction: how sure am I?

Certainty Present Past Example
sure it's true must + V1 / be must have + V3 You must be exhausted. She must have fallen.
possible may / might / could + V1 may / might / could have + V3 He might be in pain. She could have missed a dose.
sure it's not true can't + V1 / be can't have + V3 That can't be easy. He can't have taken it: the box is full.

Appearance verbs (observations, not conclusions): He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. She seems to be in pain. He looks pale.

Softening words: possibly, probably, likely, approximately, about, around, tends to.

Watch out!

  • No to after modals: ✗ He must to be tired. ✓ He must be tired.
  • maybe (adverb) vs may be (verb): Maybe it's the medicine. = *It may be* the medicine.
  • ✗ She seems is tired. ✓ She seems tired / seems to be tired.

Try it. (1) You've worked 12 hours. You ___ be tired. (2) The box is full. She ___ have taken any tablets. (3) Her fever ___ come back tonight, so check it at 10 p.m. (4) He ___ (appear) confused.

Show the answers

(1) must (2) can't (3) may / might (4) appears.
