6–24 H Teach the 10 words and NURSE. Silence is a skill: count to 5 before speaking.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak; patient lines PL1–PL5 (below), each matched to the best NURSE response.
32–50 F Round 1: respond to PL1–PL5 in your own words, one per NURSE type. Round 2: a conversation with card DN-A. Round 3 (new detail): the patient is angry, not sad: Why did nobody find this earlier? The student names the anger and doesn't defend or blame.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one statement of each NURSE type. Set homework.

Card DN-A (fictional): Mrs. Feruza Alimova, 52. An hour ago the doctor told her that her biopsy shows cancer and explained the plan. She is tearful: I keep thinking about my children.

Patient lines PL1–PL5 (fictional) and NURSE responses a–e (for matching):

Line The patient says Response
PL1 I just keep shaking. I don't even know what I'm feeling. a. You've done so much for your family.
PL2 Anyone would be upset, wouldn't they? Or am I overreacting? b. Take your time. Tell me more about what's on your mind.
PL3 I looked after my husband for ten years, and now this. c. It sounds like this has been a real shock.
PL4 I'm scared of going through this alone. d. You won't be on your own. I'll be here, and the team will be with you.
PL5 There's something else bothering me, but it's hard to say. e. I can understand why you'd feel this way. It's a lot to take in.

Key: PL1 c (Name) · PL2 e (Understand) · PL3 a (Respect) · PL4 d (Support) · PL5 b (Explore).

Observer checks: emotion named · silence used · no false reassurance (Everything will be fine) · at least one exploring question.

Stretch: combine two NURSE types in one turn. Support: NURSE card.

Homework: record 5 NURSE responses to DN-A.

Lesson 20 · B Practice · After difficult news
Goal Support a patient and family after difficult news.
New words (9) absorb, understanding, family meeting, decision-maker, palliative care, comfort, uncertainty, spiritual care, chaplain
Recycle dignity, preference, empathic statement
Language What's your understanding of what's happening? I wonder if… Would it help if…? Some people like to hear everything themselves; others prefer their family to be involved. What would you like?
Spark Listen and Answer (a family conversation)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: respond to DN-A with three NURSE types. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Palliative care = care focused on comfort and quality of life. In many Uzbek families the eldest son speaks for the family: ask the patient what they want, never assume.
16–30 I Spark: Listen and Answer (below).
30–50 F Round 1: check DN-A's understanding after the doctor's visit. Round 2: a family meeting role-play (the teacher plays the patient and the son); the student asks the patient's preference first. Round 3 (new detail): Am I going to die? The student responds (model below).
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 understanding question + 1 preference question. Set homework.

Family dialogue (teacher reads): Patient (Mr. Akbar Nurmatov, 74): My son Jasur handles these things. Tell him everything; I'll listen. Son: We'd like to know about palliative care, and my father would like an imam to visit. Questions: Who does the patient want informed? What two kinds of support are requested? Who should each request go to? Key: his son, with the patient present; palliative-care information (to the team) and spiritual care (chaplaincy can arrange an imam).

Model response to Am I going to die?: That's a really important question, and I don't want to guess. Can I ask what's making you think about that? I'll make sure the doctor talks with you about it today.

Observer checks: the patient's preference asked first · no prognosis given · requests referred to the right person · respectful of culture.

Homework: record the response to Am I going to die? and one preference question.

Lesson 21 · C Perform · A supportive conversation
Goal Hold a 5-minute supportive conversation and pass on what the patient needs.
New words (4) reflective listening, therapeutic silence, compassionate, self-care
Recycle NURSE, acknowledge, explore
Language Reflecting back: So what I'm hearing is… It sounds as if the hardest part is…
Spark Mystery Patient (a hidden concern)
Perform task Recorded 5-minute conversation and a 30-second handoff to the nurse; written 120-word note
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: How do nurses look after themselves after hard conversations? (self-care)
5–12 H 4 new words. Model reflecting back.
12–20 I Explain the task: the patient's first worry may not be the real one.
20–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient with card DN-B. Then the performance: a 5-minute conversation and a 30-second handoff to the nurse, recorded. Then 10 minutes to write the 120-word note.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the note. Brief debrief: How did that feel?

Card DN-B (hidden, fictional): Mrs. Lobar Qodirova, 67, admitted for tests. She talks first about pain (3/10, managed). Her real worry, which she shares only if the student explores and reflects: Who will look after my son? He has a disability and I'm his only carer.

Handoff model: Mrs. Qodirova's pain is 3 out of 10. Her main worry is care for her son, who has a disability; she is his only carer. Could we ask the social worker to see her?

Observer checks: the real concern found · reflecting back used · silence allowed · a correct referral in the handoff.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): a NURSE-based response to DN-A, then the DN-B handoff.

teacher.title: Complaints and De-escalation
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can respond to a complaint without blaming anyone, calm an angry relative while staying safe, and write a factual summary of a complaint.

Written task: an 80-word factual summary of complaint C3.

Prepare: complaint cards C1–C3 and angry-relative card AR1 (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 8).

The five steps: Listen → Acknowledge → Apologize for the experience → Act (or find someone who can) → Follow up with a time.

Lesson 22 · A Learn · Complaints and apologies
Goal Respond to a complaint without blaming anyone.
New words (10) complaint, grievance, patient relations, service recovery, accountability, fault, inconvenience, resolve, expectation, sincere
Recycle acknowledge, escalate, empathic statement
Language Apologize for the experience, not with blame: I'm sorry this happened. I'm sorry you've had to wait. ✗ It was the night nurse's fault. Let me find out what happened.
Spark Register Switch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Describe good customer service you've received. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words and the five steps. Patient relations = the hospital office that handles complaints.
24–32 I Model a response to C1 (below). Spark: Register Switch on C1: to the patient, to the charge nurse (factual), to the family, in Uzbek.
32–50 F Round 1: respond to C1 with the five steps. Round 2: complaint C2. Round 3 (new detail): Give me the name of the night nurse. I'm reporting her. The student answers: You have every right to raise this. I can put you in touch with patient relations.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 sincere apology without blame. Set homework.

Complaint cards (fictional): C1 – I've been waiting three hours for my pain medicine! Nobody answers the call button! C2 – My mother's meals arrive cold every day, and nobody helps her eat.

Model response to C1: I'm really sorry you've been waiting in pain; that shouldn't happen. Let me check your medicine with your nurse right now. I'll come back in 10 minutes to tell you what's happening.

Register Switch on C1 (model): to the patient: I'm really sorry you've been waiting in pain. I'm checking your medicine with your nurse right now. · to the charge nurse (factual): My patient has waited three hours for his pain medicine and says the call button wasn't answered. Could you check his order with me now? · to the family: I'm sorry your father has been waiting. I'm checking his pain medicine with his nurse now, and I'll come back to you in 10 minutes. · in Uzbek (to the patient): Og‘riq qoldiruvchi doringizni uch soat kutganingiz uchun uzr so‘rayman. Hozir hamshirangiz bilan tekshiraman va 10 daqiqadan keyin qaytib kelib aytaman.

Observer checks: all 5 steps · no blame on colleagues · a concrete action · a follow-up time.

Stretch: handle a complaint that is partly unfair, politely. Support: five-step card.

Homework: record responses to C1 and C2.

Lesson 23 · B Practice · De-escalation
Goal Calm an angry relative, set limits and stay safe.
New words (9) de-escalate, raised voice, personal space, body language, threatening, security, safe distance, cool down, limit-setting
Recycle boundary, frustrated, grievance
Language Calm and firm: I can see you're very upset. I want to help you. I can't help while you're shouting at me. Would you like to sit down and tell me what happened?
Spark Error Hunt (inflaming phrases)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: respond to C2. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Body language: open hands, side-on, at a safe distance, a lower voice. Safety first: if there is a threat, step away and call for help.
16–30 I Spark: Error Hunt; the student repairs each phrase: Calm down! · That's not my job. · You'll have to wait like everyone else. · There's nothing I can do.
30–50 F Round 1: angry relative AR1. Round 2: AR1 raises his voice; the student sets a limit calmly and offers a choice. Round 3 (unseen): a relative becomes threatening; the student steps back, leaves the room and calls the charge nurse or security.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 1 limit-setting sentence + 1 choice. Set homework.

Error Hunt key: Calm down! → I can see you're upset. · That's not my job. → Let me find the right person for you. · You'll have to wait like everyone else. → I know waiting is hard. Here's what's happening… · There's nothing I can do. → Here's what I can do right now…

Card AR1 (fictional): Mr. Jahongir Sultonov, 40, son of a patient: My father has been here since morning and no doctor has seen him! This is unacceptable!

Observer checks: no inflaming phrases · the feeling named · the limit set calmly · safety chosen over finishing the conversation.

Homework: record the AR1 de-escalation.

Lesson 24 · C Perform · Handling a complaint
Goal Handle a complaint and write a factual summary.
New words (4) verbatim, chronological, factual account, follow-up action
Recycle grievance, patient relations, de-escalate
Language Neutral past narrative: At 14:10 Ms. X stated that… I apologized… I informed… at 14:25.
Spark 60-Second Report
Perform task Recorded complaint conversation (C3) and a written 80-word factual summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: the AR1 de-escalation.
5–12 H 4 new words. Verbatim = in the person's exact words.
12–20 I Model the written summary (below).
20–50 F Spark: 60-Second Report on C3 to the charge nurse. Then the performance: handle C3 with the five steps (recorded), then write the 80-word summary in 10 minutes.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the summary. Two errors, then retry.

Complaint C3 (fictional): Mrs. Sevara Hamidova, daughter of Mrs. Dilnoza Ergasheva (room 15): her mother's upper dentures went missing during the transfer from the ED yesterday; My mother can't eat properly. She is upset and asks who will pay.

Model summary: At 14:10 on 11/07, Mrs. Hamidova, daughter of Mrs. Ergasheva (room 15), reported that her mother's upper dentures were missing after transfer from the ED on 11/06. She stated, "My mother can't eat properly." I apologized, searched the room and bedside locker (not found), and informed charge nurse Anna at 14:25. Patient relations was contacted at 14:40. She asked who would pay for new dentures. I told Mrs. Hamidova I would update her by 17:00.

Observer checks: chronological · a verbatim quote · no opinions or blame · follow-up action and time.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the C3 conversation, improved.

teacher.title: Interprofessional Communication
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can give a concise update on rounds and make a tactful suggestion, read back orders and speak up about safety, and represent the nursing view in a care conference.

Written task: a 100-word action-point summary of care conference CC1.

Prepare: the rounds script; card RN1, orders TO1–TO3 and the CC1 role cards (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 9); the unseen CUS scenario.

Lesson 25 · A Learn · Ward rounds
Goal Give a concise nursing update and make a tactful suggestion.
New words (10) rounds, multidisciplinary team, physiotherapist, dietitian, social worker, case manager, overnight events, plan of care, tactful, input
Recycle concise, attending physician, prioritize
Language Tactful suggestions: Would it be worth…? Could we consider…? I wonder whether… might help.
Spark Listen and Answer (a round)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: the C3 complaint summary. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words: who does what in the team.
24–32 I Spark: Listen and Answer; the teacher reads the round (below). Questions: What is the oxygen plan? What is the walking goal? Who leads discharge planning?
32–50 F Round 1: a 30-second nursing update on RN1 in rounds. Round 2: add a tactful suggestion. Round 3 (new detail): the physician disagrees; the student acknowledges, gives one reason, and escalates later if still concerned.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 tactful suggestions. Set homework.

Round script (teacher reads): Physician: Mrs. Yuldasheva, day 3 after admission with pneumonia. Overnight, temperature 37.6, saturations 95% on 1 liter. Plan: continue antibiotics and wean the oxygen. Physiotherapist: She walked 20 meters today; the goal is 40 tomorrow. Dietitian: She's eating about 30% of meals; we'll start supplements. Social worker: She lives alone, and her daughter is abroad, so we need to start discharge planning. Key: wean the oxygen; 40 m tomorrow; the social worker.

Card RN1 (fictional): Mr. Usmon Karimov, 77, day 2 after hip-fracture surgery. Confused 2–4 a.m. overnight and pulled at his IV; pain 4/10; eating 25%; passing urine; his daughter speaks only Uzbek. Model suggestions: Could we consider booking an interpreter for the family meeting? I wonder whether a review of his night-time confusion might help.

Observer checks: update under 30 seconds · overnight events first · suggestion tactful · disagreement handled respectfully.

Homework: record the RN1 update and 2 suggestions.

Lesson 26 · B Practice · Read-back and speaking up
Goal Read back orders exactly and voice a safety concern.
New words (9) verbal order, telephone order, CUS, two-challenge rule, speak up, safety culture, near miss, hierarchy, assertive
Recycle closed-loop communication, read-back, escalate
Language CUS: I'm Concerned… I'm Uncomfortable… This is a Safety issue. The two-challenge rule: say it at least twice.
Spark Number Catch
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Why is it hard to question a senior doctor? Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Nursing students never take verbal or telephone orders; they say: "I'm a nursing student, so I can't take orders. Let me get my nurse." Read-back is practiced here in the role of a licensed nurse, for later. Spark: Number Catch: 0.5 mg / 5 mg · 15 units / 50 units · every 6 hours · 3 L/min. Always say units in full.
16–30 I Model reading back TO1–TO3 (below).
30–50 F Round 1: in the role of a licensed nurse, the student reads back TO1–TO3 exactly. Round 2: first, the teacher, as a physician, phones the student with an order; the student declines within scope and fetches the nurse. Then, in the licensed-nurse role, the teacher gives an unclear order (Give him 10 of insulin); the student clarifies the unit and the route. Round 3 (unseen): the CUS scenario; the student speaks up twice.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one full CUS statement. Set homework.

Fictional orders and read-back (practiced in the role of a licensed nurse; students never take orders): TO1 – Give KALIXOR 20 milligrams IV once, now. · TO2 – Recheck blood glucose in 2 hours. · TO3 – Increase oxygen to 3 liters per minute via nasal cannula. Read-back: Let me read that back: Kalixor 20 milligrams IV, once, now. Recheck blood glucose in 2 hours. Increase oxygen to 3 liters per minute via nasal cannula. Is that correct?

CUS scenario (fictional): Akmal Rakhimov (room 4) and Akbar Rakhimov (room 6). A colleague is about to give room 4's medicine to the patient in room 6. Model: Excuse me, I'm concerned: this is Akbar Rakhimov, not Akmal. I'm uncomfortable going ahead. This is a safety issue: can we check the ID band together?

Observer checks: numbers and units exact · Is that correct? asked · concern raised calmly · repeated if ignored.

Homework: record the 3 read-backs and the CUS statement.

Lesson 27 · C Perform · Care conference
Goal Represent the nursing view and summarize agreed actions.
New words (4) agenda, consensus, compromise, action point
Recycle multidisciplinary team, tactful, plan of care
Language From a nursing perspective… Could we compromise by…? So, to summarize, we've agreed that…
Spark Mystery Patient (hidden team views)
Perform task Recorded care-conference contribution and summary; written 100-word action-point summary
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: the CUS scenario from memory.
5–12 H 4 new words. Model a summary of agreed actions.
12–20 I Spark: Mystery Patient; the student asks each "team member" (the teacher or classmates with role cards) for their view on CC1.
20–50 F Then the performance: a 10-minute care conference on CC1. The student gives the nursing view, suggests a compromise, and closes with a summary of action points. Recorded. Then 8 minutes to write the 100-word summary.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark the summary. Two errors, then retry.

Care conference CC1, Mr. Karimov's discharge (role cards): Daughter (through an interpreter): wants him home with her now. Physiotherapist: he needs about 2 more weeks of rehabilitation. Social worker: a rehab bed is available on Monday. Patient (through an interpreter): wants to go home. Nursing view (the student): confused at night; needs supervision at night. A possible agreement: rehab for 2 weeks, then home with his daughter; a home-safety visit; an interpreter for every family meeting.

Observer checks: everyone's view heard · the nursing view clear · a compromise offered · action points with names.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the CC1 summary of agreed actions.

teacher.title: Clinical and Academic Writing
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can write a care-plan entry with a SMART goal, an objective incident report, and a structured 250-word reflection.

Written task: the 250-word reflection (Lesson 30).

Prepare: the care-plan template, patient card PI1, incident IR1, the flawed report and the Gibbs cycle sheet (all printed in the Student Edition, Cards and texts · Week 10).

A note on terms: a nursing diagnosis is a nursing-school writing format about the patient's response and needs. It is not a medical diagnosis.

Lesson 28 · A Learn · Nursing care plans
Goal Write a care-plan entry.
New words (10) nursing diagnosis, related to, as evidenced by, short-term goal, long-term goal, measurable, time-bound, nursing intervention, evaluation, NANDA-I
Recycle rationale, intervention, outcome
Language The formula: [Problem] related to [cause] as evidenced by [signs]. SMART goals: Patient will walk 40 m with a walker by day 3.
Spark Match and Speak (care-plan parts ↔ examples)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: the CC1 action points. Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. NANDA-I = the standard list of nursing diagnoses many US schools use. Risk for… diagnoses list risk factors and have no as evidenced by.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak (diagnosis, goal, intervention, rationale, evaluation ↔ examples). Read the model (below).
32–50 F Round 1: the student explains the model care plan aloud. Round 2: writes an entry for patient card PI1 (below): Impaired skin integrity related to… as evidenced by… Round 3: fixes vague goals: Patient will feel better → a SMART goal.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: one SMART goal. Set homework.

Model care plan (Mr. Karimov, RN1): Nursing diagnosis: Risk for falls related to night-time confusion and recent hip surgery. Goal: Patient will remain free from falls during the hospital stay. Interventions: bed in the lowest position; call button within reach; hourly checks at night; the call button explained through an interpreter. Rationale: reduces the chance of unassisted getting up at night. Evaluation: no falls recorded at discharge.

Patient card PI1 (fictional): Mr. Rustam Aliev, 81, day 5 after a stroke · cannot turn himself in bed · eats about half of his meals · incontinent of urine · on assessment, a 3 × 2 cm area of red, broken skin over the sacrum (base of the spine) · pain 3/10 when turned. Model entry: Nursing diagnosis: Impaired skin integrity related to immobility and moisture as evidenced by a 3 × 2 cm area of broken skin over the sacrum. Goal: The wound will not increase in size, and no new pressure injuries will develop, by day 10. Interventions: reposition about every 2 hours; keep the skin clean and dry; check the skin over bones daily; report any change to the RN. Rationale: less pressure and moisture protect the skin. Evaluation: wound measured and documented on day 10.

Stretch: write a second goal for mobility. Support: the formula card.

Homework: write one complete care-plan entry for case CI3.

Lesson 29 · B Practice · Incident reports
Goal Write an objective, chronological incident report.
New words (9) incident report, occurrence, witness statement, contributing factor, harm, no-harm event, just culture, root cause, unwitnessed
Recycle near miss, chronological, factual account
Language Facts only, no blame or guessing. Patient was found on the floor beside the bed at 03:10 (not fell, if nobody saw it).
Spark Error Hunt (a flawed report)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: explain your CI3 care plan. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. Just culture = reports are for learning, not punishment.
16–30 I Spark: Error Hunt on the flawed report (below).
30–50 F Round 1: the student lists IR1's facts in order. Round 2: writes the report (12 minutes). Round 3: reads it aloud; the teacher, as manager, asks factual questions.
50–60 O Compare with the model. Two errors, then retry. Set homework.

Incident IR1 (fictional): 03:10, Mr. Karimov found on the floor beside his bed; bed rails down; call button out of reach. He said, I wanted to go to the toilet. A 2 cm skin tear on the left forearm. Vital signs within his usual range. Physician notified at 03:20. Daughter informed at 08:00 through an interpreter.

Flawed report: The patient fell because the night nurse forgot the bed rails. He was confused and silly to get up alone. He wasn't hurt badly. Key: blame on a colleague; a judgment (silly); fell is a guess, as nobody saw it; the injury is vague; no times.

Model report: At 03:10 on 11/07, Mr. Karimov was found on the floor beside his bed. The bed rails were down and the call button was out of reach. He stated, "I wanted to go to the toilet." A 2 cm skin tear was noted on the left forearm. Vital signs were within his usual range. The physician was notified at 03:20. His daughter was informed at 08:00 through an interpreter.

Observer checks: times for every event · found not fell · a verbatim quote · no blame or opinion.

Homework: rewrite the flawed report correctly.

Lesson 30 · C Perform · Reflective writing
Goal Write a 250-word reflection using the Gibbs cycle.
New words (4) Gibbs cycle, on reflection, in hindsight, learning point
Recycle debrief, self-care, contributing factor
Language At the time I felt… On reflection,… In hindsight, I would… This links to… Next time I will…
Spark Register Switch
Perform task Written 250-word reflection and a recorded 60-second oral version
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: What did you learn from the hardest role-play in this course?
5–12 H 4 new words. Gibbs: Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusion → Action plan.
12–20 I Spark: Register Switch: one event (complaint C3) told to a classmate in a debrief, in a reflection, in an incident report and in Uzbek to the daughter (model below). Read the model excerpt.
20–50 F The student chooses one course role-play (for example DN-B or C3), plans the 6 stages, then writes 250 words (20 minutes). Then the performance: a 60-second oral version, recorded.
50–60 O Mark the reflection for structure, honesty and an action plan. Set the weekly voice note.

Model excerpt: During a role-play, a patient's daughter complained that her mother's dentures had been lost. At the time I felt defensive, because it was not my fault. On reflection, my first sentence sounded like an excuse rather than an apology. In hindsight, I would have acknowledged her frustration before explaining anything. This links to the service-recovery steps we studied. Next time I will listen fully first and give a clear follow-up time.

Register Switch on C3 (model): to a classmate (debrief, no patient names): The daughter in my role-play was really upset about her mom's lost dentures, and I got defensive at first. · in a reflection: At the time I felt defensive; on reflection, I should have acknowledged her frustration first. · in an incident report: At 14:10 the patient's daughter reported that her mother's upper dentures were missing after transfer from the ED. · in Uzbek (to the daughter): Onangizning tish protezi yo‘qolgani uchun juda afsusdaman. Bu haqda katta hamshiraga xabar berdim va soat 17:00 gacha sizga javob beraman.

Observer checks: all 6 stages · honest feelings · one concrete action plan · 250 words, plus or minus 20.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): the oral version of your reflection.

teacher.title: Medical Interpreting (Uzbek ↔ English)
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can explain and follow interpreter ethics, interpret long turns with notes, sight-translate a short form, and interpret a full doctor–patient encounter.

Why this week matters: this is the ShifoLife signature skill. Bilingual nurses are often asked to interpret. Doing it well protects patients; doing it badly puts them at risk.

Written task: a written Uzbek translation of leaflet LF2.

Prepare: the ethics situations and the Uzbek Bridge lines (students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 11); leaflet LF2; Hot Seat turns HS1–HS3, long turns LT1–LT2 and the sample LF2 translation (Lesson 32); encounter ENC1 and the flawed interpretation (unseen). The teacher must be a fluent Uzbek speaker for this week.

Lesson 31 · A Learn · The interpreter's role
Goal Explain and follow interpreter ethics.
New words (10) accuracy, completeness, impartiality, transparency, conflict of interest, consecutive interpreting, sight translation, positioning, intervention, ad hoc interpreter
Recycle confidentiality, first-person address, cultural broker
Language Transparency statements in the third person: The interpreter needs to ask for a repetition. The interpreter would like to clarify a term.
Spark Uzbek Bridge
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: Have you ever interpreted for family? What was hard? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words as rules: interpret everything, add nothing, take no side, keep it confidential, speak in the first person, step out of the role only with a transparency statement. Ad hoc interpreter = an untrained person (often family) used to interpret.
24–32 I Spark: Uzbek Bridge (below).
32–50 F Round 1: the student explains the rules to a nurse (the teacher). Round 2: ethics situations (below); the student responds as the interpreter. Round 3 (unseen): the patient whispers something to the interpreter only.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: 2 transparency statements. Set homework.

Uzbek Bridge (C1 level):

Uzbek Model English
Doktor, uch kundan beri ichim qattiq sanchib og‘riyapti, ayniqsa ovqatdan keyin. Doctor, for three days I've had sharp, stabbing pains in my stomach, especially after eating.
Rostini aytsam, dorilarni har doim ham ichmayman, chunki ular qimmat. To be honest, I don't always take my medicines, because they're expensive.
Iltimos, bu haqda qizimga aytmang. Please don't tell my daughter about this.

Reverse: We'd like to do a blood test and an ultrasound of your abdomen today. → Uzbek. Model: Bugun sizdan qon tahlili olmoqchimiz va qorin bo‘shlig‘ingizni ultratovush tekshiruvidan o‘tkazmoqchimiz.

Ethics situations and model responses: Don't tell the doctor I smoke → The interpreter must interpret everything that is said, so the interpreter will interpret this. · What would you do in my place? → The interpreter can't give advice. Please ask the doctor. · A relative interpreting adds his own opinion → the nurse offers a professional interpreter.

Round 3 (unseen), the patient whispers to the interpreter only: Xotinimning dorilarini ham ichib yuribman. Doktorga aytmang. (I've been taking my wife's tablets too. Don't tell the doctor.) Model response: to the patient, in Uzbek: Kechirasiz, men aytilgan hamma narsani tarjima qilishim kerak. (I'm sorry, I have to interpret everything that is said.) Then to the doctor: The interpreter needs to let you know that the patient said something to the interpreter only. The patient said: "I've been taking my wife's tablets too. Don't tell the doctor."

Observer checks: first person kept · nothing added · transparency statements in the third person · no advice given.

Homework: record the 3 Uzbek Bridge lines and the reverse line.

Lesson 32 · B Practice · Consecutive and sight translation
Goal Interpret long turns with notes and sight-translate a form.
New words (9) segment, retention, omission, addition, substitution, distortion, idiom, equivalence, interpreter's notes
Recycle accuracy, completeness, transparency
Language Interpreter notes: numbers, names, negatives and time words first; symbols from Week 1
Spark Hot Seat Interpreting (3–4 sentence turns)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: the interpreter rules from memory. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words: the 4 error types (omission, addition, substitution, distortion).
16–30 I Spark: Hot Seat Interpreting: Uzbek turns HS1–HS3 (below); the student takes notes, then interprets.
30–50 F Round 1: consecutive interpreting with notes, English → Uzbek (long turns LT1–LT2, below). Round 2: sight-translate LF2 into Uzbek. Round 3 (unseen): idioms (below); the student interprets faithfully and flags the ambiguity with a transparency statement.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: name the 4 error types with an example of each. Set homework.

Idioms that can mislead: Yuragim siqilyapti can mean chest tightness or feeling anxious or sad. Ichim kuyyapti can mean heartburn or deep grief. Model: The interpreter would like to note that this phrase can mean chest tightness or feeling anxious. May the interpreter ask the patient to explain?

Hot Seat turns HS1–HS3 (Uzbek → English, fictional):

Turn Uzbek Model English
HS1 Ikki kundan beri boshim qattiq og‘riyapti. Ertalab qon bosimimni o‘lchasam, 170 ga 100 ekan. Dorim uch kun oldin tugab qolgan. Ko‘zim oldida qora nuqtalar paydo bo‘lyapti. I've had a bad headache for two days. When I measured my blood pressure this morning, it was 170 over 100. My medicine ran out three days ago. I'm seeing black spots in front of my eyes.
HS2 Kecha kechki ovqatdan keyin ko‘nglim aynidi va ikki marta qusdim. Bugun ertalab hech narsa yemadim. Insulinni odatdagidek 10 birlik qildim. Hozir boshim aylanyapti va terlayapman. Last night after dinner I felt sick and vomited twice. This morning I didn't eat anything. I took my insulin as usual, 10 units. Now I feel dizzy and I'm sweating.
HS3 Onam 78 yoshda, yolg‘iz yashaydi. Oxirgi bir haftada ikki marta yiqildi. Kechalari tez-tez hojatxonaga turadi. Men har kuni kelolmayman, chunki ishlayman. My mother is 78 and lives alone. In the last week she has fallen twice. At night she often gets up to go to the toilet. I can't come every day because I work.

Long turns LT1–LT2 (English → Uzbek, fictional):

Turn English Uzbek model
LT1 Your blood pressure is high today, 178 over 102. Because you ran out of your tablets a week ago, the doctor wants to restart them today. Please don't stop them again without talking to us. We'll check your pressure again in one hour. Bugun qon bosimingiz baland: 178 ga 102. Tabletkalaringiz bir hafta oldin tugagani uchun doktor ularni bugundan qayta boshlamoqchi. Iltimos, biz bilan maslahatlashmasdan ularni yana to‘xtatmang. Bir soatdan keyin bosimingizni yana tekshiramiz.
LT2 Before your colonoscopy tomorrow, please don't eat anything after midnight. You can drink water until 6 a.m. Tonight the nurse will give you a drink that cleans out your bowel. You'll need the toilet often, so stay close to one. Ertangi kolonoskopiyadan oldin, iltimos, yarim tundan keyin hech narsa yemang. Ertalab soat 6 gacha suv ichishingiz mumkin. Bugun kechqurun hamshira sizga ichakni tozalaydigan ichimlik beradi. Hojatxonaga tez-tez borishingiz kerak bo‘ladi, shuning uchun unga yaqin joyda bo‘ling.

Sample Uzbek translation of LF2 (key for Round 2 and the written task): Insulinni uyda boshlash. Ochilmagan shprits-ruchkalarni muzlatkichda saqlang; hozir ishlatayotgan shprits-ruchkani xona haroratida 28 kungacha saqlash mumkin. Insulinni qorin yoki son sohasiga yuboring va ukol joyini har safar almashtiring. Qondagi qandni nonushtadan oldin va kechki ovqatdan oldin tekshiring. Agar u 70 mg/dL dan past bo‘lsa, 4 ta glyukoza tabletkasini qabul qiling va 15 daqiqadan keyin qayta tekshiring. Har kuni oyoqlaringizda kesilgan joy yoki qizarish bor-yo‘qligini tekshiring. Ishlatilgan ignalarni o‘tkir chiqindilar uchun maxsus idishga tashlang.

Observer checks: notes catch numbers and negatives · no omissions · ambiguity flagged, not guessed · the register kept.

Homework: write an Uzbek translation of LF2.

Lesson 33 · C Perform · The interpreted encounter
Goal Interpret a full doctor–patient encounter.
New words (4) pre-session, post-session, three-way encounter, accuracy check
Recycle segment, omission, sight translation
Language A pre-session introduction to both parties: My name is… I'll interpret everything said, in the first person. Please speak in short sections.
Spark Error Hunt (a flawed interpretation)
Perform task Recorded 3–4-minute interpreted encounter (ENC1)
Min Stage What happens
0–5 S 90 seconds: explain the Yuragim siqilyapti problem in English.
5–12 H 4 new words. Model the pre-session introduction.
12–20 I Spark: Error Hunt on the flawed interpretation (below).
20–50 F The performance: a pre-session introduction, then ENC1 as a three-way encounter (the teacher plays the doctor and the patient, or classmates take the roles), then a post-session note to the nurse (3–4 minutes in all). Recorded. In groups, run it again with roles swapped. Score accuracy, completeness, transparency and flow.
50–60 O Play the recording back; mark any omissions or additions. Set the weekly voice note.

Encounter ENC1 (fictional):

Speaker Line Model interpretation
Doctor Good morning, I'm Dr. Brown. What brings you in today? Xayrli tong, men doktor Braunman. Sizni bugun nima bezovta qilyapti?
Patient Ikki haftadan beri chanqayman, ko‘p siyaman, ko‘zlarim xiralashyapti. I've been thirsty for two weeks, I urinate a lot, and my vision is getting blurry.
Doctor Does anyone in your family have diabetes? Oilangizda kimdadir qandli diabet bormi?
Patient Onamda qandli diabet bor edi. Men tekshiruvdan o‘tmaganman. My mother had diabetes. I haven't been tested.
Doctor I'd like to check your blood sugar with a finger-prick test and send a blood test. Is that OK? Barmog‘ingizdan qon olib qandingizni tekshirmoqchiman va qon tahlilini ham yubormoqchiman. Rozimisiz?
Patient Mayli. Lekin ignadan qo‘rqaman. OK. But I'm scared of needles.
Doctor It's a very small needle, and it's quick. Igna juda kichkina, tez tugaydi.
Patient Rahmat. Ishga qachon qaytsam bo‘ladi? Thank you. When can I go back to work?
Doctor Let's wait for the results first, then we'll talk about work. Avval natijalarni kutaylik, keyin ish haqida gaplashamiz.

Flawed interpretation (Error Hunt): I'm thirsty and my eyes are bad. · My mother has diabetes, and so do I. Key: omission (two weeks; urinating a lot); substitution (blurry → bad); a tense error and an addition (has; so do I: the patient said he hasn't been tested).

Observer checks: pre-session introduction · every segment complete · first person · no additions.

Weekly voice note (2 minutes): your pre-session introduction, then interpret 2 ENC1 patient lines from memory.

teacher.title: Exams, OSCE and Final
teacher.html:
By Friday the student can read exam-style questions accurately, follow OSCE station instructions under time pressure, and pass the five-station final.

Written task: none this week; the final OSCE replaces it.

Prepare: stems ST1–ST20 (Lesson 34; students' copies in Cards and texts · Week 12); the 2 rehearsal stations, unseen card SC1 and the OSCE station checklist (Lesson 35); final materials ML3, CP-F, LF3, DC-F and S5 (below; unseen until each station's reading time: copy CP-F and LF3 from this book); the Lesson 1 and Lesson 18 recordings; the certificate.

Lesson 34 · A Learn · Exam question language
Goal Understand what exam-style questions are really asking.
New words (10) stem, option, distractor, priority, initial action, most appropriate, further teaching is needed, select all that apply, indicates understanding, except
Recycle rationale, evidence-based, contraindication
Language Key words that change the question: first, best, most, priority, except. Negative stems: Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? = find the wrong statement.
Spark Match and Speak (stem phrase ↔ what it really asks)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: How do you feel about multiple-choice exams in English? Recall 3 words.
6–24 H Teach the 10 words. Nursing exams in the USA, including licensing exams such as the NCLEX, use this language heavily. This lesson teaches the language, not the nursing content.
24–32 I Spark (6 min): Match and Speak: further teaching is needed ↔ find the incorrect patient statement · priority / first ↔ the one action before all others · select all that apply ↔ more than one answer may be right · except ↔ find the one that does not fit.
32–50 F Round 1: underline key words in stems ST1–ST5 (below) and paraphrase each question in plain English. Round 2: work through Q1 (below) aloud, explaining why each option is right or wrong. Round 3: timed, stems ST6–ST10 in 5 minutes, paraphrase only.
50–60 O Two errors, then retry. Exit check: paraphrase one negative stem. Set homework.

Q1 (language practice, built on leaflet LF2): A patient with diabetes makes the following statements about foot care. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. I will check my feet every day. B. I will walk barefoot at home to let my feet breathe. C. I will tell my nurse about any cuts. D. I will dry carefully between my toes. Key: B, the incorrect statement; the stem asks for the patient who still needs teaching.

Stem bank ST1–ST20 (language practice, not nursing content). ST1–ST5: Round 1 practice · ST6–ST10: Round 3, timed · ST11–ST20: homework. All are built on this book's cases and leaflets.

ST1. A patient using insulin at home checks her sugar before breakfast. It is 62 mg/dL. According to leaflet LF2, what should she do first? A. Inject her morning insulin. B. Take 4 glucose tablets. C. Eat breakfast and check again tomorrow. D. Wait 2 hours and check again.

ST2. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I shake the inhaler before I use it." B. "I breathe out fully before I press." C. "I press twice quickly, then breathe in." D. "I rinse my mouth after my steroid inhaler."

ST3. According to lecture ML2, which patients have a higher risk of pressure injuries? Select all that apply. A. a patient after surgery who cannot move easily B. a very ill older adult C. a patient with poor nutrition and moist skin D. a young adult who walks every day

ST4. Lecture ML1 lists five moments for hand hygiene. They include all of the following except: A. before touching a patient B. after touching the patient's surroundings C. after contact with body fluids D. after reading the patient's chart at the desk

ST5. Which statement by a patient indicates understanding of leaflet LF2? A. "I'll keep the pen I'm using in the freezer." B. "I'll inject into the same spot every day." C. "I'll put used needles in the sharps container." D. "I'll check my feet once a month."

ST6. A patient asks a nursing student, "Am I going to die?" What is the most appropriate response? A. "No, everything will be fine." B. "That's an important question. Can you tell me what's making you think about it? I'll make sure the doctor talks with you today." C. "You should ask the doctor, not me." D. "Let's talk about something happier."

ST7. A student sees a colleague about to give room 4's medicine to the patient in room 6. What is the student's initial action? A. Report it at the end of the shift. B. Speak up now and ask to check the ID band together. C. Tell the patient not to take any medicine today. D. Say nothing, because the colleague is senior.

ST8. During a history, Mrs. Tursunova (CI3) mentions several problems. Which one should the student report as the priority? A. knee pain when she walks B. a new sore on her big toe that she did not notice for a week C. the clinic is far from her home D. she finds sweets hard to refuse at weddings

ST9. A professional interpreter should do all of the following except: A. interpret everything that is said B. speak in the first person C. give the patient advice about treatment D. use a transparency statement to ask for a repetition

ST10. A nursing student is learning to respond to complaints. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I'm sorry this happened." B. "Let me find out what happened." C. "It was the night nurse's fault." D. "I'll come back by 5 p.m. with an update."

ST11. Which actions are part of the nurse's role in informed consent in the USA? Select all that apply. A. witnessing the patient's signature B. checking that the patient understands C. explaining the risks of the procedure instead of the provider D. telling the provider if the patient does not understand

ST12. A relative phones and asks for a patient's test results. What is the most appropriate response? A. Read the results to the caller quickly. B. "I'm sorry, I can't share any information over the phone." C. Give the results if the caller knows the patient's date of birth. D. "The results are fine; don't worry."

ST13. Mrs. Ahmedova (CP3) ran out of her blood-pressure tablets a week ago. Her BP is 178/102. What is the most appropriate action for a nursing student? A. Give her a tablet from another patient's supply. B. Report the reading to the nurse and the physician. C. Tell her the reading is normal. D. Advise her to take two tablets tonight.

ST14. A patient has been taught to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which statement indicates that further teaching is needed? A. "I wait 30 seconds before a second puff." B. "I hold my breath for 10 seconds." C. "I don't need to rinse my mouth after a steroid inhaler." D. "I attach the spacer before I press."

ST15. A relative becomes threatening. The student should do all of the following except: A. step back to a safe distance B. leave the room C. call the charge nurse or security D. stand close and argue until he calms down

ST16. After teaching, which statement indicates that the patient understands what an HbA1c test measures? A. "It shows my sugar right now." B. "It shows my average blood sugar over about 3 months." C. "It measures my blood pressure." D. "It shows whether I have an infection."

ST17. Which sentences are written correctly for an incident report (IR1)? Select all that apply. A. "At 03:10 the patient was found on the floor beside his bed." B. "The patient fell because the night nurse forgot the bed rails." C. "He stated, 'I wanted to go to the toilet.'" D. "He was silly to get up alone."

ST18. A patient's son starts adding his own opinions while he interprets. What is the nurse's initial action? A. Continue, because the family knows best. B. Offer a professional interpreter. C. Ask the patient to speak English. D. End the visit.

ST19. Mr. Mirzaev (CI1) often forgets his evening doses. Which question is most appropriate? A. "Why are you non-compliant?" B. "What gets in the way of taking your evening medicines?" C. "You should have taken them, shouldn't you?" D. "Do you want to get worse?"

ST20. Lecture ML2 lists three ways to prevent pressure injuries. They include all of the following except: A. changing the patient's position regularly B. keeping the skin clean and dry C. checking the skin every day D. keeping the patient in one position all night

Key (answer · what the question really asks):

Stem Answer What it really asks
ST1 B first: the one action LF2 says to do before anything else
ST2 C further teaching is needed: find the wrong statement
ST3 A, B, C select all that apply: more than one answer can be right
ST4 D except: find the one that is not one of the five moments
ST5 C indicates understanding: find the correct statement
ST6 B most appropriate: the best of several possible answers
ST7 B initial action: what to do right now
ST8 B priority: the most urgent problem
ST9 C except: the one thing an interpreter must not do
ST10 C further teaching is needed: the statement that blames
ST11 A, B, D select all that apply: everything within the nurse's role
ST12 B most appropriate: the answer that keeps confidentiality
ST13 B most appropriate for a student: report and refer
ST14 C further teaching is needed: find the wrong statement
ST15 D except: the one unsafe action
ST16 B indicates understanding: the correct statement
ST17 A, C select all that apply: every factual, blame-free sentence
ST18 B initial action: what to do first
ST19 B most appropriate: the non-judgmental question
ST20 D except: the one that is not prevention

Stretch: write one negative stem yourself. Support: key-word list.

Homework: paraphrase stems ST11–ST20 and choose an answer (Student Edition, Cards and texts · Week 12).

Lesson 35 · B Practice · OSCE rehearsal
Goal Follow station instructions under time pressure.
New words (9) station, examiner, candidate, reading time, timed, prompt, mark scheme, global score, rotation
Recycle standardized patient, scenario, debrief
Language Candidate phrases: Before I begin, may I clarify…? I'd like to clean my hands and introduce myself. I've finished; is there anything you'd like me to add?
Spark Mystery Patient (two mini-stations)
Min Stage What happens
0–6 S 90 seconds: paraphrase 3 stems from homework. Recall 3 words.
6–16 H Teach the 9 words. OSCE = an Objective Structured Clinical Examination: timed stations with an examiner and a mark scheme.
16–30 I Explain the final: 5 stations, each with 1 minute of reading time. Model the candidate phrases.
30–50 F Spark: Mystery Patient as 2 timed mini-stations, 7 minutes each: (1) teach one LF2 chunk with teach-back; (2) give an SBAR to the supervising nurse from unseen card SC1 (below). The teacher marks with the OSCE station checklist (below), then debriefs.
50–60 O Review the checklist together; agree 2 final targets.

Observer checks: reading time used · a clear opening · finished on time · a closing question to the examiner.

Card SC1 (unseen, fictional): Mrs. Malika Rashidova, 72, room 12, day 1 after a knee replacement. At 14:00: HR 112 (84 this morning), BP 98/60 (132/80 this morning), RR 22, T 37.4 °C, SpO2 95% on room air. Fresh blood on the dressing, about 5 cm across. She says she feels dizzy. Pain 5/10. Model SBAR (to the supervising nurse): S: I'm worried about Mrs. Rashidova in room 12, day 1 after a knee replacement. Her heart rate is 112 and her blood pressure is 98 over 60. B: This morning they were 84 and 132 over 80. A: She feels dizzy, and there is fresh blood on the dressing, about 5 centimeters across. I'm concerned about these changes. R: Could you come and see her now?

OSCE station checklist (for every station; tick Yes, Partly or No):

# The candidate… Yes / Partly / No
1 uses the reading time and asks to clarify if needed
2 opens clearly: name, role and purpose
3 completes the station task (lecture summary, case, teaching, conversation or interpreting)
4 uses the right register for the listener
5 keeps facts and numbers exact, with nothing added or left out
6 checks understanding (teach-back or a question) where needed
7 stays within a student's role and refers when needed
8 finishes on time with a closing question

The checklist records evidence; the score still comes from the 4-skill rubric in section 4.

Homework: review all recordings; practice your final introduction.

Lesson 36 · C Perform · Final OSCE
Goal Complete five timed stations.
New words None. Review Weeks 1–12.
Assessment Final. Score each of the 4 skills once across all five stations, using the best evidence (total /12; note evidence on the OSCE station checklist); compare with Lessons 1 and 18; decide the certificate.
Min Station What happens (1 minute of reading time per station)
0–3 — Welcome; explain the rotation. Record everything.
3–11 S1 Lecture summary: the teacher reads ML3 once; the student takes notes, gives a 1-minute summary and asks 1 academic question.
11–20 S2 Case presentation: card CP-F; 3 minutes, then 1 question from the examiner.
20–29 S3 Patient education: teach leaflet LF3 with teach-back.
29–37 S4 Difficult conversation: complaint DC-F with the five steps.
37–45 S5 Interpreted exchange: 4 turns, Uzbek ↔ English.
45–52 Review Play 20 seconds each from Lessons 1, 18 and 36. The student names 3 improvements.
52–60 O Scores; certificate decision; a next-step plan for nursing school.

ML3, sleep in hospital (teacher reads): Today I want to look at sleep in hospital: why it matters, what disrupts it, and what nurses can do. Sleep supports healing and mood. However, patients in hospital often sleep badly. The main reasons are noise, light, pain, and being woken for checks. Consequently, some patients become confused or low in mood. What can nurses do? First, group night-time checks together where possible. Second, reduce noise and dim the lights. Third, ask patients what usually helps them sleep. To sum up: sleep is part of treatment, and small changes make a real difference.

CP-F (fictional): Sherzod Nazarov, 59; COPD (documented); has smoked for 30 years; 3-day history of increasing breathlessness and cough with green sputum; T 38.0 °C, RR 28, SpO2 88% on room air, 92% on 2 L via nasal cannula. Plan as documented: chest X-ray, nebulizers, physician review.

LF3, using your inhaler with a spacer (fictional leaflet): shake the inhaler and attach the spacer · breathe out fully · seal your lips around the mouthpiece · press once, then breathe in slowly and hold for 10 seconds · wait 30 seconds before a second puff · rinse your mouth after a steroid inhaler.

DC-F (fictional): a daughter is angry that her father was moved to another room at night and nobody told the family.

S5 lines: Patient: Kecha kechasi uxlay olmadim, nafasim qisildi. (Last night I couldn't sleep; I was short of breath.) · Nurse: Did you use your inhaler during the night? · Patient: Ha, ikki marta ishlatdim, lekin unchalik yordam bermadi. (Yes, I used it twice, but it didn't help much.) · Nurse: I'll tell the doctor straight away.

Final voice note: your 2-minute introduction as a future nurse: who you are, what you can do now in English, and your next goal.

teacher.title: Grammar Handbook
teacher.html:
How to use this handbook

This is the grammar companion to the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 books. Each lesson card names one grammar point; this handbook explains it in full. Teachers use it to prepare the 4-minute grammar slot. Students use it for homework and revision.

Most units follow this layout; reference units use tables instead:

  1. When we use it: the meanings, in short bullets.
  2. Structure: formulas for + (statement), − (negative) and ? (question), each with a healthcare example.
  3. Short answers and short forms.
  4. Keywords: the time words and signal words that go with it.
  5. Watch out!: the mistakes students make most, including typical mistakes of Uzbek speakers. ✗ = wrong, ✓ = right.
  6. Try it: 4 quick items, with the key underneath.

Symbols

Symbol Meaning Example
S subject The patient, she, I
V1 base form go, take, feel
V2 past form went, took, felt
V3 past participle gone, taken, felt
V-ing -ing form going, taking, feeling
(Q/W) question word (optional) what, where, when, how
+ / − / ? statement / negative / question

Part 3 · C1 Professional

Unit 28 · Discourse markers

When we use it: to show how ideas connect in lectures, presentations, essays and seminars.

Function Spoken / neutral Written / formal
Adding also, and, plus furthermore, moreover, in addition
Contrasting but, though however, in contrast, whereas, nevertheless, on the other hand
Cause because, since, as due to (+ noun), owing to
Result so therefore, consequently, as a result
Sequencing first, then, after that, finally firstly, secondly, subsequently, lastly
Example like, for example for instance, such as, to illustrate
Emphasis especially, the main thing is in particular, notably, the key point is
Conceding OK, but admittedly, while it is true that
Summarizing so, basically to sum up, in summary, overall

Grammar of linkers

  • However, Therefore, Consequently start a new sentence and take a comma: Hand hygiene prevents infection. However, it is often forgotten.
  • although, whereas, because join two clauses: Although she was in pain, she walked to the bathroom.
  • despite / in spite of + noun or -ing: Despite* the pain, she walked. Despite feeling* dizzy, she walked.
  • due to + noun: …due to time pressure (✗ due to people are busy).

Watch out!

  • ✗ Although she was tired, but she worked. Use one linker: ✓ Although she was tired, she worked.
  • ✗ despite of ✓ despite / in spite of.
  • Moreover in a conversation sounds like a lecture. Match the register.

Try it. (1) The test is painless. ___, it takes an hour. (2) ___ the noise, he slept well. (3) She missed her insulin; ___, her sugar rose. (4) ___ the leaflet is short, it is hard to read.

Show the answers

(1) However (2) Despite / In spite of (3) consequently / as a result (4) Although.

Unit 29 · Nominalization and compact clinical style

When we use it: in case presentations, handoffs and notes, where time and space are short. Verbs become nouns; long sentences become phrases.

Verb / clause Noun / phrase
she was admitted admission
her breathing got worse worsening breathing / deterioration in breathing
we assessed her assessment
he refused the medicine refusal of medication
it improved improvement
she has had a cough for three days a 3-day history of cough

Compact patterns: presents with · a history of · notable for · associated with · secondary to · on admission · following surgery.

She came in because her breathing got worse after she caught a cold three days ago. → Admitted with a 3-day history of worsening breathing following an upper respiratory infection.

Compound adjectives take a hyphen and no plural -s: a 64-year-old woman · a 3-day history · a 2-cm wound · a 12-hour shift.

Watch out!

  • ✗ a 64-years-old woman · ✗ 3 days history ✓ a 64-year-old woman, a 3-day history.
  • Compact style is for colleagues. With patients, turn nouns back into verbs: Your breathing has got worse.

Try it. Compress: (1) He has had diabetes for 10 years. (2) She fell, and after that she couldn't walk. (3) The patient is 47 years old. (4) His pain got better after he had pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) a 10-year history of diabetes (2) unable to walk following a fall (3) a 47-year-old patient (4) improvement in pain following analgesia / pain relief.

Unit 30 · -ing and -ed forms; reduced clauses

The same verb form can do four different jobs.

Form Job Example
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb She was sleeping at 3 a.m.
Gerund (V-ing as a noun) subject, object, after a preposition Smoking* increases the risk. She enjoys walking. Wash your hands before eating*.
Participle I (V-ing as an adjective) describes an active process a bleeding wound · the patient lying in bed 3
Participle II (V3 as an adjective) describes a passive or finished state a broken wrist · the prescribed dose · a revealed secret

Verb + gerund or verb + to-infinitive?

+ V-ing + to + V1
avoid, enjoy, finish, keep, mind, consider, stop, suggest want, need, decide, plan, refuse, agree, hope, forget
Avoid lifting heavy things. She refused to take it.

Stop, forget and remember can take both forms, with a change in meaning: She stopped smoking (she no longer smokes) vs She stopped to rest (she stopped in order to rest) · I forgot to take my tablet (I did not take it) vs I will never forget meeting my first patient (a memory).

-ing or -ed adjectives: -ing = the cause, -ed = the feeling: The instructions are confusing. The patient is confused. · a tiring shift / I'm tired · a worrying result / she is **worried.

Reduced relative clauses (C1 presentation style):

  • the patient who is lying in bed 3 → the patient lying in bed 3
  • the tablets which were prescribed yesterday → the tablets prescribed yesterday
  • a woman who presents with chest pain → a woman presenting with chest pain

Participle clauses at the start of a sentence (same subject): Feeling* dizzy, she sat down. Admitted* yesterday, he is now stable.

Watch out!

  • The -ing phrase goes after the noun when it is longer than one word: ✗ the playing football boy ✓ the boy playing football · ✗ the talking professor (unclear) ✓ the professor who is talking / **talking now.
  • Same subject only: ✗ Walking to the bathroom, the floor was wet. (the floor wasn't walking) ✓ Walking to the bathroom, she slipped on the wet floor.
  • ✗ I'm boring (= I make people bored) when you mean ✓ I'm bored**.

Try it. (1) She stopped ___ (smoke) last year. (2) The ___ (break) arm needs an X-ray. (3) The patient ___ (sit) by the window is Mr. Rakhimov. (4) The news was ___ (worry), so the family was ___ (worry).

Show the answers

(1) smoking (2) broken (3) sitting (4) worrying … worried.

Unit 31 · Cleft sentences and emphasis

When we use it: to put the most important information first, to prioritize in a summary, or to correct someone politely.

Pattern Structure Example
What-cleft What + S + V + is / was + focus What concerns me most is the new sore on her foot.
It-cleft It is / was + focus + that / who + rest It's* the evening doses that* he misses.
The thing / reason The thing that… / The reason (why)… + is (that) The reason* she stopped is that* the tablets are expensive.
All All + S + V + is All she needs is a little more time.

Correcting politely: It wasn't the morning dose she missed; it was the evening one.

Watch out!

  • No extra it: ✗ What concerns me most it is the sore. ✓ What concerns me most is the sore.
  • Keep the order: ✗ Is the evening dose that he misses. ✓ It's the evening dose that he misses.

Try it. Rewrite with emphasis: (1) The cost worries her. (What…) (2) He missed the Tuesday appointment. (It was…) (3) She needs a social worker. (What…) (4) She stopped because of the side effects. (The reason…)

Show the answers

(1) What worries her is the cost. (2) It was the Tuesday appointment that he missed. (3) What she needs is a social worker. (4) The reason (why) she stopped is (that) she had side effects.

Unit 32 · Tentative and diplomatic language

When we use it: to make suggestions to seniors, to disagree in a seminar, and to ask sensitive questions without pressure.

Function Phrases
Polite requests I was wondering whether… Would it be possible to…? Would you mind + V-ing?
Suggestions to the team Could we consider…? Would it be worth + V-ing…? It might be helpful to…
Sensitive questions I was wondering if you could tell me a bit about… What gets in the way of…?
Disagreeing I see it slightly differently. While I take your point,… I'm not sure I agree, because…
Not knowing I'm not sure, but I think… As far as I know,… I'd need to check.

Why the past tense sounds polite: I was wondering and I wanted to ask talk about now, but the past form adds distance and sounds less direct.

Softeners: a bit, slightly, perhaps, possibly, just (Could I just check…?).

But not for safety. When a patient may be harmed, be clear and firm (CUS): I'm concerned. I'm uncomfortable. This is a safety issue.

Watch out!

  • ✗ Would you mind to wait? ✓ Would you mind waiting?
  • Over-softening in an emergency causes delay: ✗ I was wondering whether you might possibly come… ✓ I need you to come now.

Try it. Make more tentative: (1) Book an interpreter. (2) You're wrong. (3) Can I ask about your alcohol use? (4) Review his pain relief.

Show the answers

(1) Could we consider booking an interpreter? (2) I see it slightly differently. (3) I was wondering if I could ask about your alcohol use. (4) Would it be worth reviewing his pain relief?

Unit 33 · Mixed and formal conditionals

Mixed conditionals

Type If-clause Main clause Example
past cause → present result Past Perfect would + V1 If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be in hospital now.
present situation → past result Past Simple would have + V3 If he weren't so afraid of needles, he would have had the test last week.

Formal inversion (leaflets, letters, academic writing): drop if and invert.

  • Should you notice any redness, contact the clinic. (= If you notice…)
  • Had I known about the allergy, I would have said so. (= If I had known…)
  • Were the patient to refuse, the team would discuss alternatives. (= If the patient refused…)

Other ways to say if

Word Meaning Example
unless if not Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
provided that / as long as only if You can go home as long as someone stays with you.
in case as a precaution (≠ if) Take your inhaler in case you need it.
otherwise if not, then… Keep the dressing dry; otherwise it may get infected.
supposing / what if imagining What if the results are positive?

Watch out!

  • in case ≠ if: Take your inhaler in case you get wheezy (take it with you now anyway) vs Use your inhaler if you get wheezy (only when it happens).
  • No would after if in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known…

Try it. (1) If I ___ (study) harder last year, I ___ (be) in nursing school now. (2) ___ you have any questions, please call. (3) Bring water ___ the wait is long. (4) You can drive ___ you don't feel drowsy.

Show the answers

(1) had studied … would be (2) Should (3) in case (4) as long as / provided that.

Unit 34 · Academic grammar: reporting verbs and the passive

When we use it: in summaries, care-plan rationales, essays and reflections.

Reporting verbs, from weak to strong

Strength Verbs Example
tentative suggests, indicates, implies The research suggests that lifestyle change can delay onset.
neutral states, reports, describes, notes The textbook states that…
strong shows, demonstrates, confirms, establishes The study demonstrates a clear link…
arguing argues, claims, maintains The author argues that…

The academic passive and impersonal structures

  • It is recommended that patients… It has been shown that…
  • Patients are advised to… Pressure injuries are associated with…
  • There is evidence* that… There is* a need for…

Tenses in academic writing

  • Present Simple for general facts and what a source says: Hand hygiene reduces infection. The author argues…
  • Past Simple for a specific study: The study found that…
  • Present Perfect for research up to now: Several studies have shown…

Style: no contractions (does not, not doesn't); avoid I think in essays (reflections are the exception: they use I); hedge claims (appears to, is likely to, may contribute to).

Watch out!

  • Too strong: ✗ This proves that… ✓ This suggests that…
  • Copying the source's sentence with small changes is plagiarism. Paraphrase fully and cite.

Try it. Make it academic: (1) Lots of studies show exercise helps. (2) Doctors say patients should check their feet. (3) I think the patient didn't understand. (4) This proves the leaflet works.

Show the answers

(1) Several studies have shown that exercise is beneficial. (2) Patients are advised to check their feet daily. (3) The patient appeared not to understand. (4) This suggests that the leaflet is effective.

Part 1 · B1 Foundation

Unit 1 · Grammar words and the alphabet

Grammar words used in this handbook

Term What it is Example
Subject who or what does the action The nurse checks the chart.
Verb the action or state The nurse checks the chart.
Auxiliary verb a helper verb for questions, negatives and tenses: be, do, have, will Does it hurt?
Noun a person, thing or idea nurse, chart, pain
Pronoun a word instead of a noun she, it, them
Adjective describes a noun a sharp pain
Adverb describes a verb or adjective; often how, when, how often breathe slowly, always, very tired
Preposition place, time, direction in, on, at, under, before
Article a, an, the the patient

Tense names. Each tense has two names; both are correct. Simple = Indefinite · Continuous = Progressive · Perfect · Perfect Continuous. Each one exists in the Present, Past and Future: 12 tenses in total (see Reference table A).

The alphabet: 26 letters

  • 5 vowel letters: a, e, i, o, u.
  • 21 consonant letters. Y can work as a consonant (yes) or a vowel (happy, dizzy).

Learn the letter names in sound groups. It makes spelling names on the phone much easier.

Sound Letters
"ay" (as in day) A H J K
"ee" (as in see) B C D E G P T V Z
"eh" (as in bed) F L M N S X
"eye" I Y
"oh" O
"you" Q U W
"ar" R

In the USA, Z is "zee"; in the UK it is "zed".

Watch out!

  • A, E, I are the most confused: A = "ay", E = "ee", I = "eye".
  • G ("jee") and J ("jay") are often swapped.
  • W is "double-u". For two of the same letter together, say "double": Anna → A-double N-A; Rassul → R-A-double S-U-L.
  • Abbreviations are spelled letter by letter: MRI = "em-ar-eye", ECG = "ee-see-jee".

Try it. Spell aloud: (1) Karimova (2) Yusupov (3) ECG (4) Jasur.

Show the answers

(1) K-A-R-I-M-O-V-A (2) Y-U-S-U-P-O-V (3) E-C-G ("ee-see-jee") (4) J-A-S-U-R (J = "jay").

Unit 2 · Nouns: singular and plural

When we use it: one thing = singular (a tablet); two or more = plural (two tablets).

Rule Ending Examples
Most nouns + -s nurse → nurses · bed → beds · lung → lungs
Ends in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x + -es bus → buses · glass → glasses · dish → dishes · patch → patches · box → boxes
Some nouns in -o + -es potato → potatoes · tomato → tomatoes (but photo → photos)
Consonant + y y → -ies artery → arteries · injury → injuries · baby → babies
Vowel + y + -s day → days · X-ray → X-rays · boy → boys
Ends in -f / -fe f → -ves half → halves · knife → knives · life → lives · wife → wives
Irregular new form man → men · woman → women · child → children · person → people · foot → feet · tooth → teeth · mouse → mice
No change same form sheep · fish · deer · series · species
Latin / Greek (common in medicine) special diagnosis → diagnoses · bacterium → bacteria · vertebra → vertebrae · criterion → criteria · nucleus → nuclei

Watch out!

  • After a number, English always needs the plural. Uzbek speakers often keep the noun singular after a number: ✗ three tablet. ✓ three tablets, two days, 5 milligrams.
  • People is already plural: ✓ People are waiting. ✗ peoples.
  • Uncountable nouns have no plural: ✗ informations, advices, equipments (see Unit 17).
  • One child, two children; one foot, two feet: say these correctly in body and family vocabulary.

Try it. Make plural: (1) knee (2) diagnosis (3) child (4) injury.

Show the answers

(1) knees (2) diagnoses (3) children (4) injuries.

Unit 3 · Articles: a, an, the

When we use it

  • a / an = one, not a specific one; the first time we mention it: There's a patient in room 4.
  • the = a specific one that we both know; the second mention; something unique: The patient in room 4 is asleep. The heart pumps blood.
  • No article for plural or uncountable nouns in general: Nurses work long shifts. Blood carries oxygen.

A or an? It depends on the first sound, not the first letter.

an (vowel sound) a (consonant sound)
an apple, an injection a patient, a nurse
an hour (silent h) a hospital (h is heard)
an X-ray ("ex") a unit ("you")
an MRI ("em"), an ECG ("ee") a uniform, a European ("you")

Fixed phrases (no article): by mouth, at home, at work, go to bed, on duty. In the USA: in the hospital (UK: in hospital).

Watch out!

  • Uzbek has no articles, so learners drop them. ✗ She is nurse. ✓ She is a nurse. ✗ Patient is in room 5. ✓ The patient is in room 5.
  • Jobs always take a/an: I want to be a nurse. He is an anesthetist.
  • Don't use the with names: ✗ the Dr. Lee.

Try it. Add a, an or the: (1) I have ___ appointment. (2) She needs ___ MRI. (3) ___ pharmacy is on the first floor. (4) He works in ___ hospital in Ohio.

Show the answers

(1) an (2) an (3) The (4) a.

She gave him her card. The card is hers. She did it herself.

Watch out!

Unit 6 · To be (am, is, are · was, were · will be)

When we use it: to say what or who someone is, how they are, where they are, and their age.

Present Past Future

you / we / they are you / we / they were you / we / they will be

Structure

Formula Example

− S + am / is / are + not + … She is not dizzy. They are not in the ward.

Short answers: Yes, she is. / No, she isn't. ✗ Yes, she's. (no short form in a yes short answer)

Short forms: I'm · you're · he's / she's / it's · we're · they're. Negative: isn't, aren't, wasn't, weren't, won't be. With I: ✓ I'm not ✗ I amn't.

When we use it: to talk about possession, family, conditions and symptoms. I have diabetes. She has a fever. I've got a cough.

− S + do / does + not + have + noun He doesn't have any allergies.

Formula Example

− S + have / has + not + got + noun She hasn't got a temperature.

Unit 9 · Present Simple (Present Indefinite)

When we use it

  • Habits and repeated actions: She takes insulin every morning.
  • Schedules and timetables: Visiting hours start at 2 p.m.
  • Facts and general truths: The heart pumps blood.
  • States: I feel dizzy. He knows his medicines.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V1 (he / she / it + -s) I check my sugar daily. She checks her sugar daily.
− S + do / does + not + V1 I don't smoke. He doesn't drink alcohol.
? (Q/W) + do / does + S + V1? Do* you take any vitamins? How often does* she use her inhaler?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.

He / she / it spelling: take → takes · wash → washes · cry → cries · go → goes · do → does · have → has.

Pronouncing -s: "s" in takes, checks · "z" in feels, needs · "iz" in washes, uses.

Keywords: every (day, morning, week) · always · usually · often · sometimes · occasionally · rarely · seldom · never · once / twice a day · from time to time.

Word order: frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be: She always takes it at night. He is often dizzy.

Watch out!

  • ✗ She take insulin. ✓ She takes insulin.
  • Only one -s: ✗ Does she takes…? ✓ Does she take…?
  • ✗ He don't smoke. ✓ He doesn't smoke.

(1) has (2) Does … use (3) don't drink (4) filter.

Unit 10 · Present Continuous (Present Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action happening now: The patient is sleeping.
  • A temporary situation around now: I'm studying English this year.
  • A fixed plan for the future: She's having surgery on Monday.
  • An annoying repeated habit, with always: He's always pulling at his IV.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + am / is / are + V-ing My heart is beating fast.
− S + am / is / are + not + V-ing She isn't eating today.
? (Q/W) + am / is / are + S + V-ing? Are* you having* trouble breathing?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.

Here be is a helper. I am a nurse (here am is the main verb) vs I am working (am only builds the tense).

-ing spelling: take → taking · sit → sitting · lie → lying · breathe → breathing.

Keywords: now · right now · at the moment · currently · today · this week · these days · still.

State verbs are not normally continuous: know, want, need, believe, understand, like, hate, seem, belong. ✗ I am knowing. ✓ I know. Feel and hurt can be both: My back hurts / is hurting.

Simple or continuous? He takes insulin every day (habit) · He's taking his insulin now (at this moment).

Watch out!

  • Don't drop be: ✗ She sleeping. ✓ She is sleeping.
  • ✗ I am needing water. ✓ I need water.

Try it. (1) Be quiet: the baby ___ (sleep). (2) ___ you ___ (take) any medicine at the moment? (3) She ___ (not / breathe) normally. (4) I ___ (understand) the instructions.

Show the answers

(1) is sleeping (2) Are … taking (3) isn't breathing (4) understand.

Unit 11 · Past Simple (Past Indefinite)

When we use it: a finished action at a finished time in the past, with no link to now. She fell yesterday. He had surgery in 2015.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + V2 (regular: -ed; irregular: see table D) The pain started on Sunday. I took a tablet.
− S + did + not + V1 She didn't vomit.
? (Q/W) + did + S + V1? When did it start? Did you fall?

Short answers: Yes, she did. / No, I didn't.

-ed spelling: start → started · stop → stopped · cry → cried · use → used.

Pronouncing -ed: "t" in stopped, checked · "d" in called, used · "id" in started, needed.

Keywords: yesterday · ago · last (night, week, year) · in 2019 · at 3 a.m. · on Monday · when.

Watch out!

  • After did, use V1: ✗ Did you took it? ✓ Did you take it? ✗ She didn't came. ✓ She didn't come.
  • Ago goes after the time: ✓ three days ago ✗ ago three days.
  • With a finished time, don't use the Present Perfect: ✗ I have taken it yesterday. ✓ I took it yesterday.

(1) began (2) Did … eat (3) didn't sleep (4) broke.

Unit 12 · Present Perfect

When we use it

  • A past action with a result now: I'm full. I have eaten. (Compare: I ate pasta yesterday: past only.)
  • Experience in life (any time until now): Have* you ever had* surgery?
  • A situation from the past until now: I've had this cough for three days.
  • Something just finished: The doctor has just left.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + V3 She has taken her tablets.
− S + have / has + not + V3 We haven't finished yet.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + V3? Have* you checked* your sugar today?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've, he's / she's (here 's = has), haven't, hasn't.

Keywords: just · already · yet (in − and ?) · ever · never · recently · so far · today · this week · for · since.

For or since? for + a length of time: for three days, for a week · since + a starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since this morning.

Present Perfect or Past Simple? Ask about life with the Present Perfect; give the details with the Past Simple: Have you ever had surgery? – Yes, I had my appendix out in 2015.

Watch out!

  • Uzbek uses the present for since: ✗ I am here since Monday. ✓ I've been here since Monday.
  • ✗ for Monday ✓ since Monday · ✗ since three days ✓ for three days.
  • No finished time: ✗ I have seen the doctor yesterday. ✓ I saw the doctor yesterday.

(1) has had (2) Have … been (3) haven't taken (4) has worked.

Unit 19 · Past Continuous (Past Progressive)

When we use it

  • An action in progress at a moment in the past: At 3 a.m. he was sleeping.
  • A longer action interrupted by a shorter one (Past Simple): She was walking to the bathroom when she fell.
  • Two actions in progress at the same time: While* the nurse was checking his pulse, he was talking* to his son.
  • The background of a story: It was raining and the ED was getting busy.

The action has no link to now and no result: it was simply in progress.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + was / were + V-ing They were waiting in the waiting area.
− S + was / were + not + V-ing She wasn't breathing normally.
? (Q/W) + was / were + S + V-ing? What were you doing when the pain started?

Short answers: Yes, I was. / No, they weren't. Short forms: only in the negative: wasn't, weren't.

Keywords: while · as · when · at (3 a.m.) yesterday · all night · at that moment.

When or while? when + the short action (Past Simple); while / as + the long action (Past Continuous).

Watch out!

  • ✗ When I was fall… ✓ When I fell… (the short action is Past Simple)
  • State verbs stay simple: ✗ I was knowing him. ✓ I knew him.

(1) was carrying … felt (2) were … doing (3) was cooking … cut (4) wasn't sleeping.

Unit 20 · Present Perfect Continuous

When we use it

  • An activity that started in the past and is still going on, with focus on how long: I've been coughing for a week.
  • A recent activity with a result you can see: Her eyes are red. She's been crying.

Structure

Formula Example
+ S + have / has + been + V-ing He has been using his inhaler more than usual.
− S + have / has + not + been + V-ing I haven't been sleeping well.
? (Q/W) + have / has + S + been + V-ing? How long have you been having this pain?

Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.

Keywords: for · since · how long · all day · all week · lately · recently.

Simple or continuous?

Present Perfect Continuous Present Perfect Simple
duration, the activity itself result, a number, a completed amount
I've been taking this tablet for a year. I've taken three tablets today.
She's been waiting since 9. She's waited three hours. (finished or counted)

State verbs stay simple: I've had this cough for a week. I've known her for years. For repeated symptoms the continuous is fine: I've been having headaches lately.
