  • Uzbek uses the present here: ✗ I am coughing since Monday. ✓ I've been coughing since Monday.
  • Don't forget been: ✗ I have coughing. ✓ I have been coughing.

Try it. (1) How long ___ you ___ (feel) like this? (2) She ___ (wait) since 9 a.m. (3) I ___ (have) diabetes for ten years. (4) He ___ (take) four tablets so far today.

Show the answers

(1) have … been feeling (2) has been waiting (3) have had (4) has taken.

Unit 21 · Past Perfect and narrative tenses

When we use it

  • Past Perfect (had + V3): an action before another past moment: When the ambulance arrived, she had already stopped bleeding.
  • Past Perfect Continuous (had been + V-ing): an activity that continued up to a past moment: She had been feeling dizzy all morning before she fell.

Structure (Past Perfect)

Formula Example
+ S + had + V3 He had taken his insulin before lunch.
− S + had + not + V3 She hadn't eaten since breakfast.
? (Q/W) + had + S + V3? Had* you felt* dizzy before the fall?

Short answers: Yes, I had. / No, she hadn't. Short forms: I'd, she'd (here 'd = had), hadn't.

Keywords: before · after · by the time · already · when · until · by (10 a.m.).

Telling a story in order: three tenses together

Tense Job Example
Past Continuous background At 2 p.m. she was walking to the bathroom…
Past Simple main events …when she slipped and hit her head.
Past Perfect earlier events She hadn't eaten since breakfast, and she had been feeling dizzy all morning.

Watch out!

  • When before / after already show the order, the Past Simple is fine: She ate before she took the tablet.
  • ✗ She had fell. ✓ She had fallen. (use V3: see table D)

Try it. (1) By the time the doctor came, the pain ___ (stop). (2) ___ he ___ (take) anything before he came in? (3) She ___ (not / sleep) for two days before the seizure. (4) He ___ (work) for 10 hours when he collapsed.

Show the answers

(1) had stopped (2) Had … taken (3) hadn't slept (4) had been working.

Unit 22 · The passive

When we use it: when the action matters more than who did it. Very common in reports, procedures, labels and textbooks.

Structure: a form of be + V3. Add by + person only if it matters.

Tense Passive Example
Present Simple am / is / are + V3 This tablet is taken by mouth.
Present Continuous am / is / are being + V3 The dressing is being changed.
Past Simple was / were + V3 The blood pressure was recorded at 10:00.
Present Perfect have / has been + V3 Has* the dressing been changed* today?
Future will be + V3 The results will be explained by the doctor.
Modal modal + be + V3 Consent must be obtained first.
Formula Example
+ S + be + V3 The sample was sent to the lab.
− S + be + not + V3 The site has not been marked.
? (Q/W) + be + S + V3? When was the patient admitted?

Watch out!

  • Use V3, not V2: ✗ The sample was took. ✓ The sample was taken.
  • Verbs with no object have no passive: ✗ It was happened. The patient was died. ✓ It happened. The patient died. (also arrive, occur, fall)
  • Speak actively to patients: You take it by mouth. Use the passive in notes and reports.

Try it. Make passive: (1) The nurse checks the ID band. (2) Someone took the sample at 8. (3) They will remove the stitches in 10 days. (4) Has anyone told the family?

Show the answers

(1) The ID band is checked. (2) The sample was taken at 8. (3) The stitches will be removed in 10 days. (4) Has the family been told?

Unit 23 · Reported speech

When we use it: to tell someone what another person said, asked or told them to do. Essential for handoffs and notes.

Say or tell? say (something): He said he was dizzy. · tell + person: He told me he was dizzy. ✗ He said me.

Statements: move one tense back

Direct speech Reported speech
"I feel dizzy." She said she felt dizzy.
"I'm having chest pain." He said he was having chest pain.
"I took it yesterday." She said she had taken it the day before.
"I'll call you." He said he would call me.
"I can't sleep." She said she couldn't sleep.

Also change: today → that day · yesterday → the day before · tomorrow → the next day · here → there · I / my → he / his.

Questions: normal word order, no do: "Where is the toilet?" → He asked where the toilet was. · Yes/no questions use if / whether: She asked if she could eat.

Instructions: told / asked + person + (not) to + V1: The doctor told him not to drive. · Labels: The label says to take it with food.

In clinical notes the present is normal: Patient reports pain 6/10. Denies nausea. States she slept badly. For a safety concern, quote the exact words: The patient stated, "I don't see the point anymore."

Watch out!

  • ✗ He asked where is the toilet. ✓ He asked where the toilet was.
  • ✗ She told to wait. ✓ She told me to wait.

Try it. Report: (1) "I have a headache." (she) (2) "Did you take your insulin?" (the nurse asked him) (3) "Don't eat after midnight." (the doctor told her) (4) "I'll come back at 5." (he)

Show the answers

(1) She said she had a headache. (2) The nurse asked him if he had taken his insulin. (3) The doctor told her not to eat after midnight. (4) He said he would come back at 5.

Unit 24 · Conditionals: zero, first, second, third

Type Meaning If-clause Main clause Example
Zero facts, always true Present Simple Present Simple If blood sugar drops too low, people feel shaky.
First real, possible future Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction If the pain gets worse, I'll call the nurse. If you notice a fever, call the clinic.
Second unreal or unlikely, present or future Past Simple / Past Continuous would / could / might + V1 If you stopped smoking, your breathing would improve.
Third unreal past (it didn't happen) Past Perfect would / could / might + have + V3 If I had known about the allergy, I would have told the doctor.

Structure notes

  • The if-clause can come first or second. If it comes first, use a comma: If it hurts, tell me. / Tell me if it hurts.
  • Negatives: If you don't take it, … · If I hadn't checked, … · … it wouldn't help.
  • Questions: What will you do if the patient refuses? What would you do if a patient shouted at you?
  • Unless = if not: Don't eat unless the nurse says it's OK.
  • Second conditional with be: were for all persons in formal English: If I were you, I'd ask the pharmacist.

Watch out!

  • No will in the if-clause: ✗ If you will notice redness… ✓ If you notice redness…
  • No would in the if-clause: ✗ If I would have known… ✓ If I had known…
  • First or second? First = it may really happen. Second = imagined: If I win the scholarship, I'll… (I applied) vs If I were the surgeon, I would… (imagined: I am a nursing student).

Try it. (1) If you ___ (feel) dizzy, sit down. (2) If she ___ (have) more time, she would study more. (3) If he ___ (call) earlier, we ___ (help) him. (4) Water ___ (boil) if you heat it to 100 °C.

Show the answers

(1) feel (2) had (3) had called … would have helped (4) boils.

Unit 25 · Question tags

When we use it: to check information you think is true. Very useful in medication reconciliation and handoffs.

Structure: positive sentence → negative tag; negative sentence → positive tag. The tag uses the same helper verb (or do / does / did).

Sentence Tag
You take it twice a day, don't you?
You haven't eaten since midnight, have you?
She's allergic to penicillin, isn't she?
He took it this morning, didn't he?
You'll come back on Tuesday, won't you?
You can walk, can't you?
I'm next, aren't I? (special form)

Intonation: falling = you're confirming, you expect yes. Rising = a real question, you're not sure.

Answer the fact, not the tag: You don't smoke, do you? – No, I don't. (= I don't smoke)

Watch out!

  • Uzbek speakers often use one tag for everything: ✗ You take it twice a day, isn't it? ✓ …, don't you?
  • Match the tense: ✗ He took it, doesn't he? ✓ …, didn't he?

Try it. (1) You live alone, ___? (2) She hasn't had surgery, ___? (3) It was this morning, ___? (4) You'll call us, ___?

Show the answers

(1) don't you (2) has she (3) wasn't it (4) won't you.

Unit 26 · Hedging and deduction

When we use it: to show how sure we are. Nurses report facts carefully and never sound more certain than they are.

Possibility: may, might, could + V1

  • This medicine may cause drowsiness. (labels, leaflets)
  • The change might be important. I'll tell the nurse.
  • Her symptoms could be related to the new tablet. (in a discussion with the team, not a diagnosis for the patient)

Deduction: how sure am I?

Certainty Present Past Example
sure it's true must + V1 / be must have + V3 You must be exhausted. She must have fallen.
possible may / might / could + V1 may / might / could have + V3 He might be in pain. She could have missed a dose.
sure it's not true can't + V1 / be can't have + V3 That can't be easy. He can't have taken it: the box is full.

Appearance verbs (observations, not conclusions): He appears drowsy. She seems anxious. She seems to be in pain. He looks pale.

Softening words: possibly, probably, likely, approximately, about, around, tends to.

Watch out!

  • No to after modals: ✗ He must to be tired. ✓ He must be tired.
  • maybe (adverb) vs may be (verb): Maybe it's the medicine. = *It may be* the medicine.
  • ✗ She seems is tired. ✓ She seems tired / seems to be tired.

Try it. (1) You've worked 12 hours. You ___ be tired. (2) The box is full. She ___ have taken any tablets. (3) Her fever ___ come back tonight, so check it at 10 p.m. (4) He ___ (appear) confused.

Show the answers

(1) must (2) can't (3) may / might (4) appears.

Unit 27 · Other future forms

When we use it

Form Structure Use Example
Future Continuous will be + V-ing in progress at a future time At 10 tomorrow you'll be having your MRI.
Future Perfect will have + V3 finished before a future time By Friday you will have finished the antibiotics.
Future Perfect Continuous will have been + V-ing duration up to a future time By June I will have been studying English for two years.
be about to am / is / are about to + V1 very near future The doctor is about to see you.
be due to am / is / are due to + V1 scheduled The doctor is due to see you at 10.

Negatives and questions follow will: She won't have finished by then. Will you be working tomorrow night?

Keywords: by (Friday) · by the time · before · for (two years) · this time tomorrow · at (10) tomorrow.

The future seen from the past (reported speech): will → would, am going to → was going to: She said she would call. I was going to phone you, but…

Watch out!

  • ✗ By Friday you will finish. (when the point is already done by then) ✓ By Friday you will have finished.
  • After by the time use the present: ✗ by the time the doctor will arrive ✓ by the time the doctor arrives**.

Try it. (1) This time tomorrow she ___ (have) her operation. (2) By 2028 she ___ (graduate). (3) The ambulance ___ (about / arrive). (4) By March he ___ (work) here for a year.

Show the answers

(1) will be having (2) will have graduated (3) is about to arrive (4) will have been working.

Reference tables

A · All 12 tenses: structure (verb: take)

Present

Tense + − ?
Simple I take · she takes I don't take · she doesn't take Do you take? · Does she take?
Continuous I am taking · she is taking I'm not taking · she isn't taking Are you taking? · Is she taking?
Perfect I have taken · she has taken I haven't taken · she hasn't taken Have you taken? · Has she taken?
Perfect Continuous I have been taking I haven't been taking Have you been taking?

Past

Tense + − ?
Simple I took I didn't take Did you take?
Continuous I was taking · they were taking I wasn't taking · they weren't taking Were you taking?
Perfect I had taken I hadn't taken Had you taken?
Perfect Continuous I had been taking I hadn't been taking Had you been taking?

Future

Tense + − ?
Simple I will take I won't take Will you take?
Continuous I will be taking I won't be taking Will you be taking?
Perfect I will have taken I won't have taken Will you have taken?
Perfect Continuous I will have been taking I won't have been taking Will you have been taking?

The pattern: Continuous always has be + V-ing. Perfect always has have + V3. Perfect Continuous has both: have been + V-ing.

B · When we use each tense

Tense Main uses Example
Present Simple habits; schedules; facts; states She takes insulin every morning.
Present Continuous happening now; temporary; fixed plans; annoying habits (always) He's sleeping now.
Present Perfect past action with a result now; life experience; up to now (for / since) I've already taken it.
Present Perfect Continuous activity from the past until now, focus on duration; recent activity with a visible result I've been coughing for a week.
Past Simple finished action at a finished time; a sequence of events She fell yesterday.
Past Continuous in progress at a past moment; background; interrupted by a short action She was walking when she fell.
Past Perfect earlier than another past moment She had eaten before the test.
Past Perfect Continuous duration up to a past moment She had been feeling dizzy all morning.
Future Simple (will) decisions now; promises; predictions; realistic hopes and fears; facts about the future I'll call the nurse.
Future Continuous in progress at a future moment This time tomorrow you'll be having surgery.
Future Perfect finished by a future moment By Friday you'll have finished the antibiotics.
Future Perfect Continuous duration up to a future moment By June I'll have been studying for two years.

C · Time keywords

Simple Continuous Perfect Perfect Continuous
Present every…, always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom, never, once / twice a…, from time to time, generally now, right now, at the moment, at present, currently, these days, today, this week, still just, already, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, today, this week, for, since for, since, how long, all day, all week, lately, recently
Past yesterday, ago, last…, in (2019), at (3 a.m.), on (Monday), when while, as, when, at (3 a.m.) yesterday, all night, at that moment before, after, by (10 a.m.), by the time, already, when for, since, before, until, by the time, all morning
Future tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, next…, in (two days), soon, later, some day, tonight this time tomorrow, at (10) tomorrow, all day tomorrow by (Friday), by the time, before for, by (June), by the time

D · Irregular verbs for healthcare

V1 V2 V3 Example
be was / were been Have you been in hospital before?
become became become It became worse at night.
begin began begun The pain began on Sunday.
bleed bled bled The cut bled for 10 minutes.
break broke broken She broke her wrist.
bring brought brought Have you brought your medicines?
come came come He came in by ambulance.
cut cut cut I cut my hand on glass.
do did done Have you done the test?
drink drank drunk She hasn't drunk anything today.
drive drove driven Who drove you here?
eat ate eaten Have you eaten since midnight?
fall fell fallen He fell in the bathroom.
feel felt felt I felt dizzy.
forget forgot forgotten I forgot my insulin.
get got got (US: gotten) It's gotten worse.
give gave given The nurse gave him pain relief.
go went gone The swelling has gone down.
have had had She had surgery in 2018.
hold held held Hold your breath.
hurt hurt hurt My back hurt all night.
keep kept kept Keep the dressing dry.
know knew known I've known her for years.
leave left left The doctor has just left.
lie (down) lay lain She lay in bed all day.
lose lost lost He lost consciousness.
put put put Put the needle in the sharps container.
say said said She said she felt sick.
see saw seen Has the doctor seen you?
shake shook shaken Shake well before use.
sleep slept slept I haven't slept well.
swell swelled swollen My ankle is swollen.
take took taken Have you taken your tablets?
tell told told She told me about the pain.
throw (up) threw thrown He threw up twice.
understand understood understood Have you understood the instructions?
wake (up) woke woken I woke up at 3 a.m.
wear wore worn Please wear a mask.
write wrote written I've written it down.

Watch out: lie (lie, lay, lain) = be in a flat position: Lie down, please. · lay (lay, laid, laid) = put something down: Lay the patient on her side.

E · -ing and -ed forms at a glance

Form Meaning Example See
V-ing in a continuous tense part of the verb I was listening to music. Units 10, 19, 20
Gerund V-ing as a noun Walking every day helps. Avoid lifting. Unit 30
Participle I V-ing as an adjective (active) a bleeding wound, the patient sitting by the window Unit 30
Participle II (V3) V3 as an adjective (passive or finished) a broken leg, the prescribed dose Units 22, 30
-ing adjective the cause of a feeling confusing instructions Unit 30
-ed adjective the feeling a confused patient Unit 30

-ing spelling: take → taking (drop -e) · sit → sitting (double the consonant after one short vowel) · lie → lying, die → dying (ie → y) · see → seeing (keep -ee).

F · Conditionals at a glance

Type If-clause Main clause Meaning Example
Zero Present Simple Present Simple always true If you smile, you start to feel better.
First Present Simple will / may / can + V1, or an instruction real future If the pain gets worse, call us.
Second Past Simple would + V1 unreal now / unlikely future If I were you, I'd rest.
Third Past Perfect would have + V3 unreal past If I had known, I would have told you.
Mixed (past → now) Past Perfect would + V1 past cause, present result If she had taken her tablets, she wouldn't be here now.
Mixed (now → past) Past Simple would have + V3 present situation, past result If he weren't afraid of needles, he would have had the test.
Formal inversion Should / Had / Were + S… as above written, formal Should you notice redness, contact the clinic.

Two rules for every type: no will and no would in the if-clause. Comma after the if-clause when it comes first.

teacher.title: Vocabulary Book
teacher.html:
This book holds every new word from the ShifoLife B1, B2 and C1 courses, with a plain-English definition and an example of how it is used. The words follow the course order: level → week → lesson.

Each entry

Column What it shows
L the lesson where the word is taught
Word the word or phrase, with its abbreviation if there is one
Type the part of speech
Definition what it means, in simple English
Example how it is used in healthcare

Types: n. = noun · v. = verb · adj. = adjective · adv. = adverb · phr. = phrase · abbr. = abbreviation · prefix / suffix = word part · phr. v. = phrasal verb · prep. = preposition.

How to study a word

  1. Read the definition, then cover it and explain the word in your own English words.
  2. Say the example aloud twice.
  3. Make a new sentence about a patient, your family or your studies.
  4. Review the week's words before the third lesson of the week, and all the level's words before Lessons 18 and 36.

C1 Professional

Week 1 · Lectures and Note-taking

L Word Type Definition Example
1 signpost n. a word or phrase that shows where a talk is going "Firstly" is a signpost.
1 outline n. a short plan of the main points The lecturer gave an outline first.
1 key concept n. a central idea Infection control is a key concept.
1 furthermore adv. in addition (formal) Furthermore, it reduces costs.
1 in contrast phr. showing a difference In contrast, the second group improved.
1 consequently adv. as a result Consequently, infections fell.
1 to illustrate phr. to give an example To illustrate, think of five moments.
1 to sum up phr. to give a short summary at the end To sum up, hands carry germs.
1 digress v. to move away from the main topic for a time Let me digress for a moment.
1 emphasize v. to give special importance to something She emphasized the main barrier.
2 Cornell notes n. a note-taking layout with notes, key words and a summary Use Cornell notes in lectures.
2 cue column n. the narrow left column for key words in Cornell notes Write key terms in the cue column.
2 abbreviation n. a short form of a word, e.g. pt for patient "Hx" is an abbreviation for history.
2 symbol n. a sign that stands for an idea, e.g. ↑ for increase Use symbols to save time.
2 condense v. to make shorter, keeping the main meaning Condense the lecture into five lines.
2 reconstruct v. to build again from parts Reconstruct the lecture from your notes.
2 key term n. an important word in a subject Underline the key terms.
2 main idea n. the most important point State the main idea first.
2 supporting detail n. a fact or example that explains the main idea Add one supporting detail.
3 elaborate v. to give more detail Could you elaborate on that point?
3 query n. / v. a question; to ask I have a query about the reading.
3 synthesize v. to combine ideas from different sources Synthesize the two lectures.
3 takeaway n. the main message to remember The takeaway is that prevention works.

Week 2 · Reading Nursing Textbooks

L Word Type Definition Example
4 etiology n. the cause of a disease The etiology involves genetic and lifestyle factors.
4 pathophysiology n. how a disease changes the body's normal functions The pathophysiology is insulin resistance.
4 clinical manifestation n. a sign or symptom of a disease Thirst is a clinical manifestation.
4 risk factor n. something that makes a disease more likely Smoking is a risk factor.
4 intervention n. an action taken to improve health Lifestyle interventions can delay onset.
4 rationale n. the reason for doing something Give the rationale for each action.
4 evidence-based adj. based on good research We use evidence-based practice.
4 contraindication n. a reason not to give a treatment An allergy is a contraindication.
4 outcome n. the result of care or treatment The outcome was good.
4 complication n. a new problem caused by a disease or treatment Infection is a possible complication.
5 hyper- prefix above or more than normal hyperglycemia: high blood sugar
5 hypo- prefix below or less than normal hypotension: low blood pressure
5 tachy- prefix fast tachycardia: fast heart rate
5 brady- prefix slow bradycardia: slow heart rate
5 -itis suffix inflammation hepatitis: inflammation of the liver
5 -ectomy suffix surgical removal appendectomy: removal of the appendix
5 -ostomy suffix a surgical opening colostomy: an opening from the colon
5 -algia suffix pain neuralgia: nerve pain
5 -emia suffix a condition of the blood anemia: low red blood cells
6 paraphrase v. / n. to say the same meaning in different words Paraphrase the sentence in your own words.
6 quotation n. the exact words from a source, in quotation marks Use a quotation only when the wording matters.
6 cite v. to name the source of information Cite every source you use.
6 original wording n. the exact words used by the author Don't copy the original wording.

Week 3 · Case Presentations

L Word Type Definition Example
7 case presentation n. a short, organized spoken summary of a patient She gave a 3-minute case presentation.
7 identifying data n. name, age, sex and other basic facts Start with the identifying data.
7 presents with phr. comes to care with a particular problem She presents with chest pain.
7 history of present illness (HPI) n. the story of the current problem The HPI began three days ago.
7 past medical history (PMH) n. earlier illnesses and treatments PMH notable for asthma.
7 review of systems n. questions about each body system Review of systems was otherwise negative.
7 pertinent positive n. an important symptom the patient does have Fever is a pertinent positive.
7 findings n. what was found on examination or tests Findings include a temperature of 38.1.
7 plan n. the next steps in care The plan is blood tests and review.
7 as documented phr. as written in the record by the team The plan, as documented, is an X-ray.
8 notable for phr. having something important History notable for hypertension.
8 significant for phr. including something clinically important Exam significant for wheeze.
8 unremarkable adj. normal; nothing important found The chest X-ray was unremarkable.
8 otherwise well phr. healthy apart from the stated problem She is otherwise well.
8 ongoing adj. continuing She has ongoing back pain.
8 worsening adj. getting worse A 5-day history of worsening cough.
8 x-day history phr. a problem that has lasted a number of days A 3-day history of fever.
8 onset of phr. the start of Sudden onset of chest pain.
8 associated with phr. happening together with Headache associated with nausea.
9 attending physician n. the senior doctor responsible for a patient The attending physician asked a question.
9 clarifying question n. a question to make something clearer Ask a clarifying question if unsure.
9 in summary phr. to sum up In summary, she is stable.
9 defer v. to leave a decision to someone else I'd defer to the physician on that.

Week 4 · Chronic Illness and Complex Histories

L Word Type Definition Example
10 chronic disease n. a long-lasting illness Diabetes is a chronic disease.
10 comorbidity n. another illness a patient has at the same time Hypertension is a common comorbidity.
10 multimorbidity n. having two or more long-term conditions Multimorbidity is common in older adults.
10 polypharmacy n. taking many medicines at once Polypharmacy increases the risk of errors.
10 adherence n. taking treatment as agreed Adherence improved with a pill box.
10 self-management n. what patients do day to day to manage their condition Self-management includes checking sugar.
10 glycemic control n. how well blood sugar is kept in range Her glycemic control has improved.
10 neuropathy n. nerve damage, often causing numbness or burning He has neuropathy in his feet.
10 retinopathy n. damage to the back of the eye Retinopathy can affect vision.
10 foot care n. checking and looking after the feet daily Foot care is vital in diabetes.
11 barrier n. something that makes an action difficult Cost is the main barrier.
11 affordability n. whether someone can pay for something Affordability affects adherence.
11 transport n. a way of traveling somewhere She has no transport to the clinic.
11 routine n. the usual order of daily activities Fit the tablets into your routine.
11 motivation n. the reason or wish to do something His motivation is his grandchildren.
11 readiness n. how prepared someone is to change Check readiness: on a scale of 0 to 10, how ready are you?
11 ambivalence n. wanting and not wanting something at the same time Ambivalence about change is normal.
11 non-judgmental adj. not criticizing or blaming Use non-judgmental questions.
11 social support n. help from family, friends and community She has good social support.
12 prioritize v. to put things in order of importance Prioritize the foot sore.
12 salient adj. most noticeable or important Give only the salient points.
12 overarching adj. covering or affecting everything The overarching problem is cost.
12 collateral history n. information from family or carers Her daughter gave a collateral history.

Week 5 · Patient Education and Health Literacy

L Word Type Definition Example
13 health literacy n. the ability to find, understand and use health information Low health literacy is common.
13 jargon n. specialist words that ordinary people may not understand Avoid jargon with patients.
13 plain language n. clear, simple words that most people understand Explain the result in plain language.
13 numeracy n. the ability to understand and use numbers Check numeracy before teaching doses.
13 chunk n. / v. a small piece of information; to divide into small pieces Teach it in three chunks.
13 visual aid n. a picture, model or chart that helps explain Use a visual aid for the injection sites.
13 everyday equivalent n. a common word with the same meaning as a technical one "Check" is the everyday equivalent of "monitor".
13 simplify v. to make easier to understand Simplify the instructions.
13 misconception n. a wrong idea or belief A common misconception is that insulin causes blindness.
13 empower v. to give someone the confidence and ability to act Good teaching empowers patients.
14 regimen n. a planned schedule of treatment Her insulin regimen is twice a day.
14 injection site n. the place on the body where an injection is given Choose a clean injection site.
14 rotate v. to change in a regular order Rotate the injection sites.
14 storage n. how and where something is kept Insulin storage matters.
14 sharps container n. a hard box for used needles Put the needle in the sharps container.
14 glucose tablets n. sugar tablets taken when blood sugar is low Keep glucose tablets in your bag.
14 foot inspection n. checking the feet for cuts, color changes or sores Do a foot inspection every evening.
14 return demonstration n. when the patient shows the skill back to the nurse Ask for a return demonstration.
14 reinforce v. to make learning stronger by repeating it Reinforce the teaching at discharge.
15 briefing n. a short meeting to prepare someone before a task Give the interpreter a briefing first.
15 pacing n. the speed at which you speak or give information Good pacing helps the interpreter.
15 first-person address n. speaking directly to someone as "you" Use first-person address with the patient.
15 cultural broker n. someone who explains cultural meaning between two sides The interpreter may act as a cultural broker.

Week 6 · Consent, Ethics and Rights

L Word Type Definition Example
16 informed consent n. agreement given after understanding the risks and benefits Informed consent is needed before surgery.
16 capacity n. the mental ability to make a decision Does he have capacity to consent?
16 autonomy n. a person's right to decide for themselves We respect patient autonomy.
16 voluntary adj. done by free choice, without pressure Consent must be voluntary.
16 witness n. / v. a person who sees and confirms; to see and confirm A nurse witnessed the signature.
16 withdraw v. to take back or stop You can withdraw consent at any time.
16 advance directive n. a written statement of care wishes for the future She has an advance directive.
16 health care proxy n. a person chosen to make health decisions for someone Her son is her health care proxy.
16 confidentiality n. keeping private information private Confidentiality protects patients.
16 HIPAA abbr. the US law that protects patient health information HIPAA limits what we can share.
17 dilemma n. a hard choice between two options This is an ethical dilemma.
17 stance n. a position or opinion on an issue What's your stance on this?
17 counter-argument n. an argument against another argument Consider the counter-argument.
